She said: Mr. Speaker, in preparing my speech for today, my assistant and I went through the newspaper clippings we have on the Montreal massacre and on violence against women in general. There was much there. There is so much to say that I cannot possibly include even a small fraction of it in my speech today.
The news photos of the night of the massacre recalled to us the horror and the shock we all felt on December 6, 1989, when we first heard the news report that a man had entered into the engineering classroom at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal, separated the men from the women and shot the women with a legally purchased semi-automatic weapon.
Afterward, a disturbing debate took place about whether this was just the isolated act of a madman or if it was connected to the death of 100 women every year in domestic violence situations, connected to the death and the injuries to women as a result of being sexually assaulted by men who hate women, men who do not see women as equal human beings.
Some people sought to reassure themselves that the massacre was an isolated act by a madman so that they could think that it would never happen again. It has happened before, it happens now and it will continue to happen.
The different thing about this massacre was that it was 14 young women killed all at once. Theodore Bundy murdered 36 women. Edward Jackson, a regular churchgoer, a respected doctor and father, raped 32 women. Larry Takahashi was found guilty of raping 16 women, and another 122 rape charges against him were never heard. It is these names we remember, the names of the people who do violence against women.
We do not remember the names of the victims. The victims are nameless and faceless to us, just as they were to the killers and to their attackers. I want to name the names. I am glad and appreciative that the members of this House wish to stand alongside me, and commemorate those who died. They are: Genevieve Bergeron, Helene Colgan, Nathalie Croteau, Barbara Daigneault, Anne-Marie Edward, Maud Haviemick, Barbara Marie Klueznick, Maryse Leclair, Anne-Marie Lemay, Sonia Pelletier, Michele Richard, Annie St. Ameault, Annie Tbrcotte, Maryse Langaniere.
I want to express my deepest sympathies to the families of these young women, to the families of the students, one of whom committed suicide shortly after the massacre and to the families of women and young people who have died of abuse, hatred and the madness in our society that does nothing to prevent this violence from taking place. These events have left us all with scars of pain.
December 6 will be remembered as a horrific and grisly day but I and many others wish something positive to come of it.
I want to talk about one of the survivors of the massacre, a young woman whom I admire very much. Heidi Rathjen has become one of the leaders in Canada on the issue of gun control. This young woman, who went on to graduate from the Ecole Polytechnique, has appeared before two parliamentary committees on gun control. She has helped to amass over 500,000 signatures on a petition for stricter gun control. She has engaged in public speaking right across this country about this issue.
Just like Ms. Rathjen, I think we must all become active on the issue of violence against women. We cannot just continue to talk about it. People are dying.
Marc Lepine had a list of 19 women whom he wanted to kill. He called them "radical feminists" and he wanted them dead because he thought they had ruined his life.
These women were high profile, successful people. Talent and hard work counted very little to Mr. Lepine. He felt that they had taken his place in society because he was a male and deserved the best even without their talent, even without hard work, without any of the skills and abilities that had got these women to the place they were. Some people still maintain the Montreal massacre had nothing to do with sexism.
Lepine's suicide note said his rampage was due to "political reasons". He said: "Even if the mad killer epithet will be attributed to me by the media, I consider myself a rational person, forced to take extreme acts." He accused women of wanting to keep all the advan-
September 30, 1991

tages of being women while seizing the advantages that were men's.
These attitudes are out there. Lepine did not invent them. They are the attitudes that promote violence against women. The attitude that women have a place in life and if they step out of that place, they can be targets for abuse from name-calling to being beaten and murdered, that women are a proper target for the rage and the frustration that is felt by some men, that women are not real human beings with real feelings and real ambitions with just as much right to pursue them as men, that men have some sort of right to sex and other services from women are attitudes that must be changed.
This year a newspaper article discussing date rape said: "Meeting a woman in a bar and drinking with her for several hours before going to her place is not a date. That's a pick-up."
A so-called pro-family newspaper blamed violence against women on the feminists just as Marc Lepine blamed them. He blamed everything on the feminists. The newspaper wrote that the cause of violence against women is the destruction of the family. How does this explain the cases of violence that we have all seen in families in the 1800s, even in the 1500s?
Wife beating was legal in Canada and elsewhere at one time. Women could not even receive a divorce even though they had been repeatedly beaten and beaten to a pulp.
Some right wing groups have commandeered the term "family values" to mean something sick and twisted. They do not want to promote the health and well-being of family members at all. They only want to provide a justification to male family members to abuse women and children and get away with it.
A co-ordinator for a sexual assault support centre has said that the issue of violence against women was brought to the forefront by the Montreal massacre, and that many women did not realize the extent to which angry men would take their fury out on women. I think that is especially true of young women. You just do not grasp that anyone, anyone you think is a friend, or even a stranger, would want to hurt you, or would have so little regard for your own wishes.
Private Members' Business
Many survivors of sexual assault are simply in shock that any one would want to do that to them. It does not matter how they dress, how old they are, or who they are, they are targeted simply because they are women.
That crisis centre received 2,327 calls in six months, and it is one of only two crisis centres in a small city. Some calls were from women who had been abused in childhood and were just beginning to come to terms with that abuse.
Chia-Tsu Liu was an abused wife in Toronto who was hacked to death by her husband when she left him and refused to return.
Nina de Villiers went jogging one day and never came back. She had been active in the movement to end violence against women and she was found dead.
A 13-year old girl was doused with gasoline by her former 15-year old boyfriend and set on fire. She had reported threats to the police before this horrible situation but no one had helped her.
Twenty people watched as an 11-year old girl was gang raped at a party in Toronto.
One female Toronto city councillor thinks violence against women is exaggerated because she does not know of anyone among her friends or family who have told her of an assault.
A young woman in my circle of friends told me that she told her mother that she was sexually assaulted when she was 17 and her mother asked her what she had done to deserve that. That same young woman escaped the sexual advances of her uncle when she was only 14 and never told her family. She was afraid she would not be believed.
Mr. Speaker, I hid from my own mother the advances of a family "friend" when I was less than 12 years old.
With society's "blame the victim attitude", many women feel uncomfortable and embarrassed about telling anyone they have been abused. They fear they will not be believed and they blame themselves.
Front line rape crisis centre workers say only one in 20 women who contact them report the crime to the police. When they do, they are often put on trial every bit as much as the assailant.

September 30,1991
Private Members' Business
We have seen recent stories of abuse in residential schools, orphanages, assaults which occurred up to 20 years ago. All the allegations made at the time were hushed up, covered up, and ignored. This is not the way to solve a serious problem in our society. We must talk about it. We must tell survivors of abuse that there is support for them, that they do not have to face this alone and face society alone. We must discuss the solutions and, more importantly, we must act on them.
I hope that the bill I have introduced will go a small way towards that, to call attention to the problem and to implement some solutions. I did not call it a day of remembrance and action for nothing. Without the action the bill is worthless.
There are very few women who are untouched by violence, women of all ages, of all physical types, from every culture, every racial group, every religious and socioeconomic background. All are assaulted. Disabled women and aboriginal women are particularly vulnerable to assault. Not only is there evidence to show that disabled women are more often the targets of abuse, but they are treated very poorly by the courts.
This year a man was acquitted of raping a deaf mute woman who kicked and fought him. She tried to defend herself. The man was acquitted because the deaf mute victim did not tell him- that she did not want to have sex. How is a deaf mute woman supposed to verbalize that she does not want sex? Should not the kicking and the fighting be enough?
Sixty-two per cent of all women murdered in Canada are victims of domestic violence. Yet in Alberta, 911 operators would not send police to a house in which a man was beating down the door to rape a woman because they thought it was a domestic dispute.
One in four women is sexually assaulted. Others who have not been assaulted or harassed still feel fear when walking, particularly alone, at night.
This cycle of violence must be stopped. Marc Lepine grew up being beaten by his father. In one study, 25 per cent of the children in a shelter for battered women said it was okay for a man to hit a woman if the house was messy.
Violence against women is not natural behaviour, it is learned behaviour. We hold up violent heroes for young boys to emulate. We treat women with a lack of respect in the work place and in the home. Women are the butt of jokes. Women are used as objects to sell products.
Women who succeed are often accused of sleeping their way to the top. I do not think anyone has accused a successful man of that.
Boys are given unrealistic expectations of what it means to be a man. Physical strength and power over others is seen as manly. Expressing one's feelings, taking care of others, resolving problems in a non-violent, supportive way, are not considered to be manly attributes. The bravado, the strutting and the machismo put on to male children hurts those male children, hurts women and hurts all of society. Children learn these attitudes all too well and the whole cycle of violence begins again.
Instead we need to teach children that every individual is different. There are men and women who are physically strong and men and women who are not. There are men and women who are intelligent and there men and women who are less so. Whatever you are, it does not make you better or a worse human being than anyone else.
The House of Commons subcommittee on the status of Women, of which I am a member, released many positive recommendations that received all party support at the subcommittee level. These included strong and consistent violence prevention and media literacy education in our schools across the country; gender equality issues should be part of the school curriculum in elementary, junior and high schools; mandatory gender equality training for judges and for the RCMP; and gender sensitivity training programs for members of Parliament. MPs decide which programs stay, which ones go, how money will be spent, what benefits people have. They have a direct impact on the lives of 26 million Canadians, over half of whom are women. I am sad to say that some members here do not have adequate knowledge and sensitivity to the problems women face to make those good decisions about women's lives.
Another recommendation was for an effective, affordable housing policy and to look into removing the assailant from the family home, rather than removing the victim from the home.
It called for a strong rape shield law and for the repeal of the honest belief defence for rapists. The subcommittee called for stronger gun control legislation. Most important, for the short term, the subcommittee called for adequate funding for services for abused women and children. Shelters for battered women are still turning
September 30, 1991

away abused women and their children because of a lack of space.
We can start by restoring the funding to the Canada Assistance Plan which funds, among other social programs, shelters for battered women. We can take action on the subcommittee's recommendations now and not await until December 1992, when the Panel on Violence Against Women reports and probably restates many of the same recommendations that we made on the subcommittee.
I want to extend my warm appreciation to the Minister responsible for the Status of Women for her support and for ensuring the support of her party. I want to extend my appreciation also to the hon. member for Halifax, my friend, for her support and for her party's support and also to the House leader of the Bloc Quebecois for his party's support.
I would also like to thank my own New Democrat colleagues. I want to thank them for their understanding and for their support on these issues. I want to thank the people across Canada who have written some very wonderful letters to me, letters of encouragement and support.
Most of all I want to thank the women who have worked so hard all of these years, staffing shelters for battered women, raising funds for shelters for battered women; the women who have worked in rape crisis centres; and the women and men who have marched in the streets and have lobbied the government on issues of violence against women. These people, these caring men and women will be the real agents for change in our society. Without them, it will not happen.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise in support of this bill to establish December 6 as a national day of remembrance and action on violence against women.
On December 6, 1989, 14 young women at the University of Montreal were killed by a gunman who did not know them but who singled them out because he hated women. The shock and the horror of the tragic event was felt throughout our country. This tragedy touched all Canadians, women and men alike. Many Canadians felt a personal sense of loss. Many Canadians, and particularly women, lost a sense of safety and security they had fell all their lives. Many Canadians saw in this brutal
Private Members' Business
slaying an extreme example of the terror and the violence inflicted on women every day.
Violence against women takes many forms, including emotional and psychological abuse, physical assault, sexual assault and murder. It does not respect any boundaries but threatens women of all ages, cultures, backgrounds, abilities, geographical locations and economic situations.
Women centred violence exist in a continuum in our society that includes sexless jokes, pornography, harassment, prostitution, date violence, child abuse and incest.
The statistics on violence against women in Canada are shocking. One in ten Canadian women is assaulted by her male partner. One in four girls will be sexually assaulted before reaching the age of 18. Eighty per cent of aboriginal women have experienced violence and almost half of the disabled women in this country have been sexually abused during childhood, while 40 per cent have been raped, abused or assaulted as adults. Nor are elderly women free from violence. Female victims of elder abuse outnumber male victims two to one.
These statistics are considered only modest estimates. Many abused women and girls are often too ashamed or frightened of reprisal to speak out or seek help. Some victims try to bury the violence deep in their thoughts and deny its existence. They do not fully understand the deep-seated trauma that such violence inflicts and that it will, in all likelihood, stay with them for the rest of their lives.
We make a serious mistake if we think that the effects of this violence are strictly personal. Its legacy is widespread throughout our society. Not only do innocent victims pay the price long after the physical abuse is over, but we pay along with them.
When the results of this violence are chronic depression, high incidents of addictions and eating disorders, deliquency, crime and suicide, we all pay and our society is diminished by this cost.
I would like to quote the words of a Manitoba woman who, as a child, endured an estimated 2,600 incidents of sexual abuse at the hands of her father. She said: "My father took away my childhood. I still mourn for it and I will always miss the innocence. I will miss the opportunity to have the choices that were taken away from me. When I think back to certain situations I was put into as a

September 30, 1991
Private Members' Business
child, I keep thinking to myself that poor little girl, that poor little girl".
Violence against women is a thief, stealing away the things that are most precious to us: love between husband and wife, trust between parent and child, the ability to live without fear, and a state of emotional health that allows us to enjoy and participate in life to the fullest.
Many of us take pride in our Canadian sense of equality and fair play. We have long believed we live in a progress society, one that places compassion and respect for people from all walks of life at the centre of our national ethos. But the tragedy at the Ecole Polytechnique and the violence that occurs daily in our homes and on our streets are reminders of how far we have yet to
go-
Violence against women is deeply rooted in our society. It is based on attitudes and stereotypes that encourage the belief that women are subordinate to men. Stereotypical views hold that a man is the head of the household, that a woman must honour and obey her partner, and that children are to be seen and not heard. These stereotypical views create a serious imbalance between men and women and between adolescent males and females. On the other hand, men are expected to control and dominate; on the other hand, women and girls are expected to be dependent and vulnerable.
When such stereotypes combine with a societal tolerance for violence, the result is an exposure and sometimes deadly mixture: men who abuse their power, men who turn on those closest to them, men who use violence as a means of dealing with their anger and frustration.
Canadians have long been tempted to look away, to say to themselves it is someone else's problem, and to believe that the dirty linen of domestic violence should not be aired in public. Some still assume that such violence should be dealt with behind closed doors.
However the truth is that violence against women is not someone else's problem. It is our problem. It belongs to all of us. When we look the other way, we become silent accomplices. When we think of violence as belonging to someone else, we deny our responsibility for its existence. When we do not want to air the dirty linen, we ignore the plight of the thousands of women who need our help and compassion.
When we hide violence behind closed doors we are guilty of encouraging the sexist view of women as persons who can be abused, raped and murdered. As long as some women are beaten by their husbands, as long as others are sexually assaulted on dates, as long as still others experience harassment at their jobs, women are being denied the basic right to security of person.
When a person is denied this basic right she suffers on many levels. She cannot walk the streets without being frightened. She cannot be safe in her home or at a university or in the work place. She cannot function without continually looking over her shoulder and worrying about the people with whom she has to deal.
There is a tragic link between violence against women and the inability of women in Canada to achieve equality in our society. Violence against women is deeply rooted in our socializing processes, our power structures and our institutions. This is a systematic problem touching on all aspects of our society including the justice system, the media, the health system, education and social services.

It should come as no surprise to us, then, that women are kicked and slapped, hit with hard objects and cut with knives. It should come as no surprise that each year in Canada an average 100 women are murdered by their male partners or that in 1990 there were 27,000 reported incidents of sexual assault. It should come as no surprise that 14 innocent women could be brutally gunned down simply because they were women.
Equality for women goes hand in hand with the eradication of violence. Economic equality will provide women with the freedom to leave abusive situations and rebuild their lives and those of their children. Political equality will allow women to participate in decisions that affect their lives and the lives of their families. Societal equality is key to breaking down stereotypes and eliminating the traditional sexist attitudes that promote violence against women.
September 30, 1991

Our efforts to address violence against women must recognize the social, economic and political structures that currently confine women to unequal roles. At the same time, we must continue to find ways to expand the opportunities and choices available to women.
When Canadians learned about the massacre in Montreal they responded in many different ways. The government provided leadership and vision through its commitment to Canada's first national inquiry into violence against women and its $136 million renewal of the family violence initiative. In a struggle to eliminate violence against women the government recognizes that it is essential to co-ordinate our efforts with provincial and municipal governments, women's groups, service clubs, business and labour and professional associations.
Many Canadian organizations responded to the Montreal tragedy by a renewed commitment to opening career opportunities for women, particularly with respect to science and engineering. The Canadian Federation of University Women, Canadian Council of Engineers, Memorial Foundation, Societe Alfred Dallaire and the Ecole Polytechnique are among the organizations, institutions and corporations that have established scholarships in memory of the victims.

Mr. Speaker, when tragedy invades our lives, we tend to react first with a feeling of horror, a feeling of helplessness, and over all the questioning as to why this has taken place. On that December night almost two years ago, a night that I think all of us will remember with exceptional clarity all of our lives, I remember the particular horror, the particular feeling of helplessness and over all the questioning as to why this had happened.
On that night in December it happened that I was dining with a group of my colleagues and one of our colleagues was late. As we waited for him we wondered why he was late. When he joined us he gave us the terrible news that was just then coming across the television screens and the radio airwaves in Canada. As he told us, one could tell in the crowded restaurant in Ottawa that the news was filtering to other tables, to other people. As we all remember, it seemed to deepen the horror that this took place in the pre-Christmas season when at least on the face of it we are all supposed to be mirroring a feeling of both peace on earth and good
Private Members' Business
will toward all of humankind. When evil takes place, we are left with a feeling of what can we do, how can we combat it, but when good comes out of evil there is always a sense of accomplishment and a feeling that terrible as the originating event was, there is some sense of balance restored if some good takes place.
I think that in both the existence of this bill brought forward by my friend, the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby, and in the kind of co-operation that took place among the three parties in the House, from the Minister responsible for the Status of Women and, in some small part, from my own participation, we saw an indication of how a horror cannot be redressed, cannot be cured, cannot be obliterated, but can be the catalyst for something that will, in the long run, please God, improve what is a terrible situation.
The tragedy at Ecole Polytechnique was the most extreme symptom, result, reaction if you will, to an epidemic running not just through our country, but through world society. The fact that we have managed to grow a few blossoms on the graves of those wonderful young women who were cut down at the very beginning of what should have been wonderful and fulfilling lives sometimes does not seem as if it is nearly enough. And, of course, it is not nearly enough, it is just the first few steps of what must be concerted action.
This is a private member's bill supported by all parties and all of us in all parties are happy, I even say delighted, that this has taken place.
But, Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby brought forward this bill, as she herself said in her speech, it is not just to have a day of remembrance, it is to have a day of action.
I am not going to go through a litany of the grotesquer-ies that have taken place against women just since I came into this House. My colleague has given a number of examples, examples that we are all too familiar with. My colleague from the government party talked about the fact that it is not something that can be confined to one particular cultural group, to one particular socio-economic class, to one particular geographic region, it is something that runs rampant throughout the world.
I think that there was always violence against women. I think this was one of the prices that women paid for being in the nurturing position, for being the maintained of home and hearth and, therefore, not being those

September 30, 1991
Private Members' Business
who provided the wherewithal for home and hearth and the protection.
I think that what has happened, particularly in the last 20 years, when we have seen the women's movement become, as many of us who have worked in it have always believed, perhaps the most cataclysmic drive for social change that this world has ever seen. It changes those things that many of us believe to be unchangeable, immutable and many of us feared changes to what we believed was immutable. Many of us feared it because it changed the way families are structured. It changed the way our daily, personal and private lives went on. That is why I say it was cataclysmic.
In the face of cataclysmic change, there is obviously going to be cataclysmic reaction.
Even though there was always violence against women, the influx of women into the work force, the changing of the face of national institutions such as this one-40 may not change the face and its features, but at least it changes it to a degree in its topography.
It frightens people and when people are frightened, they behave in a manner that is unacceptable. Sadly, in the case of this society and societies around the world, some of them are behaving in a manner that is lethal.
I applaud the government and most particularly the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women on the appointment of the blue ribbon panel. When I heard the names of the participants on this panel, I knew that their work would result in the kind of report on the issue of violence against women that all of us, the member for New Westminster-Burnaby and all women in the House, have been asked for in one form or another. Many men in the House as well have supported us on this.
That is only one aspect. I bring forward today, along with my support of this bill, two other areas that need government action, not through the avenue of private members, but through government policy.
The first is one that the government is working on, the House is dealing with, but that all of us are very, very concerned about. I refer to the whole question of gun control.
We all know that there are very strong feelings and opinions on both sides of the gun control issue, but there are certain facts that are just not changeable. They are there.
One fact is that in the case of spousal murder, guns are the single most common cause of death, the single most common. That has to be stopped and it can only be stopped by tougher gun control legislation, legislation with teeth.
The second area that has to be taken care of is that of the rape shield which fell last month under the Supreme Court of Canada. I agree with the Legal Education and Action Fund and with various other women's groups in this country that we do not wish the Minister of Justice to be precipit, because this is a difficult and challenging area of law.
We in this Chamber and the women and men of Canada, the vast majority of whom I know are supportive, need to hear that the minister is working on this, that women in fear of assault will have legislation to protect them.
In closing, I want to once again commend the member for New Westminster-Burnaby, the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women and those men in all parties of this House who continue to be supportive of what is a mainstream, serious and frightening issue. It may be the single most serious issue that any of us have been called on to deal with in our political lives.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with my colleagues on all sides of the House in speaking just for a couple of minutes on this issue.
It is now two years since 14 young women were massacred in Montreal for the sole reason that they were pursuing a professional career that is stereotypically denoted as a man's job. While this killing justifiably evoked shock and outrage from people all across Canada, a silence surrounds the hundreds of women who are victims of domestic violence each year.
One in four Canadian women will be sexually assaulted in their lifetimes. While 12 per cent of women in Canada are assaulted each year by their partners, approximately 100 of these assaults result in death. The figures for reported sexual assault are assumed to be lower than the actual number of crimes against women committed each year. Many women choose not to report a crime because of the trauma and difficulty involved in
September 30, 1991

prosecuting the assailant. At the moment the penalty for assault is often lower than that of breaking and entering. For example, a few years ago a 26 year old man received a suspended sentence for assaulting a 13 year old girl.
The government condones or appears to condone this warped priorization by failing to grant the necessary funding to women's groups which are working to end these crimes and to provide support for the victims.
Canada is a signatory to a United Nations document which recognizes the need to achieve a peaceful social environment for women that is compatible with human dignity.
Statistics show that most men who commit violence against women come from a background that encourages that type of behaviour. Thus education and positive preventative action is necessary to stop the vicious circle in which so many women and their families are entrapped.
The bill before the House this morning, and I congratulate my colleague for presenting this bill, represents a national day of remembrance and action on violence against women. It would be a positive demonstration of our commitment to end this violence and grant women the right to safety in our society.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, today, members of the Public Service Alliance are back on strike. Services to the Canadian public-including services essential to safety and security-are being disrupted.
The government is therefore asking Parliament to enact the Public Sector Compensation Act and put an end to the strike.
On Friday, the head of the Public Service Alliance broke an agreement he had made with me on September 17, not to strike as long as negotiations continued. This action, Mr. Chairman, is most unfortunate. Only 13 days ago, the parties agreed to return to the table, without preconditions, and to make every reasonable effort to reach a settlement.
During this past week, negotiators on both sides held a total of 35 meetings at the various bargaining tables. Treasury Board negotiators bargained seriously and in good faith, Mr. Chairman, and I say this with no hesitation. The offers we brought to the tables were reasonable and within the government wage restraint policy.

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
The government's wage policy, Mr. Chairman, is well known and has not changed-it was announced in the Budget last February. Its details are a matter of record and familiar to most members of this House. They form part of a series of measures announced in the Budget to bring the country out of the recession while containing the deficit and inflation.
These measures, I may recall, included capping payments to the provinces, freezing total federal program spending, reducing the number of managers, setting inflation targets and constraining wages.
On June 19, before the summer recess, I advised the House that we could not afford to negotiate any increase in wages this year.

I want to remind hon. members that whatever views they may hold on the current situation with the alliance, the government and the country are faced with a fiscal situation that must be addressed. We owe it to the Canadian public to live within the measures announced in the February budget. The deficit and inflationary pressures must both be contained so that interest rates can be brought down and economic recovery can continue.
The measures announced in the budget are working. The recovery has begun and it is now being jeopardized by the strike. I can sympathize with the alliance leadership and understandably they are unhappy with the government's zero and three per cent wage offer.
I said in June, and I repeat today, that the government's offer is not very palatable to the Public Service unions any more than it has been to the government. Yet, we have signed agreements with other unions which have taken what I believe is a very responsible approach. They chose to negotiate settlements within the government's wage restraint program. In doing this, they have agreed to join the ranks of public servants in four other provinces, and that must not be forgotten, that have a wage policy of zero per cent for at least 12 months and, in some cases, for two years.
The Public Service Alliance may be the reason Parliament is now considering passage of Bill C-29, but this union has not been singled out in our application of zero and three. Everyone is subject to the zero, three program.
As I stated in the House last week, performance pay is being suspended for 1991-92, not only for senior management, but for Governor in Council appointees, including the heads of Crown corporations.
When combined with the freeze in salary for this year, the suspension of performance pay results in an average reduction of 5 per cent in compensation for this group of employees. These are harsh, but necessary, measures in times of restraint.

The question of wage restraint, Mr. Chairman, has been a most difficult issue for the Public Service Alliance. We knew it would be and I personnaly wish that the government could offer more money to its employees.
As I have said on numerous occasions, 0 and 3 is not what our employees deserve, and it is certainly not a measure of their contribution to public service. It is, however, all that Canadian taxpayers can afford.
Knowing that the government must remain firm in its resolve to restrain spending, we have been as generous as we could in offering to improve the benefits to employees. The offer we placed on the table last week provided for substantial improvements in areas important to the Alliance, such as employment security and protecting the purchasing power of certain groups of employees.
We offered improved benefits in many other areas, and I wish to review these for hon. members, Mr. Chairman, because there is evidence of the very serious efforts Treasury Board has made to reach a fair and reasonable settlement.
My strong preference has always been to negotiate rather than legislate, and I provided our negotiators with the best possible mandate that we could provide as a responsible government under the circumstances. The Public Service Alliance has been greatly concerned about the employment security of its members, especially as it relates to future contracting out and privatization. I think that the concern has been overstated, because the federal government's Work Force Adjustment Policy is one of the best employment protection plans in Canada. About one half of one per cent of employees have lost their jobs through work force adjustment.
September 30, 1991	COMMONS

The policy provides six months' notice of loss of a job, and employees are given priority for other jobs in the Public Service for which they are qualified or can be retrained.
Retraining can be given for up to two years. Even after being laid off, employees retain their priority for new Public Service job openings for one year. We know of very few other employers, if any, which provide better employment security.
Yet the alliance is asking for more guarantees. In an effort to reach a settlement, we put more guarantees on the table. We told the alliance that we were prepared to guarantee the employment of employees whose jobs are transferred to the private sector as a result of contracting out or privatization.
We also said that those who choose to work for the contractors would receive six months' salary to compensate for lower benefits in the private sector. Finally, we said that a reasonable job offer would be made to any other employees affected by work force adjustments.
On another matter, the alliance argued that some employees would be seriously affected by the zero per cent this year, and that employees earning higher incomes are more easily protected from the increases in the cost of living.
We responded to this concern by offering a one time lump sum payment of $500 to all indeterminate employees in the Public Service earning less than $27,000 a year, which is roughly equal to the average earned income in Canada at the present time.
Some 35,000 employees would qualify for this payment.

The Alliance complained that the government was not commited to the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. This is a complex issue that we have worked hard with all unions to resolve.
In January 1990, when the Alliance withdrew from a joint study and when we saw that the outcome was being delayed further, we decided to go ahead and pay out retroactive lump-sum payments of $317 million to 73,400 Public Service employees. Equalization adjustments worth $81 million continue to be paid yearly.

Government Orders
These were the amounts, Mr. Chairman, that, based on current data, the government calculated to be required under the equal pay for work of equal value provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
Because the method of calculation is presently under dispute before a human rights tribunal, the payments were not being incorporated into salary, but provided as seperate equalization payments. However, Mr. Chairman, in an effort to reach a settlement, we offered to incorporate these equalization payments into the base salaries of our clerks and secretaries. Doing this would provide these employees with a larger salary base from which future salary increases would be calculated, giving them more money and, eventually, a better pension.

Treasury Board offered improved benefits in other areas. It offered to pay 100 per cent of the premiums of the Public Service health care plan. It offered to raise the level of reimbursements claimable under the dental plan. It offered to increase the employer's contribution to the premium for disability insurance to 85 per cent from 75 per cent. It offered to increase the number of work place day care centres to 15 from 10. It offered to improve, among other things, vacation leave, shift and weekend premiums and meal allowances.
There is only a limited amount of money available. The cost of any improved benefits would have to be paid out of the departmental budgets established at the time of the last budget. For this year, it would mean that some departments would have to reduce their rate of hiring to replace public servants who retire.
We made, I am convinced, the best offer that a responsible government can make today. To the alliance, it is not enough. We must not forget that the country faces a $400 billion national debt. The interest on that debt amounts to more than $40 billion a year. The cupboard is bare and the alliance is calling for a mediator. The cupboard is bare and the alliance is asking for more.
The wages and benefits that federal employees currently enjoy are a cut above that of the average Canadian worker. Employees represented by the alliance earn an average salary of $33,500 a year, including equal pay, compared to a national average earned income of $27,100. They have a pension plan that is fully indexed to the cost of living. They enjoy, as I mentioned earlier, one of the highest levels of employment security in

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
Canada, and their over-all benefits are at least comparable to other major employers.
This week Treasury Board is publishing in newspapers across the country an outline of the offer that the alliance rejected. The government has a responsibility to Canadians who must be made aware of the serious efforts we made to reach a negotiated settlement.
It is important that Canadians understand the kind of wages and benefits federal employees already enjoy. It is important because the government and all Canadians have endured serious disruptions in service earlier this month, disruptions that began again this weekend as the alliance called its members back to the picket lines.

These disruptions put safety and security at risk, and jeopardize economic recovery. I have already reported to this House that grain terminals could no longer handle this year's harvest, that businesses were facing imminent layoffs because of delivery delays, and essential services were being affected.
We cannot allow these disruptions to resume. The Public Service Alliance of Canada is unwilling to accept the best offer that can be made. The Government must therefore assume its responsibility and legislate an end to the strike.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Hon. members are already familiar with Bill C-29. We debated its provisions in this House not two weeks ago. I will therefore be brief in reviewing its provisions.
Bill C-29 would extend all collective agreements and compensation plans, so that all strike activities will become illegal. All employees would have to return to work or they could face fines of up to $1,000 a day. Union representatives could be fined as much as $50,000 a day and union itself, $100,000 a day.
As I indicated earlier, the legislation would ensure that everyone is subject to the 0-3 program. This includes the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers, members
of Parliament, senators, Parliamentary staff, the Canadian Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The heads and employees of other government bodies that are non-commercial in nature and not normally self-financing are also covered.
The wages of two groups-the Auditing Group and the Computer Systems Administration Group-would be adjusted for the period preceding the current fiscal year, but increases would be limited to zero and three per cent for the following years.
The agreements signed with four unions-agreements that, I am happy to say, are within the 0-3 guidelines- would not be changed by C-29. The bill excludes benefits and services provided under the terms arrived at through the National Joint Council, a union-management consultative body. In this way, Treasury Board can continue to discuss them with all the unions.

Many of the improvements contained in the offer to the alliance relate to items normally discussed at the National Joint Council. These include improvements to health insurance, disability insurance and the dental plans. These improvements were not accepted by the alliance and will not be included in the legislation. To give due regard to the consultative process set up through the National Joint Council, we would like to extend for 30 days the work force adjustment policy and bring these matters back to the National Joint Council and discuss them with all Public Service unions.
The other improvements contained in the offer to the Public Service Alliance would normally be lost to employees. The government is prepared, however, to make one exception. The government agrees that it is easier for higher income earners to protect themselves from cost of living increases when their salaries are frozen.
I am prepared to provide for a one time $500 lump sum payment to all indeterminate employees earning less than $27,000 a year. The cost of this provision will be absorbed within existing departmental budgets.
I am sure that hon. members will agree that these employees deserve special consideration and I urge them to vote in favour of this amendment.
September 30, 1991

In conclusion, the Public Sector Compensation Act is based on the premise that all of us working in the public sector should contribute to national economic recovery. Because of current economic conditions, the government cannot offer more.
It is unfortunate that we were unable to reach a settlement and had to resort to legislation. Parliamentarians, the Canadian public and our employees, the vast majority of whom are hard working and dedicated to public service, hope for a negotiated settlement.
We must now turn our attention to the task of bringing order back to the Public Service. I ask for the co-operation of all members in ensuring speedy passage of this legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understand from the rules that because we are in Committee of the Whole members get a maximum of 20 minutes to either raise questions or to make statements and, in this particular instance, the President of the Treasury Board to clarify certain aspects of his remarks.
I would like to begin my remarks by asking the minister if he can confirm or deny as to whether over the weekend representatives of the union attempted to get in contact with him for the purposes of exploring various avenues which were open to both parties concerning this particular dispute.
While the minister is on his feet, will he indicate to the House as to why he and his representatives were not available to respond to the concerns raised by the other side?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to answer this question. You will recall, as I stated in my opening remarks, that on September 17 we came to an arrangement between the union and Treasury Board, an arrangement that was so positive that all sides in this House agreed that we would postpone legislating and give negotiation a chance to succeed.
We proceeded in good faith. We had during the week 35 meetings at different tables. We made on Thursday evening two new offers and we expected them to be considered. We did not walk away from the table. PSAC did and called a strike, thereby changing the terms under which we had agreed to go back to the table unilaterally.
Government Orders
Under those circumstances we felt that it did not act in good faith and we have to go back to the original plan and legislate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister has confirmed for members of the House that by his very answer, or lack of details and precision in his answer, representations were made to him over the weekend and that the minister as President of the Treasury Board, who stood in this Chamber not more than a week ago and talked about examples of bargaining in good faith, did not make himself available this weekend, or his staff members, to entertain any proposals from the other side in order that there might be a resolution of this particular issue.
I am somewhat puzzled and annoyed that the President of the Treasury Board would not avail himself of every opportunity to try to bring some peace and dignity to the collective bargaining process.
It does not stop there. I understand that the minister would like to be part and parcel of this debate. He will have his opportunity to participate in the debate. We would love to hear from the minister in his usual colourful language.
I want to put on the record that it was not all that long ago that a decision was made by the Public Service Staff Relations Board which charged that this government and this minister were bargaining in bad faith.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. minister says: "That is not true". He will have an opportunity to explain the raison d'etre of that particular decision and how it affects the collective bargaining process between the government on the one hand and members of the Public Service on the other hand.
The minister knows very well that they have been bargaining in bad faith. What they offered to the unions to go back to the bargaining table was nothing more than a sham to buy time so that they could come back into this House and provoke a situation across this country. That underlines the Tory agenda. I stood in this Chamber not more than 10 days ago and said as much as that and now, today, we have clear, unequivocal evidence that we are in that kind of situation as viewed by the decisions and the actions of the President of the Treasury Board.

September 30,1991
Government Orders
I want to ask the minister a second question. Can he share with members of this House the amendments that are being rumoured in terms of what he intends to amend in this particular statute?
I am fully aware that he does not have to do that until we get into a clause-by-clause situation, but I ask the minister this because members of the government House leader's office have been informing us that we will be receiving copies of the amendments which the minister intends to table on the floor of the House of Commons. Could we hear those amendments?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member finds some comfort in listening to himself. I could very easily ask him to telephone the president of the Public Service Staff Relations Board and ask him: "Did you or did you not find the government acting in bad faith?" His answer will be no.
He was asked two questions by the union: did the government act in bad faith and, second, did we make every reasonable effort? The board said we have acted in good faith but we had not made every reasonable effort.
We said: "Okay, let's find a way to go beyond that". We were convinced we had made every reasonable effort: 90 days or 60 days of negotiations, 30 days of conciliation with a union that had started initially, the day after the budget, by saying that "this is a political fight. We will never accept it. We want to fight the government".
We tried to bring back the discussion. As for offers that he described as sham, I would like him to go and tell Canadians, the 146,000 of them who lost their jobs-they have been asking questions about them for the last few weeks-how they would like to accept these offers, all of them.
Do he realize that last year only 230,000 some Canadians tried to enter this terribly badly mistreated Public Service! I tell him that our Tory agenda is to try to get the finances of this country in order; not to destroy the Public Service but to protect it. If we had continued going the Liberal way it would have been disastrous for them, by putting our fiscal situation in order at the time of recession, by doing what other Liberal governments have done. We have negotiated. They have not. They
have legislated. We spent 90 days at the table. They have legislated the first day, good Liberal governments. It is because the situation is difficult, and this is what we are faced with. We are committed to try not to raise taxes, not increase the deficit and get the economy to pick up again.
As for the amendments, I do not have the definite list here but I can say that they are reasonably minor. One of them would allow me to proceed with what I have said I would like to do: have this lump sum payment of $500 because the act would otherwise prevent it. There is an amendment which deals with a mistake in conciliation in the French version. It allows me basically to first define compensation.
We are now negotiating with some of our other employees while this bill is in front of the House, until such time as it receives Royal Assent, to continue these negotiations and possibly come to terms. We are bringing in an amendment to correct an oversight in the French version, line 31. We would complete the list of new separate employers because since the bill was printed two new ones have come on stream-it is a minor thing again-the Canadian Polar Commission and the Federal Office of Regional Development. These are the minor amendments we intend to introduce.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is interesting to note that the minister now says on the floor of the House of Commons that it is their intention not to raise any new taxes for the purposes of additional revenue.
May I remind the President of the Treasury Board and his colleagues on the front benches that since 1984 there has been a proliferation of taxes on Canadians across this country numbering some 33 new tax increases.
When the minister stands in his place and makes the suggestion that it is not their intention to raise any taxes and that they are concerned about the public purse and the management of the Canadian economy, I can only say that it is not very believable coming from the President of the Treasury Board.
There was a period of time some years ago when the Canadian economy was flourishing at a phenomenal rate, but there was no decrease in the debt of the national government.

It was not the deficit.
September 30, 1991

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Now the hon. minister behind him says: "It was not the deficit". They like to change their line of argument when it comes to dealing with individuals.
Second, this minister seems to think that he knows all the answers or would like to know all the answers when it comes to dealing with the unemployed. There are many constituencies in this country that have unemployed.
I suggest to the minister that by playing this group off against another group does very little to enhance morale in the Public Service. It does very little to enhance any economic opportunities outside the Public Service.
To make this catcall that there are all sorts of individuals out there who would like to have these jobs, we all know that. The question is: Why has the government provoked an unnecessary strike on the Canadian people? Why has the government done that?
While the minister is on his feet-because I know my time is limited-would he indicate how many of his cronies, his fat cat friends are going to be receiving their bonuses and the magnitude of their bonuses? What will they be? Will he explain that to the Canadian people?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I have great respect for the hon. member. I hope he will not get into the habit of throwing away things like that which finally tend to disgrace this place.
I am trying to explain fairly what the opposition is. I do not expect him to agree; I know that from the start. He can throw numbers around and try to convince people of things that are wrong.
I will start with his last question. I have said in this House that the government policy at budget time was that everybody would get a zero year. I have said in this House that from April 1, 1991 to April 1, 1992 everybody will have a zero year and those who get a bonus will not get it. They will get zero per cent for that year. That will come of course at the end of the year because the committee sits then. It will come when it is due. They will not get it anyway.
Second, he talks about raising taxes. Should we have taken the Liberal approach to budget making or to fiscal policy? If we had followed the same route, where would
Government Orders
our deficit be? It would be $100 billion. Where would our debt be? It would be $700 billion.
We have change the course by cutting $30 billion. Of course we have put the taxes in order. We have made cuts which were opposed each time by the opposition, all of it. We have tried to get our House in order. Each time it was never the right cut, and we managed to get as much income as possible. We have made good progress so that in a few years' time we will not need to borrow any more. It is a tough problem because of what you made of our fiscal situation.
As far as playing one group against another, I would like to remind the hon. member that we are not playing any group. We are asking everyone to contribute his or her share. Is it being against the union to announce to our managers that we will abolish 10 per cent of their positions? Is it being against the union to announce to the provinces that we would cut the growth of transfers for the following year? Is it against the union to put some order, to freeze our operating budgets?
We are asking everyone to make an effort. We did it so as to send out a signal to the others that there was some concern about the recession. There is too much government spending. Obviously, when you have to pay $40 billion interest on your debt, you have a major problem.
We sent out this message, and it was well received because good sound Liberal governments have done the same. Basically this government has tried to be consistent and do a very difficult and unpopular job of getting public finances in order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his opening remarks the minister alluded, in response to a question, to the offer was made to members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. Can he confirm that he will continue to put on the table the $500 lump sum payment to approximately 35,000 employees? Will he guarantee employment for employees whose jobs were transferred to the private sector, the improved benefits including those for the dental, health insurance, disability insurance, vacation leave, shift premiums, et cetera, as well as payments totalling $81 million a year?

September 30,1991
Government Orders
Will the minister agree that that will be included in his amendments?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Should I? It does not seem to be a very good offer. You call it a sham.
That is right, and now he wants it assured.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Maybe I should withdraw it. If he had listened to me, I said just a little while ago that we are prepared to pay the $500 because we find that reasonable, but we will find the money from within the operating budget.
All the other issues can be dealt with. It is provided for in the bill, through the NJC. We will do it then and discuss with all unions the job security issue and the other issues.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the President of the Treasury Board said in his remarks that the chair of the Public Service Staff Relations Board did not find him in fact to have bargained in bad faith.
I would suggest that was the minister's interpretation of the ruling that the chair of the Public Service Staff Relations Board made and not the widely held interpretation.
The minister spoke of citizen safety. I have never, in 30 years as a worker who has worked in the area of collective bargaining, seen an employer who has been so provocative, who has been so sinister, who has been so double dealing as the negotiators from the employer's side in this dispute.
Last Friday the minister said Mr. Bean broke his agreement with the government. In fact, last Friday Daryl Bean from my office, late in the afternoon, spent three hours attempting to reach the minister. During a number of those hours we were aware that the minister was on the third floor of this very building. Mr. Bean wanted to speak to the minister about negotiations, about a new package, and the minister refused.
There have been a large number of people over the weekend who have attempted in fact to arrange for a meeting, or at least discussions between the union and the employer over the weekend so that we could in fact avoid this process we are going through today.
There was a call by Shirley Carr to the Minister for International Trade who assured her that he would in
fact pass the message on to the minister. There was a call from Jack Munro who is going to a convention in Toronto today. He was most concerned and called Mr. Spector and was assured that the minister would be advised. Our own leader's office attempted to reach the minister on Friday night.
On Friday, at a meeting between Mr. Capello and Daryl Bean in the evening, there was a meeting set for 2 p.m. on Saturday for further discussions and negotiations. Mr. Capello went to the telephone and returned and said he did not have a mandate to pursue the negotiations and come to the bargaining table on Saturday. This was in spite of the fact that Mr. Bean on Friday night had advised Mr. Capello that he had in fact a new proposal to put before the minister.
I think that the question that was asked by my hon. colleague, the House leader for the Liberals, was a very fair and a very legitimate question. That question was: Did the minister get those messages and, if in fact he got the messages, why did he choose not to make any effort to try and resolve this dispute until it became full blown again today?
There was a meeting on Sunday that the minister spoke to me about earlier, but that meeting was not with Mr. Capello nor with the minister. That meeting was with Mr. Ian Deans of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, who does not have a mandate to negotiate.
Although Mr. Bean had told the minister and told Mr. Capello that he had a new proposal to put on the table, this government took this dispute, put it into the political forum, and then took the weekend off.
I would ask the minister to explain to Canadian people, to this House, and to the Public Service Alliance how, when so much was at stake in this country, the government side could take the weekend off.
The minister said he preferred to negotiate rather than legislate. He said it a few minutes ago in his remarks. We just outlined a whole weekend of people, parliamentarians, people from the labour movement, the President of the Public Service Alliance, and heaven knows who else, who have urged this minister, through various people, to come to the bargaining table. This minister has the temerity to get up in this House and expect us to believe that he would rather negotiate than legislate.
September 30, 1991

The minister spoke about a one time lump sum for all those earning less than $27,000. He was speaking rather quickly, but I think he said less than $27,000. That would be 35,000 employees.
What about the other 120,000 employees who work for this government? Is the minister seriously suggesting that he expects the union to accept worker pitted against worker? Does he expect the union to accept a proposal that includes 35,000 people, but excludes 120,000 people? Does the minister sincerely believe that any union negotiator could take that back to their membership and expect a ratification? If the minister knows so much about collective bargaining, I find it very hard to believe that he would believe that that was possible.
The minister spoke about equal pay for work of equal value and lump sum payments. That is laudable. I really appreciate that the minister believes in the concept of equal pay for work of equal value. If that is the case, I would like to ask the minister another question: Will he withdraw this government's appeal to the Human Rights Board of the equal pay for work of equal value decision?
The minister talked about Treasury Board improving benefits. I share the question of the member from the Liberal Party who asked whether those benefits would be incorporated into this bill.
The minister spoke about the cost of any improved benefits which would have to come out of departmental budgets. I would ask the minister if that means there will be job losses as a result of those improvements coming through departmental budgets.
The Treasury Board ads this weekend say what the union walked away from. I would suggest that the minister should have a meeting with the Public Service Alliance and see what the minister has refused to look at coming from the union.
The minister referred to safety and security being at risk and that the union is unwilling to accept the best offer that can be made. Surely the minister would, at the very least, take a look at what the union's offer is.
If the minister is not willing to take a look at this offer, we can only conclude that the minister has another agenda, and it is not bargaining with the Public Service Alliance of Canada. I would suggest that the other agenda is a fight for the hearts and the minds of the
Government Orders
Canadian people, and that it is a cynical, devious way to impose its will on every group within the public sector: those who were at the table and those who were not, those who are unionized and those who are not, including the RCMP, the military, CSIS and a three-page list of others.
I think it is time for the minister to fess up and not try and fool the Canadian people about what his agenda is. I would, as the last question in this part of my intervention, ask the minister if he does have an alternate agenda to get this legislation through so that he has everybody encompassed, not just the Public Service Alliance?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the president of PSAC was in the hon. member's office when he decided, as an answer to our latest proposal, to go on strike.
No? Well he must have been very close then, from what I hear.
We did not leave the table, PSAC did. We made offers on Thursday evening and the following day. As an answer, they went out on strike. We took it that our offer did not seem to be agreeable to them and, therefore, we said: "What choice do we have?"
We had an arrangement. They say we have new proposals now. We had been at this for 90 days before the strike. We had 35 meetings last week, extensive meetings at many tables. Where were these offers? It sounds a little strange to me that suddenly some new offers would emerge that would be acceptable.
Mr. Bean knew, before we went back to the negotiations, exactly what our position was. We said that we had a limited margin of manoeuvre but we would do everything we could to make it as positive as possible, and that is what we did. We do not seem to be able to reconcile this with his request. Therefore, we have no choice but to proceed with the bill.
The hon. member says: "I have never seen an employer who acts in such a provocative way." I could give you names of dozens of employers who had to lay off people all over Canada.
Let's hear them.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
They were in a much better financial position than we are. We have a debt of $400 billion, and a deficit of $30 billion, and we are trying, all around our

September 30,1991
Government Orders
budget, to tiy to make these cuts and lower the deficit as we have been over the last few years.
The hon. member said that at the last minute Mr. Bean wanted to make offers. Well, I personally found it rather surprising that he decided to go on strike at ten o'clock on Friday, and to learn, as we are still at the table, on television that the negotiations are over. We did not break the negotiations, he did. Now he can always claim that he could have acted otherwise, but I do not agree with that.
The hon. member says that we are pitting members against members and we may have a secret agenda. We have only one agenda. It is to try to get the finances of this government and of the country in order. It is a difficult agenda. It makes for very, very difficult decisions that affect everybody. Of course, it is at a time when we are in a recession, as we were at budget time, where we knew there would be some recovery in the summer and early fall, but that could be threatened by governments losing control over their finances, because during a recession you have more money going out and less coming in. But these are considerations we took into account. We also saw that there was a great threat to the inflation path, which is a great menace to our employees and to our workers. So we decided to send out a clear signal, to set inflation targets, and to act accordingly.
One of the greatest threats in the analysis that was made of the over-all economy was that the unit labour cost had increased by 25 per cent in Canada over the last few years, compared to zero in the United States, and we were not being competitive.
Therefore, we decided that as part of a package, dealing with managers, transfers, and operating budgets, we would ask our employees to make an additional sacrifice, thereby sending a message which was received.
Most provinces have taken difficult decisions. Some of them have gone beyond. They have not negotiated, as we have, and tried to get the best possible deal. They have legislated. In some instances, zero per cent for two years. Therefore, I consider that we acted, not in a provocative way, but in a responsible way.
The member referred to equal pay for work of equal value. I am glad that she recognized that this government, at least, has done something very important to
conform itself to the law, by giving, in one lump sum payment again, $370 million, which is a considerable effort in our present circumstances.
Then we said that we would continue to contribute to some 75,000 employees $81 million a year. This is our analysis of our commitments.
The member asked: "Will you withdraw your appeal"? What are we appealing? We disagree very strongly with an interpretation that has been given of the meaning of these principles which were approved by the House. We are just trying to get confirmation that our interpretation is right. This is what we are doing.
The alternative proposal would cause a lot of ratcheting, where averages would be made, and would cause all kinds of destruction within the system. We feel that is not at all what the House intended. Therefore, we are proceeding in a way we think is right.
We say that we will be taking these additional resources for the $500 one time, lump sum payments out of the operating budgets, and that some positions will be threatened. Of course. I do not disagree with that. Do we start printing money, borrowing more money, or raising taxes? We are trying to manage within our existing resources. It is tough, but we are doing it. It will mean that posts will stay there, but they will not be filled as quickly as they would otherwise. We will try to come up with these sums through a better allocation of the existing resources.
Again, I would repeat that when the member says we have not made every reasonable effort over the weekend, I would ask where she has been over the last few months. We have been at the table for 60 days. We have been at conciliation 30 days. We went back and stayed for 35 different meetings and not one offer came from PSAC.
In the still of the night, having decided to go back on strike against the solemn agreement we had reached in my office, she says maybe we should sit down and talk. Well, I do not agree with that at all. I think the only way now is for us to legislate.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister answered one or two of my questions. I noted that he referred to everything I referred to, but chose not to answer most of what I asked.
September 30,1991

I want to make it perfectly clear to the minister that when I referred to Daryl Bean being in my office, I referred to him being in my office on Friday, late in the afternoon. The minister said to me, earlier today, that he was aware that letters went out from the union on Thursday. Do not try to confuse when anybody made decisions about things, or when people decided to start bargaining or not to bargain.
The minister said he wanted to make it clear that he thought it was unfortunate that the union brought in a last minute offer. Well, I would think that if the minister has ever been to the bargaining table: "It ain't over until it is over". People continue to try until the last minute to avoid a labour dispute.
Mr. Bean called a strike, which is very usual. He has a legal right to call a strike and he then had an offer.
All the way through bargaining people change their offers based on what gets put in front of them, what will fly, what will not fly. It is not unusual to have new offers all the way through bargaining to take something and try to change it, massage it so that it will be acceptable to the other side.
The minister should not try to infer that they are the only puritans here who ever tried to settle this dispute.
The minister referred to the Human Rights Commission and that he wanted to make sure his interpretation was right instead of the Human Rights Commission's decision. It is so like this government. If it does not like the Human Rights decision, it appeals it. If it does not like the conciliation, it ignores it. If it does not like the union, then it hammers it.
I think what is important here is for us to take a look at why we are at this point in this dispute. I would really like an answer from the minister: Was it his plan to end up having this legislation passed so that he could encompass everyone and not just the Public Service Alliance?
