speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is obviously a somewhat philosophical disagreement. The hon. member is giving me pointers on how to conduct bargaining. I would point out that, last Thursday night, we tabled new and improved proposals and that, as far as we were concerned, Mr. Bean had gone to consult with his member-
Govemment Orders
ship and would be back to let us know what they said. The decision was his to go on TV at 10 o'clock on Friday to advise us that they were going on strike.
He chose to put an end to the bargaining process, which I deplore because we did try to bargain. Sixty days of bargaining following the tabling of the Budget, 30 days of conciliation, 35 meetings during which the union obviously never intended to accept the government wage policy. As a matter of fact, Mr. Bean stated publicly: "This is no ordinary strike. It is a political strike. We are after the government's skin." Still, we did not make a fuss. We said: "Listen, he is entitled to his opinion. We will give it a try." We could have done like several provincial governments and refuse to bargain, but now we are being blame for not having bargained enough. Those governments, Liberals and others, legislated zero per cent wage increases on the very day of the Budget and, in some instances, reopened collective agreements that had already been signed. And now they come and take us to task! They imposed zero per cent settlements for two years and they come and give us a lecture! And we are told that it was provocation to act responsibly in the administration of our budget! Go and ask the Canadian people who were laid off these last few months how they would feel about accepting such offers. And how do you explain that 234,000 people applied last year to join this public service of Canada which treats its employees so poorly according to the hon. member?
We have bargained in good faith. Mr. Bean gave his answer when he announced they were going on strike. Now, our answer to him is: "We had an understanding. If you strike, we will legislate you back to work. The strike is on and so is the legislative process.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make some introductory comments and ask some information of the minister before moving an amendment to clause 2. It seems to be something that the minister himself has failed to deal with in the amendments that he has suggested will be moved.
I want to go back to the process. Some time earlier this year, five, six, seven months ago, depending on the particular group in question, the government was in a position to negotiate with its employees. The minister keeps saying that it did negotiate. He tries to deny that

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
the Public Service Staff Relations Board made a finding of bargaining in bad faith.
I can only quote from the findings of the Public Service Staff Relations Board: "The insistence on conditions precedent to negotiating terms and conditions of employment at the bargaining table is incompatible with the requirement to make every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement. Accordingly, the board declares that the employer has acted contrary to section 51 of the act and orders the employer to comply with section 51 of the act".
That is precisely what bad faith bargaining is. The board ordered this government to comply with the law of Canada. The government instead chose to use this decision and its legal obligation to go back to the bargaining table as a bargaining tool, another sledgehammer to hold over peoples' heads to force them back to the bargaining table under conditions which would see the bill that is now before us passed very quickly, with little debate and with no amendments.
Send the Tories packing.

The key issue here is that problems should be resolved by talking. The minister has refused, as President of the Treasury Board, to speak directly to the president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada since last week.
He has not returned calls from the chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, whose responsibility it is to make sure this system works. Mr. Deans is chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board and is anxious to offer his services in an attempt to reach a fair settlement here without having to resort to strikes and back to work legislation.
The government has adamantly refused to take a reasonable step of appointing a mediator who might shine some light on this situation, who might actually lead us through the tunnel to a conclusion.
Where is the mediator, Gilles?

One has to ask why the government refuses to appoint a mediator. I can only conclude that it is precisely for that reason that it does not want light shed on this situation, that it does not want an objective view of the situation made available to the Canadian public which can then determine whether the government is acting fairly. I believe it has already passed judgment on that.
People know it is not fair when somebody earning $500,000 gets a bonus of $80,000, which is equivalent to the full and entire salary of four Public Service employees.
I want to touch on a few things that the minister has touched on before I come to some questions. I want to touch on this very generous "$500" that is being offered to the lowest paid employees.
I wonder if the minister when he responds to some of these points can tell us why he thinks it is fair that somebody earning $26,999 under his offer would get a signing bonus of $500, but the person earning $27,000, one dollar more, would get no such bonus. The person earning $26,9999 ends up earning more than the person earning $27,000. That seems like a little bit of an "Alice in Wonderland" scenario and perhaps the minister could explain it to some extent.
That is Tory economics.

The minister knows perfectly well that $500 on a $20,000 income that gets spent entirely on goods and services that a family needs-you do not have any money to save and you have no money for luxuries- does not pay the increase in costs brought about by the goods and service tax for that same family or individual in the past year.
The minister also knows perfectly well that if people were out on strike for a matter of seven days, the savings to the government were far more than the cost of that $500. The savings were far more.
Members across the way keep shouting: "Where are we going to get the money, where are we going to get the money to treat people responsibly who are responsible for no more in their payroll than 3 per cent of the entire national budget".
I guess I would ask the minister to look at the other 88 per cent of the budget and say: "Are these the people who really have to carry the burden of this government's mismanagement of the economy?"
In six consecutive budgets this government, increasingly tightening the ratchet, has said to the people: "We are going to get rid of public servants", and it brags about cutting 90,000 jobs and affecting 34,000 individuals, "we are going to restrain their pay so that they are losing
September 30, 1991

money against inflation." They are actually losing purchasing, not just staying even. That is going to solve the government's deficit and debt.
People might have believed that in the government's first budget in 1988 or its second budget in 1989 or its third one in 1990, but by 1991 and 1992 they are starting to get a little suspicious that this government does not know what it is doing. It keeps proposing the same solutions and it never solves the problem. The problem continues but it keeps proposing more extreme versions of the same solution.
Anybody who has not been able to solve the problem in six years knows it is time to start looking for another solution.
I would like to hear the minister explain why the employees of the government get nothing this next year, but people on contract-and people on contract are earning more than the entire payroll of the Public Service Alliance-have no limits placed on them. I would like to hear the minister's explanation for that.
Finally, I want to talk about pay equity. I make it absolutely clear that for the Liberal Party, pay equity is not negotiable. I resent, on behalf of every woman in Canada, that this government is placing pay equity on the bargaining table to be bargained away in exchange for other benefits. This is a legal right that women in Canada have, the right to equal pay for work of equal value.
We will be proposing amendments that require Treasury Board to immediately implement a roll into salaiy of those equalization payments which it has been making to women instead of full wages and salaries in recognition of the work they do and to, within a year, fully implement pay equity.
There are a number of issues that will be raised, but given that we are now on clause 2, I want to talk particularly about the bonuses. The minister has done an absolutely phenomenal amount of skating in the last week, having introduced a bill just two weeks ago that specifically exempts bonuses and any other type of premium differential, other emolument or benefits paid in respect of circumstances specified by the Treasuiy Board, i.e. $80,000 extra for people who are already making $500,000.1 did not hear him mention, and maybe
Government Orders
I missed it, that he is taking that exception out of the bill now.
Having specifically exempted those bonuses from the application of the zero, three per cent budget guidelines, he was then faced this week with having to say: "Well, no, no, no, they are not going to get any increase on those, they are not going to get any bonus or any performance pay or any of that stuff at all."
Until I see it in legislation, I do not really know what the minister means and I do not think anybody out there knows what he means. They know that two weeks ago he tabled legislation that exempted bonuses from the zero per cent freeze and the 3 per cent cap and then they saw him this week trying to skate around that and pretend that he was going to do something else. If he is going to do something else, let him do it in legislation.
Before the President of Treasury Board responds to some of the points I have made and allows me perhaps the opportunity to make other changes, I know it is highly unusual to move amendments to the definition clause of a bill, however there is really no other place in the bill where this is dealt with.
I move:
That Clause 2 be amended at page 3 by deleting lines 2 through 6
and substituting the following therefor:
- amount of pay-
What we are taking out is that this bill does not include allowances, bonuses, differentials, premiums or other emoluments or benefits paid in respect of circumstances specified by Treasuiy Board. That makes it very clear that the commitments and statements the minister made this week that zero and three apply to bonuses are in fact true in legislation and not just in rhetoric.
The minister has often commented-and I would not use personal examples except that the minister uses it so often-that he has been through a 20 per cent reduction in his salary. I suspect that that 20 per cent reduction was not on a $20,000 salary. The next time he uses that example he might want to tell people exactly how much he was earning after his 20 per cent reduction and how that compares to so many of the people who are now without a contract.
One final comment: One thing I have found most discouraging this week was when the President of Treasury Board refused to speak directly to the president of the Public Service Alliance and communicated through his staff. He had staff report that they were prepared to

September 30,1991
Government Orders
give this $500 bonus to 35,000 members of the alliance. Wow, 25,000 of those were women! How any employer can brag that 25,000 of 35,000 of its lowest paid employees are women and that it has not implemented full pay equity, I fail to understand.
You have the motion moved, Mr. Chairman, and I would appreciate the minister's comments on some of the points I have raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The Chair will consider the amendment moved by the hon. member for Ottawa West and will take the admissibility of this motion under advisement.
That being said, I again recognize the President of the Treasury Board.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has made a great number of points. I will try to address them as succinctly as possible. I think one of her first points was to deny that we had made, I would say, an honest effort at negotiating.
I would like to remind the hon. member that this sounds a little strange inasmuch as we have reached settlement with some of our unions within the zero-three range. We have reached agreement with unions. We have even obtained conciliation board reports recommending acceptance of settlements within the zero-three range.
It is not so far-fetched. We have made efforts and we have been successful. For example, with PIPS the board report recommends acceptance of a settlement within the range. Therefore, I should not think that we were not throughout the exercise failing to try to achieve a settlement. Far from it. We have tried from the start. We knew that the zero-three perspective was not a pleasant one, and we understand that.
The hon. member referred then to article 51 in which she said that we had been found, therefore she concludes, guilty of acting in bad faith. I would insist that this is not the case. The union asked the Public Service Staff Relations Board two questions: Did Treasury Board act in bad faith and, second, did they make every reasonable effort?
Article 51 contains these two possibilities. The board came to the conclusion that we had not made every reasonable effort, not that we had acted in bad faith. I think that should be clearly stated.
The hon. member then said that I refused to meet with the president of PSAC. I must admit that we have been in touch with PSAC at the table away from the table. My negotiators have been talking to Mr. Bean on an ongoing basis. I have been kept fully informed. I met him before we decided to sit down, and I told him how it would unfold and what the limits were of our mandate. He agreed to sit under those conditions, that he would bring his members back and we would end the legislation. Then the negotiations took place and the information was that no counterproposal was coming. What is the point of having a mediator? We had our proposal on the table and the answer we got is that they went back on strike. Therefore I do not see any point in having further negotiations since we have not been making progress for the last few months.
The hon. member mentioned once or twice the bonus question. I suggest that her salary and her allocations are higher than those of many members of PSAC, and I suppose there is a reason for that. So is mine.
We have also chairmen of large corporations who have to compete in the real world. Of course when somebody gets $300,000 in salary it is seen as a very high amount. I must say that it is. That being said, managers also have a component which is performance pay. This is a valid way. We have set out a board to grant them.
What will happen for 1991-and I would like this to be very clear-is that we have frozen everything. We have frozen everything. These bonuses are given at the end of the year, from April 1991 to April 1992. They will be evaluated and, whatever the recommendation, they will get zero. I cannot recommend them now, but I guarantee at budget time the decision was everybody would have a zero year.
We will come to members of Parliament. We begin on January 1. This is our year. Bringing it forward will cause all kinds of problems, like it will cause Parliament to have a higher increase but for a shorter period of time. We said let us maintain it as we have with the unions. They did not get their contract ended at budget time. Some of them ended in August and others in September.
September 30, 1991

For the managers, they already started in April to have their salary frozen. Their bonus will be paid at the end. They will be paid zero dollars.
I would like that to be put to rest. In my view even for our managers in the Public Service, I think it is a good idea to have this combined salary and performance pay. This is a very good way of rewarding our managers. This was done anyway by taking the money from within. That being said, this year they will also get zero, which is indeed going back 5 per cent.
She talked about the money we could have saved by people being out on strike and not being paid. I would tell her with respect that when people are out on strike-public servants are important persons-they create a vast amount of destruction in the country. This has occurred, so it is far from clear at this time that the over-all balance will be positive. When you have in the grain industry the destruction we have seen, when we have in the airports the destruction we have seen, there is much less money coming into the government. In the end we may end up losing and not gaining any money.
As far as saying that $20,000 is not much money, I would not disagree with her at all. Of course it is not much. That is why these agreements, these salaries have been negotiated in the past. That is where we are through good negotiations.
I would say that this year we will freeze everyone, but we understand that for a certain group of people it is more difficult. We decided to make an effort within the capacity we have by freezing and taking the money from within the operating budget.
We can throw more money out, pay more money, grant higher salaries, but the alternative is a greater problem for us or for any government down the road. Next year we will be paying close to $41 billion in interest on the debt. We can of course go out and borrow $1 billion and make people happy for a little while, but this is a road to disaster. Our own employees would be very quickly threatened. They cannot be immunized from the overall problem that is facing this economy and they should be part of the solution, as other Canadians are part of the solution.
She referred to people on contract. If they are hired on contract, they usually have the same treatment as the
Government Orders
indeterminate employees and other contracts where you try to get, whatever contract you give, the lowest possible cost.
As for pay equity, I would like to know where her party has been all these years. We are the government that has given $317 million for pay equity and which year after year is committing $81 million for pay equity, not the Liberal Party. This problem has been an ongoing one and at long last we are doing something about it. The member should congratulate us instead of blaming us.
The member said that I took a cut. There was a decision taken by the Quebec government. I must say that I do not remember how much money I was making. I can probably confirm that it was not $50,000 but, whatever it was, it was a substantial cut. I did not like it. It was certainly much worse than a freeze and it went throughout the system. Some of those who had lower salaries did have to take this in their stride.
As for cutting off, why cut at $27,000? Of course there has to be a cut-off point, but we are managing as you will see in our proposal a gradation so that we will try not to have people pass over others and so on.
Basically the hon. member has raised a number of points. I have tried to answer most of them. I would like to go back to the basic principle. We made this decision at budget time because we needed to be sure that the finances of this country and our management would not be derailed. There was a recession with far fewer taxes coming in and far more money going out. There was a danger that when the economy started picking up again, the governments would be there scooping all the money available. We did not want that. We sent out a clear signal that we were committed to clear inflation targets.
Do you know what, Mr. Chairman? It works. The recession is ending and the economy is picking up again. That is why we cannot allow this strike to disrupt this very fragile recovery.

Mr. Chairman, I find it a very unusual process we are going through today, listening to the minister. The government sounds like it is willing to negotiate. It sounds as though somehow the Public Service Alliance has forced them into this horrible situation of back-to-work legislation. It some how

September 30,1991
Government Orders
tries to give us the impression that it has been reasonable.
However, the whole record of what has happened since budget day in February indicates that the government itself has been reluctant to negotiate openly, has been stonewalling and is trying to have its own definition of what the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruling was all about.
When it knows that there is an offer by the Public Service Alliance, and it has known for a number of days now, it is refusing even to look at that offer.
The minister any number of times today has said: "Mr. Bean called the strike". Somehow he says that that means we do not have to negotiate any more. The government knew at ten o'clock Friday morning that there would be a strike. Their negotiator had meetings scheduled even after the strike was called, and they met. The government had not said: "Okay, there is a strike. We stop meeting". They actually had a meeting at seven o'clock Friday evening. At that time, after the strike had been going on for over five or seven hours, depending on which part of the country you were in, the government said: "We are walking away from the table". It did that knowing that there was something coming from the workers, from their union.
It is as if this government does not want negotiations to succeed. It is as if it was afraid that it might get an offer which was reasonable. We know that any progress that has been made to date has not been made at the government initiative.
The government said: "Zero, that is what we are offering". We will have an amendment today which says that it is going to give a lump sum payment of $500 to those at the lower end of the pay scale, not to be rolled into their wages, not to count for their pension plans or any other benefit they may have in the long run, but it will give them this lump sum payment.
It did not do that out of generosity, because that has not been the government position from day one. It did in in reaction to public opinion. This government knew it was being devastated by public opinion on how it was treating its employees at the low end of the pay scale. All of a sudden it starts to move.
Why did it go back to the negotiating table two weeks ago? Not because it wanted to negotiate, but because it had a ruling by the Public Service Staff Relations Board that indicated it was violating its own laws, that it had not made every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement.
Again, the government knew it was not winning the battle of public opinion. It could not defy its own laws. As the ruling of that board stated, it is an employer like other employers and should be expected to follow the laws of Canada.
When I listen to the minister saying: "Well, it's the union's fault. It wanted too much. It said our budget was political and it was going to fight this political budget", I think he should actually listen to what he is saying. It did not want to negotiate. It refused to negotiate money until it had to negotiate money. It was not going to do anything for the employees at the low end of the pay scale until, again, the public forced it into it.
Now we have a situation in which members of cabinet have been called, people in the Prime Minister's Office have been called saying: "Get back to the negotiating table". My colleague from Mission-Port Moody went over to him earlier and said: "You know you've got an offer. Why don't you go see what it is".
I hear one of the Conservative backbenchers, pardon me, he is a member of the cabinet now and that is the Prime Minister's mistake, saying: "Why didn't the union make that offer Friday morning?" The point is, we have had time.
This government did not announce to the public that it was bringing back this legislation until this morning. It had time Friday to consider this offer. It had all day Saturday to consider this offer. It had all day Sunday to consider this offer. It is unreasonable for the government not to make every reasonable effort to resolve this dispute in a peaceful manner.
Whether there was a strike Friday afternoon or not, the government has had the ability to listen to its employees, to sit down with its employees. As the heckling and hackling from across the way indicates, that is not its chosen route. It does not want to sit down and negotiate. It does not want to work in good faith.
September 30, 1991

The minister does not have to withdraw the legislation from the House. He could be meeting right now. He could be sitting and trying to work this out, but that is not the government's way. That is not this government's way.
I find it ironic that at the same time that the Prime Minister and others from the government have called upon Canadians to try to work things out with regard to the Constitution, saying we should be listening to each other, talking with each other and not prejudging the situation, this government is not doing exactly that with its own employees. It is refusing to talk. It is refusing to consult. It has prejudged the situation because it will not even look. It will not even meet with the workers to see what the workers are now offering.
I find it ironic that this morning we have some indication that with the mediator we are having some progress in the talks between CUPW and Canada Post.
One of the things that has been suggested over the last two or three weeks is that we have a mediator to try and resolve the dispute with the Public Service Alliance. The government has refused to do that, and yet it was its own Minister of Labour who insisted that Canada Post and CUPW sit down with a mediator and try to resolve their dispute. Again, the federal government is saying: "We don't play by the rules that everybody else must play by". It does not play by the same rules that it expects everybody else to play by with regard to our Canadian Constitution. It does not play by the same rules that it expects Canada Post and the postal workers to play by. It sets its own rules. That has been its approach from day one.
I am going to give the minister a chance to respond. I want to ask him a very simple question: What harm does it do if, while we are proceeding with this legislation, he should sit down and meet with the senior people from the alliance and hear what they have to say? What harm would that do to the public of Canada?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not share at all the inteqrretation put on our negotiations by the hon. member. He seems to forget that this did not start Friday; it started some months ago. We have been at the table with PSAC for 90 days. We were at it again this week. What good faith can we have in PSAC?
Government Orders
Let me read you a document signed jointly by the two of us:
PSAC has agreed-and directed its members to return to work at
that time and for as long as negotiations continue.
It left the table. We did not. We put new offers which it did not want, and we feel it is useless to continue this process because it has acted in bad faith, indicating to us that it was not at all interested in pursuing these negotiations. We did not walk away from the table, it did.

The minister has refused to answer the question I asked. I cannot force him to do that in the House.
I do not think we should spend time worrying about whose fault something is right now. If you take a look at the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruling, whether the minister likes it or not, many people would certainly perceive that he and the government were found guilty of bad faith bargaining, whether the words were specific or whether it was general, saying that the government did not make every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement, and those words are found in that ruling.
I again ask the minister the question that many reasonable Canadians would ask: What harm does it do him, what harm does it do the government, to sit down and meet with the leadership of the alliance-while this legislation is proceeding, if necessary-and why will he not do that for the benefit of the public of Canada?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while we had chosen to negotiate-that is why I find my colleague's accusations strange-several other governments facing situations similar to ours chose to legislate.
Answer the question!

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
That is precisely the question. The government chose negotiation. It did so in good faith. We returned to the table; we made new proposals and the union chose to leave the table, saying that our proposals were unacceptable-I suppose so, otherwise why would they have quit? Therefore, I do not see how this process could serve any purpose whatever, except to waste our time again.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Before recognizing the next speaker, the Chair, after considering the motion presented by the hon. member for Ottawa West, declares it in order.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity this afternoon to speak to Bill C-29, introduced by the President of the Treasury Board.
I have been covering my riding for many weeks. In fact, in three months, I took part in 12 open-line shows and heard a number of comments from the average working man in my riding and, and today, Mr. Speaker, we are proud to support a bill that although it may hurt one group of citizens, those citizens enjoy considerable security, unlike many others who have lost their jobs, are living on welfare and are constantly looking for work, not just in Beauce but across Quebec and Canada.
When I was elected a second time in 1988, this government was elected to make certain decisions. Canadians and Quebecers were saying: "You must reduce the deficit, you must deal with the deficit and with excessively high government spending. You must control inflation. Interest rates are too high".
Since that time, since November 21, 1988, we have taken steps that were not popular but they were necessary. The Prime Minister has said, both inside and outside the House, that our government was faced with a disastrous situation as far as the country's finances were concerned. We know this government's record, and we know the measures we took were not popular. However, we had to do this, we had to take corrective action, and I think we are on the right track.
Mr. Chairman, we are now experiencing a recession. Economic recovery may still be fragile and perhaps hardly noticeable, but at least there are encouraging signs across the country and especially in my region. I would like to point out, however, that this recession is a global phenomenon. Today, if the government does not take the necessary action, it may end up like other countries that have faced problems even worse than those we are facing today.
It is not easy to defend the government's bill. It isn't easy to tell people: You won't get a raise this year. Your wages will be frozen during the first year, and you will get 3 per cent the next year and 3 per cent the year after. It isn't easy, but in the circumstances it is the sensible thing to do. It takes a lot of courage to support this kind of decision by our government but I do so willingly, because I know it is in the best interests of the people of Beauce and the people of Quebec.
In Beauce yesterday afternoon, I saw 132 people at a meeting, where I was asked all kinds of questions about this bill. Finally, I asked how many of these 132 men and women, all adults, had job security. One had job security: he was a federal employee who worked in Quebec City for Agriculture Canada, so he wasn't even a resident of my riding. So out of 132 people, 131 did not have job security.
Mr. Chairman, today we are faced with a situation that will get completely out of hand if we do not take corrective action. When we talk about the problems facing all regions across this country-in Quebec for instance, in Central Quebec, Abitibi, the Gaspe, the Montreal area, the Lower St. Lawrence-in all these regions the economy is in trouble, and people are doing everything they can to keep existing industries alive.
In the private sector, sacrifices are made to keep businesses afloat, to avoid going bankrupt. Some employees have accepted not just a wage freeze but wage cuts to keep jobs that pay $6.50, $7.00 or $7.50 an hour, so I think our federal employees are not being treated that badly.
Mr. Chairman, let me give you some figures. I believe that federal public servants now, if I am not mistaken, have an average annual salary of $37,621-yes, that is the average-fully indexed pensions, one of the best job security plans in Canada.
Furthermore, they have a dental plan fully funded by the government and benefits like health insurance and disability insurance. I asked the people of Beauce whom I saw yesterday, "How many of you have such benefits?' ' Not one. These programs are fully paid for by the government. Sick leave with full salary, generous leave and vacation benefits, family benefits like paid maternity leave.
So, Mr. Chairman, when we talk about wall-to-wall protection, of course there is room for improvement. If we were in a better financial position, we could give
September 30, 1991

them increases of 2, 3 or 4 per cent this year, but we decided to set a zero increase for one year.
Mr. Chairman we have a job to do here, all of us, whatever party we belong to. We must consider the interest of the country, that is, the interest of those who live here. I am encouraged that many people support us. You will read the editorials this morning in the various newspapers, and I know that the English-language editorials throughout the other provinces encourage us to continue this debate and end this purely political strike.
Mr. Chairman, there are ways to solve these political strikes. Mechanisms exist, customs and traditions must be observed. It is called democracy. In two years, if these public servants are not satisfied, they will vote against the government and will express their opposition democratically, not by coming to invade Parliament with people who are not even public servants but have been brought together to disrupt the atmosphere of Parliament.
Here is what the editorialist of Le Soldi, which is quite a serious newspaper in Quebec, called our civil servants this morning: the government's spoiled children. That was not written by a Conservative MP but by an independent editorialist, who more often than not has been strongly critical of the government. "Donahue closes brand-new plant in Matane." "Massive layoffs at Dom-tar." "Number of welfare recipients and unemployed reaches new high." "Montreal's economy literally collapsing." That was how he began his editorial.
Day after day, the headlines are full of layoffs the private sector is forced to go through. But I must tell you that I do not believe that Conservatives dominate the political situation in England, Germany and France, but they still have the same recession we do.
Job security has become a priceless asset in recent years, what with two recessions. This protection is even more valuable in the public sector, sheltered from the economic difficulties related to competition and productivity, which can lead private companies to lay off workers even though they have a job security clause on paper.
Government Orders
The only ones who have not been hit by the recession in the past two years are public servants at all levels- municipal, provincial and federal. Name me some people who have been hit by the recession! Mr. Chairman, the people of Beauce listening to us today are shocked at the attitude of public servants who act in this way and do not agree to make the sacrifice imposed on other Canadians and Quebecers.
Here is another editorialist, Pierre Gravel in La Presse. As far as I know, he is not connected to the Conservative Party. "Nothing works any more. A miraculous eleven-day strike was not enough to establish a productive dialogue between Ottawa and its 150,000 public servants and nothing indicates that a new miracle will produce results in the short term."
His editorial, which is too long to read in full, Mr. Chairman, says: "The confrontation has ceased to be just a labour conflict between the government and its unionized employees and again become what it always was: an essentially political debate with the government over its budget priorities."
.
In the present situation, exacerbated by constitutional tensions, Canada cannot afford, Mr. Chairman, to have its public service tied up for a long period of time. Neither can it put up with its devastating effects on industrial or business concerns which are already in a sorry state.
Therefore, the government must have the courage, the guts, of seeing its logic through and must pass as soon as possible special legislation to suspend the right to strike of civil servants and to set their conditions of employment.
About the union members, and I will close with this, as far as the author of an editorial published in La Presse this morning is concerned: "they must understand that it is no longer on the picket lines that their political fight is to be fought but at the place where democratic societies pass judgement on governments' decisions, that is in the polling booth. Make your views known at the next election."
Now, I have a piece of advice for Mr. Daryl Bean, president of our civil servant's federation. I heard Mr. Bean say on television this week end that they were going out on strike, leaving the table because the other side as bargaining in bad faith-a fact the President of the Treasury Board denied earlier-and that there would be acts of violence. I think that his role is to prevent such acts of violence and to tell his members to demonstrate publicly but peacefully.

September 30,1991
Business of the House
Mr. Bean even declared to a Hull radio station this morning-I heard him-that he would defy the law and was ready to go to jail. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the legislation can subdue these people who are giving Canadians, Quebecers and people from Beauce a bad image with their exaggerated demands.
Why does the government offer zero-three-and-three to civil servants while the inflation rate is at 6 per cent? We were asked that question. That fact of the matter is that this country and this government are facing a difficult financial situation. Members opposite know it full well, particularly those from the Liberal Party to whom we owe this accumulated deficit going back to nearly 25 years. The wage restraint policy affecting government employees is but one of the steps taken by this government to reduce the deficit and the inflationary pressures. We are going to succeed, no doubt about that, Mr. Chairman.
I must warn you that my colleagues are going to speak in favour of this bill. We will pass it, even if it hurts, because we are not here to win a popularity contest but to administer public funds as best we can with the tools at our disposal.
In my opinion, based on what civil servants from my area told me over the weekend and last week on the phone, in letters or in person when they came to meet me at my office, people are not ready to go on strike, they do not want to strike. Daryl Bean makes decisions alone with his senior executive for the major cities, but in our area, in the riding of Beauce, our civil servants accept their working conditions. Sure we have secretaries earning $27,000 or $28,000 a year, but in our area, some heads of families do not even earn that much. They do not get half or even one quarter of that amount in UI or welfare benefits.
So, when I see hundreds of people lined up at Employment and Immigration offices today to try and find out if there are jobs left in Quebec and in Canada, I tell myself these people must be protected.
There is one thing the opposition failed to mention earlier: four unions did accept the zero-three-three formula which was also put forward in seven of the Canadian provinces. I am referring to the civil service unions representing engineers, controllers, translators, physicists and merchant officers. All of them have accepted the policy. They submitted to it. How many of the strikers would rather be back at their desks, working and receiving their salary at the end of the week? There
are thousands of them, but they are forced today to follow the lead.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, there is a degree of urgency. I hear that the legislation could be in effect by the end of the week but that is much too late. We should be sitting night and day to put an end once and for all to this strike that should not be going on in the present political circumstances.

I think you will find acceptance for the following motion.
I move:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order or usual practice of the House, during the proceedings in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-29, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada and to amend another act in relation thereto, whenever consideration of a clause, schedule or any amendment is completed, it shall forthwith be stood until later this day for further debate or amendment, or for the question to be put, and
That any amendment tabled with the Chair prior to 9 p.m. this day be deemed proposed and be put without further debate at 10 p.m. this day.
If members were to adopt this motion, that would in effect put forward until ten o'clock this evening any amendments that any members want to make on the bill. Then, we would have any standing votes needed to take place to separate on any of those issues take place at ten o'clock, therefore leaving members free during the day to attend committee meetings, of one kind or another, that normally occur on a Monday.
That would not, by the way, disturb the votes that have been deferred until 6:15 this evening with the six o'clock bell. Those votes would take place at the scheduled time of 6.15 p.m. All votes on Bill C-29 would then take place at ten o'clock this evening.
Mr. Iain Angus (Thunder Bay-Atikokan) Mr. Chairman, I just want to confirm that we have had the discussions and to ensure that the people watching understand that this in no way reduces the amount of time available for debate on this very important issue. In
September 30, 1991

fact, it ensures maximum debate within the time that the House has allocated to us.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just to clarify, I assume that this will not preclude members of Parliament from introducing their amendments, and thereafter, giving a short, succinct explanation of those amendments.

Under the normal rules for Committee of the Whole, if ten o'clock came because of the closure, then no further amendments could be put. They become votable, even though we never get to that particular clause where that amendment could then be put. We are making it a fairer system for all members because of the time constraints. There is more time for debate, and any amendment can be put. That is the thrust of what we are trying to do.

Since the President of the Treasury Board has, I believe, circulated copies of his amendments to members of the House, and we will be doing the same with all parties with regard to our amendments, perhaps we could have just a brief moment or two to explain what that amendment would be.

Mr. Speaker, Constable Irving Kurz of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was honoured this weekend by the Red Deer Chamber of Commerce when it selected him as citizen of the year.
Constable Kurz has dedicated over 1,990 hours of volunteer time, setting up a program for victims of crime. He is recognized nationally for the instigation of this program.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, did you know that this government is denying millions of dollars to Canadians who qualify for certain programs?
For example, I met a gentleman of 81 years of age who should have been getting the supplement, yet he had not been. It was made retroactive for three years but he lost 13 years of compensation he should have had.
In another case, I met a widow of a veteran who raised five children, the oldest being 12 years, by herself and did not get any of the assistance to which she was entitled. Through that process she lost her home. She is trying to get some of that money back to educate one of her children and she cannot even get that.
When will the government stop this practice? When will it start being fair to Canadians who deserve the money they should get?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past weekend it was interesting to hear the leader of the Reform Party take some credit for the constitutional proposals introduced in this House by the government almost a week ago.
Included in this self-attributed victory was the issue of property rights which are now proposed to be entrenched in the Constitution. It would be very nice if Preston Manning stopped rewriting history. I wonder where the Reform Party leader was on July 1, 1960 when Prime Minister John Diefenbaker proclaimed the Canadian Bill of Rights by saying: "Every individual has the right to life, liberty, security of person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law."
The right to own property was on the Conservative agenda 31 years ago, as it is today. Canadians, in particular western Canadians, will be very familiar with the work done by the Chief, and no doubt are surprised at what Mr. Manning said.
It makes one wonder what the Chief would say if he were in this House today, probably something about the south end of a horse, looking at it from the north.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian public does not support the federal government's autocratic and authoritative method of dealing with its public servants. The public knows that the civil
September 30, 1991

servants are dedicated, hard working and deserve respect and fair treatment.
The public wishes the government to return to the bargaining table and offer its employees a fair and equitable wage settlement. Thousands upon thousands of residents in my riding of Surrey North and British Columbia have signed petitions opposing the back to work legislation, urging the government to return to the negotiating table and enter into a fair contract.
It is time for this government to come to its senses, to show some leadership, and to settle this strike fairly and equitably.

Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one can deny the strong correlation which has developed between the rise of cross-border shopping and the level of taxation on gasoline in Canada. This relationship is supported by a number of recent studies and surveys on cross-border shopping.
In Ontario, John Winter Associates developed a model for cross-border shopping based on consumption patterns. Close to the border there is a 15-minute convenient zone where consumers are willing to cross the border for every-day items, such as gasoline, on a weekly or biweekly basis.
A recent Ontario small business survey of seven border community regions found that one-third of those interviewed confirmed shopping in the United States in April 1991. Of this figure, 80 per cent purchased gasoline on a regular basis in the United States. Consistently gasoline was the most frequent cross-border purchase.
These results represent a very dangerous trend for Canadian consumers. It is now time for the federal government to act to rectify this situation. Retailers in our border communities look forward to such action.

Mr. Speaker, across Canada this fall, certainly across Prince Edward
Island, minor hockey associations are gearing up for another season.
This year the GST will be a factor many of them would rather not have to face. Hockey associations must pay GST on expenses like ice time and hockey equipment. They are not eligible for a tax rebate.
These are non-profit organizations. An extra 7 per cent in expenses therefore must come either out of their budget, from the players or their parents. That is the bottom line.
This policy is unfair and stands in sharp contrast to the government's stated goal of recognizing the important role of non-profit organizations in Canadian society.
I call on the government to review the effects this new tax is having on non-profit organizations like minor hockey and figure skating associations and to establish a policy that treats these valuable organizations with the fairness they deserve.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most pressing issues facing Nova Scotia today is the construction of a four lane highway from the border of Nova Scotia on to Truro. This highway has a high rate of accidents, all too often resulting in deaths and injuries.
Nova Scotia is unique in that it has only one main highway into the province and this highway also serves as the only road on to Newfoundland.
With the elimination of the railroad in Newfoundland and the reduction in rail service in Nova Scotia, the burden on the present system is no longer acceptable. The Hon. Kenneth Streatch, Minister of Transport for the province of Nova Scotia is in Ottawa today to negotiate with the federal government for funding to proceed with the highway.
As one who travels this over-burdened route regularly I can personally attest to the unacceptable situation first hand. I urge the federal ministers involved to come to agreement with the province so that this project can proceed quickly.

economy standards set and enforced by the federal government.

and will undoubtedly result in a reduction of staff at Extendicare Hearst or possible closure of the facility.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first anniversary of the World Summit for Children. The summit, chaired by our own Prime Minister, promised the children of the world that 50 million of their number would be saved from death within the next decade.
Tragically 14 million children did not live to see this anniversary. They led lives bankrupt of the care and comfort necessary for survival. They died from starvation or preventable diseases. Many were the victims of war.

Mr. Speaker, I don't think the present situation is helped any by statements that may be clever politically but do nothing to solve the problem.

He said they would start getting ready for a strike the day after the Budget speech, if the federal government dared to cap public service wages. The next
day, he added that he didn't care whether the government brought in legislation or not. It didn't make the slightest difference because he had no intention of obeying the legislation.
If you think this creates a climate that is favourable to negotiations, I can't say I agree. We tried to resume negotiations in a spirit of calm, within a restricted mandate, because raising taxes or increasing the deficit was out of the question. We are trying to reduce spending, and we have done so in all areas, as many other governments have done, including liberal governments in similar circumstances. However, instead of negotiating as we did, they brought in legislation immediately. We tried to reach a settlement through the bargaining process.

If the minister were serious-he was just telling us that he knew since before the budget that the union was in a mood to have a confrontation-why was he negligent in not making sure that in between there was a mediator who would have been able to make some suggestions to the government and the union to resolve the difficulties? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only thing we sought to confront was the deficit and the debt of this country.
The Leader of the Opposition, and I am surprised at his position, tried to make cheap political gains by talking about the bonus. It is not true. He knows it very well. I can reaffirm here in this House very solemnly that none will get an increase in salary and nobody will get any dollar in bonus. That should be put to rest.
As for taking these difficult decisions, our choice at budget time because of the recession with less money coming in and more going out was not to say: "Well, let us carry this over, borrow the money the Liberal way". We decided to tighten the belt. We did not tackle the union. We took 10 per cent of manager jobs away. We capped the transfers to the provinces. We took many, many difficult decisions including the zero, three. We wanted to show leadership. Provinces have followed and it is working.
September 30, 1991

Mr. Speaker, what this country needs right now is a spirit of tolerance and understanding. Yet the government is pursuing an agenda of confrontation and dissension among Canadians and with its own employees, bent on increasing what little sagging popularity it has left now.
I ask the minister: When will the government start managing responsibly and stop disrupting the lives of Canadians? I appeal to him, even now at the eleventh hour: Will he appoint a mediator? Will he try to settle this fairly and justly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think of the two, the employer and the employees, particularly PSAC. It is PSAC which is not being responsible. When you see things as we saw Saturday and again this morning in a veterans' hospital where people are prevented from providing services to people badly in need, this is not being reasonable.
As for the mediator, this is a process which can be useful-of course, I would not deny that-providing there is a chance we can get some agreement.
We sat with PSAC for 60 days of negotiations and 30 days of conciliation. They went on strike. We said: "Well, let's go back and have a last try at it". We were at it for 35 different meetings. We put offers on the table, very important offers given the restraint we have to live under, on Thursday evening. We got the answer the next day: they were on strike. What had they agreed to? They agreed not to go back on strike until negotiations were terminated, and they were not.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows very well that the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruled that the government wasted months not bargaining well. I urge him, now that he has mentioned the chance of negotiations, if there is even a chance, surely we can spare Canadians the agony that they are going through and the agony that his employees are going through and appoint that mediator and take that small chance, however little it may be, instead of publishing advertisements all across the country, at great cost to the taxpayers. They are only bound and determined to tell Canadians what to believe at their own expense.
Oral Questions
I ask the minister: Will he immediately withdraw these ads, concede that there is a chance, appoint a mediator and use this money to reach a reasonable settlement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member will agree that the citizens of Canada who have been considerably disturbed by these strikes have a right to know what we have offered. Let them decided about that.
As far as, again as the hon. member said, going back to the negotiating table, I will read a joint agreement from Treasury Board and PSAC which said: "It will remove its picket lines and direct its members to return to work at that time and for as long as the negotiations continue". We did not leave the negotiating table; they did.

Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board said today that the government's only option was to go ahead with back-to-work legislation. I believe that it is this government's last resort. It is a failure for this government. The strikers have said that they would return to work if the government named a mediator. Will the government appoint a mediator immediately and sit down at the table?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I already explained that the government would not accept a mediator because PSAC had already shown its bad will by refusing to follow a very clear negotiating process. They left the table. During months of negotiations, in the 90 days leading up to the strike and at 35 intense meetings, they never put a single proposal on the table. All of a sudden, faced with this legislation, they show that they have a particularly fertile imagination. Personally, I have lost confidence in the leaders of this union. I deeply regret it, and we will be prepared to negotiate, if you want. But when the conditions of the agreement we have are respected, the public servants will be at work.

Mr. Speaker, the government's continuous refusal to reach beyond and sit down at the table ensures that Canadians are going to lose confidence in this government. In fact, they already have lost confidence in this government.

September 30, 1991
Oral Questions
I would ask the President of the Treasury Board again, if the minister truly wants to see a resolution in the interest of those farmers for whom he has expressed concern and for whom we all have concern, if he wants to see a resolution to this for small business and those who may be hurt: Is the government's position so weak that he refuses to go in front of a mediator? Why will he not appoint a mediator now and sit down with one?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if our intention had been to deal with the unions without negotiation it would have been very simple. We could have legislated. Many other provinces have done the same. We chose to negotiate. We have done it in an open way. We thought there was a fair chance of explaining our position.
Canadians across this country have been going through a very difficult recession. Hundreds of thousands of them have lost their jobs. We wanted our public servants to make an additional effort. I know they deserve better conditions, but paid how; by increasing taxes or increasing the deficit? This is the greatest threat to our Public Service, a mismanagement of the fiscal situation.

Mr. Speaker, all we are asking on this side of the House is that this government make an extra effort.
We know that the legislation can be passed within 48 hours, yet there is nothing preventing this government now from continuing to negotiate. Tougher agreements than this have been negotiated in 48 hours.
Will the minister use the remaining time to negotiate an agreement with the Public Service Alliance, rather than settle for the failure of back-to-work legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are certainly committed-I made it very clear this morning- to proceed with the legislation. We will see how events unfold until then, but the legislation is going to go through.
Now that it is inevitable, I hope for the good of our own employees who are losing pay-and this is again a
sad result of these strikes-we will deal with it expeditiously.
As I have said, if we go back to our original agreement which was applauded by everyone in this House, we will then consider what to do.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
This afternoon in Rosetown, Saskatchewan, over 1,500 farmers are gathering to protest the lack of action by the government because they face the worst financial crisis in a generation for Canadian farmers.
Last winter, the government committed itself to providing a third line of defence financial assistance to these producers. When is the government going to provide this
assistance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed the hon. Minister of Agriculture will be attending this meeting in Rosetown. He will be putting forth very clearly the litany of programs and support that this government has provided to the agricultural industry.
The hon. member knows that a third line of defence program was announced this spring that has exceeded $500 million. He also knows that moneys will be flowing very soon under the Net Income Stabilization Account program and under GRIP. Something in the order of $1.5 billion plus will be flowing into the hands of the farmers before Christmas.
The moneys that are flowing under the programs that have been established under the safety net program, the special program designed with the farmers in the spring, will provide in excess of $2 billion over the next 12 months.
That is not chicken feed, as we say out in western Canada. Those are real, hard, cold dollars. I think it clearly demonstrates that we are in fact dealing very co-operatively with the producers of Canada, recognizing the very serious difficulties they face primarily due to the trade war.
September 30, 1991

Mr. Speaker, last year the Farm Credit Corporation seized over 600 farms in Saskatchewan worth over $160 million.
The Deputy Prime Minister knows that most of the programs he has been talking about now do not provide the support for the losses that farmers suffered in the 1990-91 crop year. They are asking for special assistance, a third line of defence. The government has not met that commitment.
When is the Deputy Prime Minister going to stop stonewalling? When is he going to stop taking up more and more time? When he is going to stop the smoke and mirrors show that he has been putting on and provide the cash that the farmers are asking for?
These farmers are not rallying 2,000 or 3,000 at a time for the fun of it. They are rallying because they are in a desperate financial situation, and they are asking the government for help.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether the hon. member understands the significance of $2.5 billion, because it is $2.5 billion that will flow into the hands of the agricultural industry over the next 12 months.
Some $550 million to $600 million has indeed been provided under a special third line of defence program that was announced in the spring. There is money that is now flowing under the Net Income Stabilization Account. There is money that will be flowing under the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, GRIP, the interim payment of which will be in the hands of the producers sometimes between the middle of October and the end of October.
That is cash.
Those farmers haven't received one red cent, and you know it.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: They may not have received the cash, but that is cash that is flowing to the farmers right now. Why would the hon. member try to discard that? $2.5 million is not chicken feed. That is hard, cold cash and the farmers will appreciate it very much, I am sure.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture, but in his absence I will direct it to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Oral Questions
The drought committees in Essex and Kent counties, comprised of the Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, commodity groups and agricultural sales groups, have all worked very hard for two months to put together reports of the impact of the drought in Kent and Essex counties.
When the Essex County committee requested to meet with the minister to present this very comprehensive report, it was asked to meet with the minister's policy advisor.
Will he today make the proper commitment and make certain that the federal Minister of Agriculture takes the time to meet with the farm community and the individuals who are showing tens of millions of dollars lost this
year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, there is a process in place which evaluates these situations. It is a third line of defence committee that is composed of farmers, representatives of the provincial government and the federal government. The work of that committee is ongoing.
As a matter of fact, my understanding is that it will be meeting in Winnipeg, I believe, later this week. It is my understanding that there will be-
The wrong province.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
We are dealing with this on the basis of a national program, and the third line of defence committee does not deal only with the province of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta. It deals with the national situation.
It is under that auspices that we will attempt to ascertain the losses and to determine what sort of cash flow will be necessary, what kind of cash flow will be in the hands of the producers, and evaluate it on that basis. That is the established process to avoid the business of ad hoc programs which that member and other members have sought to discontinue. We agree with that. We have a process in place. Let us follow it.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Deputy Prime Minister.

September 30, 1991
Oral Questions
In recent newspaper accounts, the U.S. trade representative implicitly threatened to levy a retaliatory tariff on Canadian plywood entering the U.S. Her remarks were, and I quote:
Unfortunately, history proves that in our dealings with the
Canadians in timber issues, nothing less than a hard headed
approach by our government appears to ensure fair resolution of
disagreements.
Has the minister investigated this issue? Will he ensure that Canada will not be bullied by the Americans when it comes to plywood like we were with the softwood surtax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is helpful for the hon. member to tremble every time an American speaks about trade with Canada. I want to give him some facts to help him relax and he will not be so concerned.
We have removed the surtax. This has had a very strong positive effect already on the Canadian ecpnomy. We have marshalled our arguments very well. We do not think the Americans have any possible reply which will stand up. Thank heavens we have the bi-national panel to enforce it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
At the meeting of the provincial, federal and territorial ministers of health held in Winnipeg, the standards of the Canada Health Act were upheld, including the prohibition of user fees.
The province of British Columbia did not send its minister of health to this important meeting and the premier of B.C. continues to advocate user fees.
My question is: Has the federal minister of health informed the premier of the province of British Columbia that user fees in that province will not be tolerated?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to comment on any declaration coming particularly from a premier in a province where there is an election.
I want to repeat what I said in Winnipeg. I said that of course we are opposed basically to any user fee. As long as there is none applied-and there is none to my
knowledge, no user fee in the country that is being applied now-there is no reason to to do or say that we will do something. But if anything occurs, I will take my responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. The reduction of Established Programs Financing to the provinces and territories continues to cripple their ability to uphold the standards of the Canada Health Act.
What assurances were given to the ministers of health at their recent meeting that the federal government will restore and maintain the federal funding for health care?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the member quoted what has been said in Winnipeg. However, he missed a part of the declaration which said that we should take into account the fiscal reality of the country. It was also in the declaration by the ministers of health.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It has become painfully obvious that the Canadian airline industry is in a serious nosedive, thanks to the government's combined policies of deregulation, open skies, and its high interest, high dollar monetary regime.
Given that our two remaining national air carriers, Air Canada and Canadian, will continue to struggle to survive unless there are some major concessions from the federal government, what immediate plans does the government have to assist our airline industry and to protect the tens of thousands of Canadian jobs that are dependent on it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume that the hon. member knows that Air France is not a Canadian airline and that it had to lay off a large number of employees last week. I presume he also knows that the four or five American airlines that have had to do the same thing are not of Canadian origin. Therefore the aviation industry throughout the world at the present time is in great difficulty because of the gulf war last year, the tremendous increase in gas prices and the number of people who are not travelling at the present time.
September 30, 1991

Mr. Speaker, the minister ought not to be concerned about Air France, he should be concerned about Air Canada and Canadian and start at home.
Given that the government continues to maintain that an open skies agreement is part of the answer, can the minister explain to Canadians how Air Canada and Canadian will be assisted by allowing the large American carriers which he just quoted to come into Canada, fly across our country freely without any restrictions? Why not say no to cabotage and yes to a healthy Canadian controlled airline industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I presume that the hon. member is aware that at the present time American carriers handle over 60 per cent of transborder traffic and earn $500 million more annually from this market than do Canadian carriers. About 13 million passengers move annually between the two countries, generating $2.3 billion in revenue. Scheduled air services between Canada and the U.S., including local and regional services, are provided to 84 cities.
The present open skies agreement is flawed. We have entered into open skies discussions with the Americans because we want to improve the level playing field for Canadian airlines and give them a better lease on life.

speakerposition: subtopic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Transport. Canadian National is scheduled to sell its rail line from Truro to Sydney, Nova Scotia by the fall of 1992.
Will the Minister of Transport explain to the House why the Government of Canada is allowing Canadian National to privatize this essential transportation link in Atlantic Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, CN has been given a mandate by this government to be as commercially profitable as possible. Therefore, CN is properly trying to find all the means of making sure that it will be competitive and will be able to stay in business. They are examining at the present time the possibility of making the line more profitable and therefore they are examining the possibility of privatizing that line if they can get a good deal that would provide improved service for the area. No decision has been made.
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister.
The minister knows that this railway line is the lifeline for many of our industries; coal, steel, lumber and fish, in order that they can move their products to essential Canadian markets.
I ask the minister why the sale, why the cause of uncertainty? Will he not now do the right thing and order CN to rescind this privatization order and keep this railway line intact? Will he tell them to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I repeat that the intention of CN is to improve the performance of that line to give better service to the clientele at a better rate, making themselves more competitive and making the industry they serve more profitable and therefore be able to maintain better commercialization.
There is no cause for alarm. CN is examining the situation and the possibility of improving the service at a better price and I think they should be commended for doing that.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of health.
The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child requires the government to ensure the development of institutions, services and facilities for the care of children.
In recent weeks the government House leader and the minister of health have made contradictory statements on the government's willingness to fulfil its many promises to Canadians on a national child care program.
Since the Prime Minister has committed Canada to ratifying the UN convention and it is now the first anniversary of the UN summit on children, which our own Prime Minister co-chaired, will the minister tell Canadian parents and their children who have been waiting for so long when will you implement their national child care program? When, Mr. Minister?

speakerposition: Speaker pro tempore
speechtext:
I know it was probably a momentary indiscretion but I would ask hon. members when they put their questions to address the ministers through the Chair.

September 30, 1991
Oral Questions
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I believe we are particularly sensitive to the problems of children, who are the most vulnerable part of Canadian society. I think we have done a lot but we we want to do still more, particularly at different levels.
With regard to the question on child care, I want to remind my colleague that we did in 1988 present something that was turned down particularly by the Liberals in the Senate. So far, we have presented the exemption of tax for Canadians.
We are looking now at new strategies, bearing in mind that since 1988 many problems have arisen on the issue of children, particularly in terms of child poverty and violence. Last year we put $136 million in these areas. We want to do more.
At the same time we have to take into account and put in perspective the previous comments of the President of Treasury Board. We can only do what the fiscal reality of the country allows us to do.
I hope that she will not ask me to raise taxes, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, Article 24 of the UN charter guarantees a child's right to health care services. Article 27 guarantees a child's right to an adequate standard of living. Article 28 guarantees the child a right to an education.
How can this government comply with those articles since it has deindexed the family allowance, capped the Canada Assistance Plan which funds child care services, cut back on funds for medicare and cut back on funds for post-secondary education? How can this government comply with those articles of that UN convention?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said before. We all agree in this House that all that can be done for children should be done. But I think a lot of members of Parliament agree that it has to be done in light of the country's capacity to pay. We have to provide the resources.
I am surprised that my colleague and her party does not understand that we can spend money forever, as did
the former government, but there is a time when we have to pay for the services we give. We need the resources. We still believe, as do a lot of Canadians, that the better we manage the fiscal reality and the resources, the better service we will give to Canadians. It cannot be sorted out in the way that will not consider both, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport and it concerns railway safety.
The CN rail crossing at Stewiacke, Nova Scotia is a complex intersection of five roads intersected by a rail line. Over many years there have been a total of 11 accidents resulting in deaths and injuries. The residents of the area have been demanding barrier gates for years and even decades.
I wonder if the minister could give us an update. Is there any progress towards eliminating this dangerous situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member has raised this point. Like the hon. member, I am also very concerned about railway safety. This particular item has been raised with my department and a decision is being made. I think the hon. member will receive a very favourable answer very shortly.
