speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of his colleague, the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology.
I am sure the minister is aware that the National Research Council has been looking at a proposal to establish the Institute for Instrumental Diagnostics in the city of Winnipeg, a very important research development for the entire country.
The governing council of NRC met last week to make a decision which was contingent upon the federal government providing $7 million of special financing to take care of the capital cost.
September 30, 1991

I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister in that capacity or as Minister of Finance if the federal government has now committed its support to that new research centre, and can he tell us if the decision has been a favourable one so we can go ahead and start this important work in the city of Winnipeg?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to answer on behalf of the Minister for Science.
In no way are we pulling back from Winnipeg. I am happy to tell the hon. member that NRC's presence will remain very strong there. It is a question though of whether we will have a new institute or not. The whole question of expanding NRC programs and putting them into a new institute is what they are currently reviewing. What they are reviewing is an expansion and not a withdrawal. Their commitment to stay in Winnipeg for its present services is, of course, very firm.

Mr. Speaker, I never thought the question of withdrawal of services was the issue. What I was asking about was this: Is this federal government prepared to match the offer of the National Research Council to establish a special Institute for Instrumental Diagnostics, which is a field of substantial growth around the world, which Canada can take a world-class leadership role in, for the sum of $7 million contribution? Compared to other contributions that have been made, I would say that is a good bargain.
I want to know this, perhaps from the Minister of Finance: Has he committed through his own department to make that commitment so that the NRC can go ahead and expand and develop that new research centre in the city of Winnipeg?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows that the NRC is resolved to continue the strength of its program in Winnipeg. There is no doubt about that. However, in terms of creating a new institute, it has not made a decision to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. Three weeks ago, on the Great Whale issue, the court ordered the government to meet its responsibilities arising from the James Bay Agreement. My question is, Will the Minister finally get with it? Will he comply with the federal court's judgement?
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
It
is done, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of the Environment. When? You have had three weeks to make this announcement and you have been forced into it. The reason that this-

speakerposition: Speaker pro tempore
speechtext: The hon. member must address the question to the Chair. The hon. minister may want to answer it.

Mr. Speaker, Great Whale is only one project. There are two others, one in Manitoba and one in Ontario. It was a year ago that we asked this government to appoint a panel to study the cumulative effects of the three projects.
It has been a year and the government has not acted. It is still sitting on its duff. When is it going to act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, in the case of Great Whale, the Federal Court ruling was quite clear in ordering the federal administrator to act immediately in enforcing the ruling. As I previously answered, that has been done.
The decision on whether to appeal or not has not yet been made. We are examining the ruling. The Department of Justice is examining the ruling and we will be informing the member accordingly.
Now on the issue of doing an assessment on the cumulative impact of different projects on James Bay and on Hudson Bay, we have had discussions with the provinces and we will continue to have discussions. I am happy to inform the member that we have not abandoned the idea of undertaking such a project. Quite the contrary, we expect to be able to make an announcement as soon as we have completed our discussions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
The government has claimed that the recession is finished, but the growth of output figures which were released today show that recovery in fact is very slow; only .2 per cent in July, the same slow rate which existed in June.
Will the government not try to speed this recovery up to help people across this country, to get people back to work, to reduce interest rates significantly and to see to it that the value of the Canadian dollar is brought down to help our exports so that people are helped across this country?

September 30,1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is encouraging is that this is the fourth consecutive month in which there has been an increase in the Gross Domestic Product and I think that is a clear indication that we are on the road to recovery.
What is also very encouraging is that the output of the goods producing industries expanded by .6 per cent, led by a strong growth in the manufacturing sector. The manufacturing sector is showing strength, expanding in July for the fourth consecutive month. Since its trough in March, we have experienced an increase in the manufacturing sector of 5.1 per cent.
We have never said that this was going to be a robust turn around. We said that we would have a recession that would be much less severe than the one in 1981-82 and that has been the case. The peak to trough decline in 1981-82 was over 5.5 percentage points. In this particular case, it is about 2.5 per cent to 2.8 per cent. So the decline was not as severe and it was not as long. We have had a good second quarter and we anticipate, for the third and fourth quarters, we will have moderate recovery and that is what the statistics are proving. We should be very satisfied with that.

Mr. Speaker, if this government is satisfied with the rate of growth, which will not decrease unemployment in this country, then this government should quit today.
Is the minister prepared to accept a .2 per cent rate of growth per month, which is not one month now but two months in a row of slow growth? Is he prepared to accept that when it means that unemployment in this country will stay over 10 per cent until well into next year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I am not prepared to accept that and I certainly have not.
What I am saying is that we are on the road to sustainable recovery and durable recovery which will produce growth at a rate of about 3.5 per cent. Incidentally this seems to be one of the best anticipated growth
rates of all industrialized countries in the world, certainly of the OECD. That I think is good news.
He asks about interest rates. Interest rates have come down by more than 5.5 percentage points. We saw a 9 basis point decrease last week. We expect, with the inflationary pressures receding, that interest rates can come down further still. If that is the case then we will be on the road to sustainable recovery with price stability, and that is the goal and the objective of this government. It will provide jobs. It will provide sustainable growth and will preserve the integrity-

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
I have received a number of calls from people in southern Nova Scotia who are concerned about the speculation that the search and rescue helicopter and fisheries patrol helicopter contract will not be renewed when it runs out.
I wonder if the minister could assure fishermen and others in southern Nova Scotia that this very important service will continue to be there and operating out of southern Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the helicopter contract in question was entered into several years ago. The period of the contract does not expire until March 1992.
There was certainly no decision made that once the contract expires there will be no further helicopter service there. The contract and the experience are now being evaluated by the department, and a decision will be made before next March as to whether this service will continue. It is a $2.35 million annual contract providing about 700 hours of fishery surveillance and it is available for search and rescue work.
I understand the feelings of the hon. member with respect to this matter. Certainly his views will be given every consideration when the time comes for a decision to be made with respect to this matter.
September 30, 1991

speakerposition: subtopic

TRIBUTES TO THE LATE JEAN-THOMAS RICHARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with respect and affection, I wish to point out today the death of an outstanding fellow citizen, Jean-Thomas Richard, my predecessor in this House for 27 years. Bom in Sandy Hill, where he always lived, Jean-Thomas Richard married Margaret Maloney and was the father of John, Michael, Maria, Suzanne, Pierre, Tom and Adele.
A lawyer by profession, he was a member of this House from 1945 to 1972. The riding was called Ottawa East and in 1972, Mr. Speaker, I had the honour to succeed him.
A hard-working man of the people, always available to his constituents-it would be hard not to admire and respect him. I know that he had many friends in this House. Those who had the privilege to really know him as more than the energetic, ever-present member of Parliament that he was, will attest to his kindness, friendliness, honesty and generosity of mind and spirit. He was present. He was also at the service of his fellow citizens.
Few challenges would have deterred Jean-Thomas Richard in his 84 years. One might even have thought that he would have defied death itself. His name Thomas suited him. He questioned a lot. He doubted everything.
I join all citizens of Ottawa-Vanier, Mr. Speaker, in extending to the Richard family our sincerest condolences.

Twenty-seven years in the service of his constituents in this House stands by itself as an achievement of note. J.T., as we called him and as he was called affectionately by his friends, sat in your chair, Mr. Speaker, on many occasions on Friday afternoons. He always ended his Friday duties by bidding his fellow parliamentarians "a

September 30,1991
Tributes
good safe trip home and a pleasant weekend with your families and your constituents".
Speaking for all those who loved him, speaking for all citizens of my riding of Ottawa-Vanier, we say to his family, his numerous friends, Jean-Thomas Richard will be sadly missed. He was a great Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege and I ask your guidance in terms of how we can best deal with this issue respecting an ad that appeared in The Ottawa Citizen today, September 30, 1991, concerning the government's dispute with the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
I understand from the minister's comments earlier this morning that this ad also appeared in other papers across the country.
I have provided you with a copy of this advertisement. The section of it that causes me concern is this. The advertisement begins with a description of the offer made by the Government of Canada to the Public Service Alliance of Canada and it refers to:
A wage offer consistent with the Government's budgetary
guidelines -
It goes on to describe those guidelines as applying to:
- Public Service employees, Ministers, Members of Parliament and Senators, as well as their staffs, the Canadian Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; 0 per cent in the first year, and 3 per cent in the second year.
My concern about this ad arises from the fact that it describes the wage offer to the alliance as a wage offer consistent with the government's budgetary guidelines. It then goes on to say: "Guidelines which apply to all the following," as I have just read.
In fact, the government's budgetary guidelines, to the best of my knowledge, did not apply to the Canadian Forces and to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and
Privilege
may not, except by inference, have applied to the staff of members of Parliament and senators.
It is my view that in stating that the budgetary guidelines do apply to those two groups, in particular the forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the government, in this advertisement, is anticipating passage of legislation which is still before this House, still subject to amendment, and still subject to whatever disposition this House may make of it and whatever disposition the other place may make of it.
To state that these guidelines, as offered to the Public Service Alliance, do apply, I believe is not consistent with actions that have been taken by the government in Parliament, and indeed pre-empts decisions that this House may take in its debate today and tomorrow.
I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that you have a careful look at this advertisement, in particular that section of it, and determine whether there is a question of privilege, in which case the proper motion would be moved.
I know, Mr. Speaker, you have dealt with similar situations in terms of public advertising, anticipating decisions of Parliament in this and in the previous Parliament. I wonder if you could advise as to whether there is a question of contempt involved in this advertisement and what the appropriate action would be if you find so.

Mr. Speaker, on the same question of privilege, I would urge you to take this matter very seriously as you have in the past when it has been raised in other forms, that the judgment of the House of Commons not be anticipated by the government, either by the kind of ad which has been referred to by the hon. member, or in advertising, or in any other way.
To do so is, in my judgment, a breach of the privilege of the House of Commons. It does not enable us to do our job as we are called upon to do. That is to make decisions when government is, in the course of advertising or in the course of placing the kind of ads referred to by the hon. member, basically predicting what the outcome will be and anticipating what the outcome will be and declaring the process of this House to be irrelevant.
It is basically saying that it will have its way and it is so confident of having its way that it can take out this kind of ad. I think that shows a contempt, not only for this

September 30, 1991
Privilege
House, but for the entire democratic process. I hope that you would take these things into account when you render a judgment on whether or not this is indeed a question of privilege.

The ad states, I think, rather clearly that the President of the Public Service Alliance has called for a resumption of strike action rather than respond positively to the following offer made by the Government of Canada. So it is an offer made by the Government of Canada.

As for the Canadian Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, there are acts that allow the government certain prerogatives when it comes to these issues.
We may, indeed, be superseding those acts with a piece of legislation that is before us, but at the moment, there is nothing in the offer that was not possible for the government to bring into being. speechtext:
I am going to deal with the matter now because of what is before the House and I think it is better to deal with it rather than delay.
First of all, the hon. member for Ottawa West is raising a matter which has been before the House before and especially in a ruling which I had to give many months ago with respect to certain ads that were published by the Government of Canada relating to the
September 30, 1991

goods and services tax and which was done in quite explicit language and, in my opinion, quite improperly. They were printed in such a way that anybody reading it would assume or could easily assume that the legislation had, in fact, been passed by the House of Commons and would come into effect on a certain date which was stated in the ads. After listening carefully to certain remarks I decided then that the ad was not appropriate because it was doing exactly what ought not to be done, and that was making a very clear indication to anybody reading it that the legislation had in fact been passed.
I decided that it stopped just short of a contempt for reasons which I explained in that judgment. Nonetheless the matter gave the Chair a great deal of concern and, as has been said on a number of occasions since by both sides of the House, it is a matter that we should watch very carefully.
That is of course the point that the hon. member for Ottawa West and the hon. member for Winnipeg Trans-cona are making, that this is much the same.
I want to thank the hon. member for Ottawa West for bringing the matter to my attention and, as I say, these matters are not always easy to be absolutely sure of at first glance, but a principle and a serious one is of course involved.
I have had a chance to consider the ad very carefully. First of all the ad is, as the hon. member for Calgary West said, indicating an offer made by the government to the Public Service staff, the Public Service Alliance, during the discussions which have been taking place over a number of days.
The paragraph to which the hon. member for Ottawa West takes exception reads:
A wage offer consistent with the Government's budgetary guidelines which apply to Public Service employees, Ministers, Members of Parliament and Senators, as well as their staffs, the Canadian Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police: 0 per cent in the first year, and 3 per cent in the second year.
It may well be depending on how one wants to analyse that sentence-and I do not intend to be a grammar teacher here-that the hon. member for Ottawa West is
Privilege
pretty close to the mark when she says that this might give somebody the idea that the Canadian Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, members of Parliament and senators' staffs were included in the government's budgetary guidelines. I would say that is an argument which certainly is a credible one.
One might also argue on the other side that it depends on how you read it. But I certainly have to say in my view that the hon. member for Ottawa West has put forward a credible argument and I think that, depending on how much one knows about the background, the sentence in itself does create some confusion.
But I have looked at the ad carefully and where it falls away from being exactly the same or even nearly the same as the ad on the GST is that this is not talking about in my view legislation which "has been passed or is in place". It is talking about an offer made under circumstances in which I think it would be reasonable to assume the government would then have to do whatever was imperative to place that offer into effect in the event that the offer was accepted. I find that it stops short of the contempt that the hon. member for Ottawa West is asking me to find.
However, I again say that there is some confusion even in my mind, and I of course am not in a position to argue the facts on it, about that original paragraph. I do not think it is a confusion which leads to a contempt, although it certainly may lead to a question of debate in the House.
I want to thank the hon. member for Ottawa West for bringing it to my attention. I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona for intervening, and I thank the hon. member for Calgary West.
I would ask hon. members, whenever possible, when dealing with those who write these ads to take care that what is in the ads is accurate and to take very great care that what is in the ads does not anticipate beforehand something that this House may or may not do.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment in front of us is quite simple and will allow members of the government and the President of the Treasury Board to tell us what their offer is made of.
In fact, Mr. Chairman, the amendment proposed by my colleague for Ottawa West suggest to apply the wage freeze to the following definitions, and I quote clause 2, page 2: "-does not include-and this would be eliminated from the bill-any allowance, bonus, differential, premium or other emolument or benefits paid in respect of circumstances specified by order of the Treasury Board."
The object of this amendment is specifically to give the President of the Treasury Board the opportunity of being
September 30, 1991

clear about the position of the government regarding bonuses, premiums and other benefits.
You will recall that last week, there was quite an outcry when we learned that big shots, people already so well paid that they needed a yearly bonus, were about to receive or had already received bonuses which in the case of Mr. Lawless of CN Rail amounted to $84,000, when his annual salary is a mere $365,000. Not bad! The bonus for Don Lander would be about $62,000 for an annual salary of $250,000. Nothing to complain about! And the list goes on. Atomic Energy of Canada: $50,000 on a $208,000 salary.
The general public and the Public Service employees feel somewhat disgusted when they see how generous this government, which refused to recognize the needs of its own employees, could be, how it could so freely give away the taxpayers' money to the big shots at Crown corporations.
Mr. Chairman, that is the first thing you have to acknowledge. Were it not for this government's lack of integrity, as we perceive it back home, we could still be at the negotiating table today. The civil servants and the unions were shocked, Mr. Chairman, and I don't blame them. It is insulting to be told that legal, logical collective bargaining is out of the question, while the government tries some new tricks, as was the case with the chairman of Canadian National and the chairman of Canada Post.
I think Bill C-29 which is now before the House, Mr. Chairman, puts an end to 25 years of collective bargaining between civil servants and the federal government. Things will never be the same. The Conservative government has now created such an awful mess that I do not see how we can solve this, unless we go back to the table and negotiate in good faith and, after this unfortunate experience, go back and rewrite, review, and revise all the legislation relating to the civil service, such as the Public Service Employment Act, the Public Service Staff Relations Act in particular, and the Financial Administration Act.

Parliament passed the Public Service Staff Relations Act in 1967. It established the Public Service Staff Relations Board. Parliament set the bargaining process in motion with a deliberate preference for the operational principle of the adversarial system. It was a choice that was made by this House in 1967.
Government Orders
Certain areas are restricted from collective bargaining and others by arbitration. Certain members of personnel were excluded from union membership. Others were designated as those who performed services essential to the public health and safety and could not join their fellow unionists in the event of a strike.
Public Service unions were given two possible routes to resolve disputes. One is binding arbitration. The other is the appointment of a conciliator who assists in nonbinding recommendations for settlement. If an impasse exists and no resolution is possible, Public Service employees have a right to withdraw their work, that is they have a right to strike.
In my opinion, public servants have a good case to make when they complain that collective bargaining granted to them in 1967 is too restrictive.
Those of us who have been in this House for some years know and recall how this Progressive Conservative Government in 1984 said: "We are going to review the Public Service Staff Relations Act. We are going to try and give you more in terms of flexibility".
I want to remind the House that under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, such things as bargaining, promotions, demotions, staffing levels, or what we call classification positions, lay-offs and pensions are nonnegotiable. You cannot bargain on those things. Those are things that can be bargained under the Canada Labour Code, but they cannot be bargained under the Public Service Staff Relations Act.
Federal public sector employees are usually dead last when compared to the private sector, when compared to municipal or provincial employees' salary packages. The last time I looked at it, it was clear to me that this so-called fat cat image that was promoted by some right-wing politicians in Canada was making people believe that Ottawa public servants and 75 per cent of the others who work outside of Ottawa-the National Capital has about 25 per cent of the total public servants of Canada- were fat cats, that they were over-paid and under-worked.
In those days the government did not help the image. I can recall and I am sure everyone in this House can what Mr. Mulroney was saying about public servants in 1983.1 will not repeat it because I thought in those days that it

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I first wish to inform the hon. member that the government is very firmly determined not to leave any doubt on the matter of bonuses and performance pay.
I repeat once again that, for the current fiscal year, the year running from April 1991 to April 1992, the salary of these people has been frozen in April 1991. When it is time for a bonus, at the end of April 1992, they will receive zero cent.
As for the legislation, I can say that I receive his proposal positively. I am told that the wording presents only one risk, by preventing the Treasury Board, for example, from adjusting travel allowances, or such other matters. Which does not worry him at all, I think.
With your permission, I will ask my counsels to discuss with Opposition members, to see if we can find a suitable wording; but, we very clearly have no intention to go back on that issue. It will be done through legislation, or another way, but it will be a matter of wording. Not being a lawyer, and I do not apoligize for that, I will not go into the subject.
However, I would remind the hon. member that, because of the present situation, it is risky to talk about these bonuses which were never given. I would thus recommend him some caution.
He also made a little exaggerated statement when he said that we are ending 25 years of negotiations. Would he have wanted us to do as two liberal governments did, those of Newfoundland and New Brunswick, and impose a 0 per cent raise in the Budget? We preferred, after 25 years of negotiations, trying to solve this problem by means of negotiation. We did sit at the bargaining table for 60 days. Then we went to conciliation. We were in conciliation for 30 days without having a single proposal from the Public Service Alliance allowing us some hope of progress.
In other words, if we made a hard decision in the Budget by establishing pay raise parameters at 0-3-3 for
three years, it is because of the difficult situation our country is currently facing. We must not lose track of what is happening in the country. Quite a number of companies have experienced hard times and as we are getting out of our recession, we must send them a very clear message, telling them that we are determined to do our share.
Further on, he said that we tried to solve our budgetary problems on the backs of public servants. No. What we are asking public servants is to do their bit, along with many others. We ask unionized workers to do their share. We also asked managers to do their bit, since we will cut their number by 10 per cent. We asked the provinces to do their share, by reducing the rate of increase of their transfers. These will continue to grow, but the growth rate will be reduced. We asked all departments to do their share, since we intend freezing their overall operating costs.
So we asked everybody, be it the Prime Minister, the ministers, the opposition leaders and all the members of this House, to do their bit. If our process was such as he describes, can it be that four unions managed to use it and sign agreements accepting the 0-3-3? How can it be that binding conciliation reports recommended settlements within the parameters we established? Is it not because the Public Service Alliance, even before the budget was laid down, and immediately after, stated that it had absolutely no intention of negotiating, that it was launching into a political fight?
As for us, we made serious efforts. I told you the number of full days we spent at the table. Only this week, we had 35 negotiation meetings.
Now we could have done like those other Canadian governments who took even harsher measures. We had to take these measures because of an extremely difficult situation. With its deficits and its debt, the government takes up too much room. It takes up all the money available. Next year, we will pay $41 billion in interests. We are taking up all the money. And all the businesses wishing to get going again are stuck because we have them nothing. At budget time, we decided to make an effort. We saw there was also a risk of inflation brought upon by a very high increase in manpower costs, an increase of 25 per cent as compared to the United States for the last few years. So we wanted to send a very clear signal to everyone: Careful! We have to get with it. And the best way to do it, as one of the major employers in Canada, would be to take our responsibilities. The hon.

member spoke of loyal employees who are being affected. He spoke of less favoured people whose salaries are much lower and who will be affected. As an employer, we have nothing to be ashamed of.
We will not excuse ourselves for trying to manage more rigorously the country's finances or to maintain services at a lower cost.
The member spoke of regional rates of pay, he said we paid certain classes of employees lower salaries in Newfoundland than we did in Toronto. Perhaps I may first comment on the tragi-comic role played by the Leader of the Opposition during Question Period today. The Leader of the Opposition rose in the House looking very stern and very angry. He was outraged that as a result of this dispute, farmers and especially Western farmers had lost up to $30 million per week. He said it did not make sense. The President of the Treasury Board said-and I am reaching the end of my speech-that he negotiated with Daiyl Bean for 90 days. Well, Madam Chairman, I can tell you that people in Shawinigan and Grand-Mere, in my riding, think 90 days with Daryl Bean is a long time.
The President of the Treasury Board was extremely patient to listen to all these complaints, especially since in February, and I think Canadians should remember this, when the federal Budget was brought down, Daryl Bean and Johane Hurens said in the lobby of the House that they were going to call a general strike. They promised Canadians they would. They would paralyse the country and get rid of this government.
I can see why members of the New Democratic Party would get involved in this kind of strategy, because strikes and demonstrations make them feel good. However, I have trouble understanding Liberal members who have been in power and know what it means to be responsible, Madam Chairman. I realize they are trying to protect their power base in ridings in the Ottawa area, where members were elected by public servants, but they should have the guts to explain to their constituents, to
those public servants, that because of the present financial situation in this country, we cannot give more. The same applies to the other provinces and a whole series of enterprises in the private and public sector.
Madam Chairman, in concluding I would like to say that Parliament should conclude this debate as soon as possible and if it does, I hope we will be ready to vote on this bill immediately, because Canadians must realize that the Parliament of Canada is ready to act in a emergency. I know that according to what was negotiated with the opposition, the debate will be extended until 10 p.m this evening and tomorrow evening, but Canadians, Madam Chairman, would have preferred a different approach.
In concluding, I wish to congratulate the President of the Treasury Board for his courage and I want to ask all Canadians to try and bring their influence to bear on Liberal and NDP members, to make them change their destructive attitude towards the Canadian government.

bloody awful and the people who perpetrated them are wrong. I want to say that unequivocally.
Some bosses within the Public Service have told their employees: "You come into work despite the fact that you are on strike or I will get you later if you do not". That is wrong. The government keeps saying and keeps pretending, telling Canadians who are unemployed and others: "Well, wouldn't you like to have the job of so and so who is employed and who is on strike." Since when do we promote that kind of envy between our citizens, pretending it is the right thing to do?
Some say that federal public servants make all kinds of money, that they are just making oodles of money doing their job. There is a story in The Ottawa Citizen and I have a copy of it here. year; in the private sector, $45,400 a year. Let us look at a receptionist in the Public Service, average salary $20,500; in the private sector, $22,500. In other words, the private sector pays $2,000 more a year.

Every morning when I come to work, I arrive on Parliament Hill at 7 a.m.. I drive on Catherine Street here on Ottawa. I want to make sure that the minister knows that we need the necessary funds in order to do that, obviously.

In closing, I just want to remind the minister of the editorial in today's Ottawa Citizen which is entitled "Bad Mistake on Both Sides". I will agree that there were bad and serious blunders on both sides.
I want to remind the minister that the public interest is his job. It is the job of this government and the job of this House to discharge what is in the best interests of the public.
Even if both sides were evenly wrong, which I do not think they are, on this count, I want to remind the minister that it is his job to administer the Government of Canada in the best interests of the taxpayers of our country. The negotiator who was appointed the other day had his hands tied behind his back and could really offer nothing in terms of wage compensation, save $500 to some of the lower salaried employees. I say that the government acted in such a way that this process was doomed to failure.
I just want to conclude by asking one question of the minister in terms of how this thing is going to work: I notice that a person making $26,999 a year will now be making $500 more, $27,499. That person's senior or supervisor, or lead hand or whatever they are called in that particular department where they happen to be working, might be making $27,300 and now you will have the more junior employee making more than the senior one. I have some difficulty in understanding how that is possibly going to work. I say to the minister that he should at least have provided some sort of a top up to
people over $27,000 a year, even if, heaven forbid, it would be on a sliding scale, but not to arrange it in such a way that someone who makes more money will make less money than someone who makes less money. I have a hard time understanding how that could possibly ever work.

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, in answer to the last question of the hon. member, I will tell him that we did exactly what he is suggesting, that is the necessary gradation to avoid any overlapping. In any case, we must not forget also that it is a lump sum. We have made that gradation so that people would not make "a step ahead" which would have messed up the pay scales paid needlessly.
That being said, the hon. member is making fun of expenditures made by the government on some items such as the GST, which are quite legitimate and quite necessary expenditures. He went on and talked about kennels, and I hope the hon. member is not against the fact that the government is fighting drugs, that he would not want that those services be deprived of the necessary tools to do that job. That is what we are doing, and I am not making any apology for it, far from it. Those are legitimate expenditures.
As for the illegitimate expenditures, I would say that it is rather the case with the union which is responsible for some big losses incurred following this useless strike which will ultimately, cause a very serious prejudice, to such an extent that it will take quite a while for those employees, for whom everybody seems to be so much preoccupied, to catch up for what they have just lost.
So, for the last time, I would ask people to get back to their sense.
As far as responsibilities are concerned, the hon. member suggested that we have-

We have a job, as president of Treasury Board, as government, to discharge our responsibilities and protect the higher interests of the country.
September 30, 1991

I would repeat again what I said earlier today: that is precisely what we did at budget time. We could have gone the Liberal way: borrow money, find money outside, spend it when we do not have it.
We ask our employees not to accept what is called a reasonable offer, but to accept what is a reasonable solution to a difficult environment. They have to consider the facts. When we talk about comparisons, we do not ask them to rejoice in the fact that they have a job, and in some cases, not so well paid as the hon. member has rightly said, but at least they have one.
During the pre-budget consultations, if there was one message that came across very clearly on all sides, it was that the government is spending too much. As a matter of fact, we will have a $30 billion deficit this year, so we needed to send out a very clear message of our determination to act. As I have said earlier, we have taken many different measures, of which one deals with salaries.
We are not asking the members of the Public Service to pay for all of this deficit, but to bring their contribution, as everybody else is doing.

He said that we tied the hands of our bargaining agent and would never budge from 0-3. I believe the government's position was clearly established in the Budget speech, which announced the government would propose a plan that would substantially reduce inflation and that one of the key measures sending this message was a decision to freeze wages this year, with subsequent increases of 3 per cent during the next two years. That is what we have done, and we did it to send a message to industry and other governments to be very prudent and avoid spoiling our chances for the economic recovery now taking place after a very severe recession. We were right, because in the weeks following the Budget, one province after another adopted our approach, with the difference that most provinces decided to legislate zero per cent. In some cases, they legislated zero per cent for two years.
We said we had some flexibility. Not much, but we would try to progress within those limits, and instead of legislating, we would negotiate. And then we heard the abrasive annoucements by the president of PSAC, who said that he was starting a great political debate. During days, weeks and months of negotiations, we tried to get back to more serious matters, but to no avail. On
Government Orders
Thursday, at 7 p.m, we put a number of new proposals on the table. We indicated new options for flexibility but our offers weren't even considered. The answer was that a strike was called.
The hon. member said we should avoid giving the impression that Public Service employees make too much money. I agree. Far be it from me to claim that Public Service wage scales are entirely out of line with the private sector, but perhaps he would like to think about what Daryl Bean said. When someone has to go to the private sector, they ask for almost a year extra. Is it because people are better off here than in the private sector? In any case, it is always the same Canadians who are strick with those problems and who have to pay taxes.
So we had to send a very serious message that we were determined to deal with the problem, and that is what we have done, Madam Chairman.

I would like to say at the outset that the government's offer of zero, three and three is fair when you consider all factors. The offer was made in the hon. Michael Wilson's budget in February of this year.
But the Daryl Beans, the Bob Whites, the Shirley Carrs of Canada have shown terrible judgement by rejecting the government's offer and forcing a strike. The taxpayers of Canada are furious at the union's decision.
This is a time for union leaders to take off their blinders and make decisions which are good for the country. This is a time when governments, management and labour must share some common goals about the economic future of this country. This is not a time for strident, militant threats by labour.
It is a time for union leaders to understand the realities of the real world. No one likes to propose a zero increase in salaries. As the largest employer in Canada, however, we must show leadership.
The total salary cost of the government is approximately $10 billion. The fringe benefits amount to 28 per cent, or $2.8 billion. The total salary and benefits, therefore, is $12.8 billion and there are approximately

400.000	employees in total, including 196,000 civil servants.
Canadians are just emerging from a tough and difficult recession. Unemployment is high. The people of Canada are fed up with high taxes. They blame all three levels of government. They expect us to show more restraint and leadership in the handling of their tax dollars.
Yet, when the government takes steps to make true our commitment of restraint and fiscal responsibility, we are met with strong protests by the unions.
The government's recent proposal applies to all
400.000	employees. It includes all Armed Forces, RCMP, judges, et cetera. It includes the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers and all MPs. There is a formula for MP's raises each year. It works out to approximately 1 per cent less than inflation. The increase this year, effective January 1, 1991, was 3.78 per cent.
When this legislation passes, it will mean that MP's salaries will be frozen for all of 1992 and be increased by 3 per cent in 1993.1 personally welcome this legislation. Obviously, Daryl Bean and his executive do not.
Marjorie Nichols' recent comments in The Ottawa Citizen were very interesting and I quote:
A private sector union boss who proposed leading his troops into the streets to protest low salary increases at auto parts plants in Ontario would be sent away for a long rest. Yet, that is precisely what the PSAC President, Daryl Bean has done and the opposition parties are applauding.
Ms. Nichols goes on to say:
It is simply not good enough for the Grits and the New Democrats to keep hurling the accusation that the government has destroyed free collective bargaining in the public service. Obviously, the bargaining process has been short circuited by the government's restraint program, which limits public service salaries to 0-3-3 per cent over the next three years. A recession has precisely the same impact on bargaining in the private sector.
I could not say it any better than Ms. Nichols. Listen to this point.
The government has a moral duty to all of its shareholders, the citizens of Canada, to set an example and hold the line against reinflation that would boost interest rates and stamp out the recovery.
And in her closing lines she says:
Anyone who believes that this strike is about money, must also believe in the tooth fairy. This is a political strike by a politicized union, supported by political parties with political agendas of their own.
This strike is not about money. It is about people playing politics with the salaries and job securities of workers, many of whom cannot afford to be on strike.
Several provincial governments have shown leadership in these difficult times by freezing the salaries of their civil servants.
Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Manitoba have all passed legislation in recent months to freeze salaries, that is, zero increases.
There have been some notable exceptions. The NDP government in Ontario is busily introducing double digit increases across the board. It has shown callous disregard for the taxpayers of Ontario and for the health of the Ontario economy.
I personally believe that the right to strike should be taken away from all public servants. I believe that all the jobs of public servants should be designated as essential services. We should not allow this chaos every few years. Strikes are too costly.
Some people, particularly small business owners, never survive. In the metro area we were burdened with a crippling TTC strike, on top of the PSAC and the Canada Post strikes.
Fortunately Canada Post workers have agreed for the time being at least to go back to work while the mediator meets with labour and management.
Once these strikes are settled, I believe we need to pause and rethink the process. There must be a better way. The economic harm inflicted by such strikes must end. The labour movement should reassess some of its outdated policies and practices. It would be very interesting to have legislation requiring a mandatory release of the public union, their executives' salaries and recent salary increases.
It would also be worth considering the merits of having all union votes, not just some, conducted by secret ballot. I believe a great deal of pressure and intimidation of fellow union members goes on now.
Government must also rethink the right to strike of Canada Post workers. I have already recommended that the right to strike be stripped away from Canada Post. It is an essential service. Strikes cause too much grief and
September 30, 1991

havoc among seniors, veterans, charitable organizations and small businesses.
An alternative to my proposal to ban strikes at Canada Post would be to end the monopoly Canada Post now enjoys. In other words, let the private sector into the game.
The most recent comprehensive study of the problems faced by Canada Post was conducted by Alan March-ment. In his report, he recommended the privatization of the corporation if Canada Post failed to achieve its objectives of service and financial self-sufficiency in
1990.
In closing, I want to say it is disappointing that it will likely take another week to pass this legislation. I am discouraged but not surprised that the Leader of the Opposition and his Liberals and the Leader of the NDP and her New Democrats could not resist the temptation to make this debate into a political charade.
They obviously do not care about the harm being done to the average Canadians who are losing their jobs. They do not care about the economic hardships being created right across Canada. The Canadian people will not be fooled by their shallow political rhetoric.
The Leader of the Opposition will probably order his Liberal senators to stall and delay Bill C-29 as long as possible, inflicting further economic hardship on Canadians.
I have had many telephone calls and letters about the strike by PSAC. Almost all the calls and letters are supportive of the government's back to work legislation. They are against the Public Service trying to hijack the government and they are very angry and frustrated by the harm being done to them.
Let me share with you comments I had from two business people from my riding of Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville. I recently spoke with Maureen Hyman who owns a business in my riding. She has struggled throughout the recession to keep her family business alive. Miss Hyman is growing very frustrated with the strikes that are plaguing Canada.
She says that this country is in total chaos. She says that the notion of job security especially during difficult

economic times is ludicrous. Nobody should have job security. Where is their job security in the private sector? Nobody should be given a job for life. That is total nonsense. Miss Hyman does not believe that workers should be given the opportunity to strike and disrupt the lives of Canadians.
I also heard from Joseph Wileman who lives and works in my riding. He called me to express his disapproval with the position taken by PSAC to strike. Mr. Wileman who was a public servant years ago insists that the Public Service should not be unionized.
They may not get a pay raise right now, but their job security more than makes up for that. He went on to say that they have a job, and they should be quite satisfied.

Here we are, just starting to recover from a severe recession; thousands of Canadians have lost their jobs, many Canadians who have jobs are worried about the security of their current jobs. They do not understand how Canada's civil servants can be so unrealistic in their pay demands.
Canadians are fed up with taxes. They blame all three levels of government, as I said a while ago. They feel angry and frustrated. They at least want their taxes which are collected to be used carefully and frugally. They certainly do not want civil servants to get salary raises at this time.

Insistence on conditions precedent to negotiating terms and conditions of employment at the bargaining table is incompatible with the requirement to make every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement. Accordingly, the Board declares that the employer has acted contrary to section 51 of the Act and orders the employer to comply with section 51 of the Act.
I cannot see anything that could be clearer than this statement. If anything, the government should have blushed, gone back to the negotiating table, discussed with the employees, and if it could not come to a conclusion then it should have gone to arbitration.
We heard quite a bit from the hon. members across the way on the government side about the fact that government employees are overpaid. Just for the record, survey after survey clearly states that the public servants, when it comes to their annual increase, are not in parity with the private sector increases.
For instance, in the private sector in 1989 the employees received on an average of 5.3 per cent, while the federal administration paid its employees 4.2 per cent. In 1990, the public sector on the average paid its employees 5.9 per cent, while the public servant received an average of 5.3 per cent. In 1991, the first quarter, the private sector paid on an average of 5.5 per cent, while the public servant received on the average of 5.4 per cent.
That is to say that all of those increases were somewhat lower than the inflation rate.
What is happening now? Why are the public servants complaining and why are they on strike? At issue are many of the points that the President of the Treasury Board was talking about, such as job security.
For instance, since 1984 until now there is in excess of
13,000	employees who have lost their jobs. The government continues to move in the direction of downsizing the Public Service. Many of those public servants are worried about the possibility of losing their jobs, like anyone else in any sector.
Pay equity is another concern. Despite the fact that a giant management-union committee came up with the results of a study that said that we have to get on with pay equity legislation, we have yet to see some sort of compliance with that.
There is another issue which has been raised by the public servants and that is the national rate of pay. It is surprising that most of the public servants are not paid for what they do, but for where they live. Some members still receive regional rates of pay. An electrician in Newfoundland, for example, is receiving approximately $4 less than an electrician who is doing the same job in British Columbia, which is highly unfair.
There is wage disparity. The pay for people who work in the federal government is lower than those who work in the private sector. As my colleague indicated a little earlier, a comparison between the public sector and the private sector clearly states that there is disparity. The reason for that disparity is because of the fact that the federal government's way of dealing with public servants has been underhanded.
On average a public servant receives approximately $11.73 per hour. When we look at the private sector, a labourer in the private sector-and I heard one of my
September 30, 1991

friends saying something unparliamentary perhaps, but we will deal with that later- earns approximately $14.56 per hour, up to $15.35.
If we are to compare specifics in both the public sector and the private sector, let us take for examples, secretaries, receptionists and telephone clerks. On average these people earn approximately $20,500 a year. While in the private sector on average people who do the same kind of work earn approximately $23,500. There is about $3,000 difference between what the public servant earns and what the private sector is paying.
We move on to the other side of things, professionals for instance in the Public Service. Take for example the computer programmers. On average a computer programmer in the public sector earns $42,500 a year, while his colleague in the private sector earns $46,400 a year. There is approximately $4,000 difference between what the private sector pays and what the public sector pays.
There are approximately 55,000 secretarial and clerical workers who deserve a 6 per cent pay increase and who are making almost $26,400. Most of those people, I might add, are women.
The government is saying: "My way or no way". It has offered the $500 one time lump sum to the public servants. I might add this $500 would be offered for one year and next year they will go back to their previous salary. They have been on strike now for about seven days. I would suggest that the government has already made $500 through savings because of the fact that the public servants are on strike. The government can solve the problem, but obviously it does not have any intention to do so.
Contracting out is one of the concerns that the public servants have. It is interesting to note that in 1990 the government itself admitted to the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee that it did not know whether contracting out was cost effective.
My suggestion to the government is that when it is spending in excess of $5 billion of taxpayers' money it had better know whether it is cost effective. It had better know whether it is saving taxpayer's money.
This whole question of government action and inaction on this issue is cause for alarm in my constituency of Ottawa Centre where many of these people live and
Government Orders
work. It is interesting to know that a poll concluded that four out of five Canadians believe they will be personally affected by cuts in government services. In many federal departments there is a need for more public servants, not less. All you have to do is go to 200 Catherine Street in my riding at 5.30 or 6 o'clock in the morning and you will be surprised to leant that there is in excess of 20 to 30 people lining up to get services from Employment and Immigration.
I would challenge my colleagues to dispute the fact that in the Department of Employment and Immigration there is need for more public servants, not less. Simply put, it is because there is an overload on the system and this is known by many of my colleagues.
A majority of 52 per cent of the Canadian public says that a reduction in the availability of federal government services due to budget cuts will have a negative affect on the future of Canada. It will because the Public Service of Canada is the most basic, fundamental infrastructure to any growth and unless you have that infrastructure in shape and in order there is no hope for anything else to function. These are the people who are making, introducing and implementing the law at the federal level.
A strong majority, which is approximately 71 per cent of the Canadian public, believes it is paying more in taxes and receiving less in services. That is certainly not because public servants are not doing their best.
Two out of three Canadians feel public employees are hard working and do an honest day of work. That is contrary to what one of my colleagues was stating a little earlier, that many public servants are fat cats. I have not seen a single fat cat public servant. If any one of my colleagues knows of a single fat cat public servant, maybe he should contact my office and let me know, or maybe he should contact the President of the Treasury Board.
We have one of the finest Public Services in the world and certainly the way we are dealing with it is not the best way.
The government should go back to the negotiating table. The Public Service wants to see the government going back to the negotiating table.
I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board one question. I know he has repeatedly answered this question by side-stepping it, by saying that he does not want to hire an arbitrator. The media asks him questions. The

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
opposition asks him questions. The Public Service Alliance union has asked him the question.
I would suggest that the majority of the people would like to see the government answer this question: Why would he not proceed with the appointment of a mediator? If the mediator is to come up with a decision that the government is not happy with, it can do whatever it wants to do then. I might suggest that the reason why the government does not want to appoint a mediator is because it knows it is going to lose. It knows that based on the fact that we have been putting suggestions in this House and before Canadians the government is really not dealing with public servants the way it should be dealing with them.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I would like to take on some of the points that the hon. member for Ottawa Centre has raised.
I am a little bit flabbergasted by some of his statements. Being from Ottawa Centre, I would expect him to be more aware of the reality of the Public Service. He said that 13,000 employees have lost their jobs. This is not the case. We have removed positions but we have been very careful to find other jobs for the employees who are there. We have done it through attrition. It is very exceptional that members have to leave the Public Service against their will.
I would give him a number. We are one of the largest employers in Canada. We have 225,000 people working for us. From 1986 to now, I would think it is in the order of 1,500 persons who had to leave the Public Service against their will. If this is not the best job security ever, I do not think you can find it.
I think the hon. member should be very careful in making statements that we are not concerned about job security. We are.
The hon. member referred to the decision of the Public Service Staff Relations Board and he again stated that the commission had found us to have negotiated in bad faith. In all fairness, I would ask him to put the question to Mr. Ian Deans, chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board.
Section 51 covers two things: "bad faith" and "every reasonable effort." The union put the two questions to
the board and the board decided that we had not made every reasonable effort, but did not say that we had acted in bad faith.
We have made additional efforts, because we had 35 different meetings last week negotiating with the union. We put forward offers to them that were not even considered. That is why I do not see the point of continuing this process.
He has given us numbers with respect to the private sector. Would the civil servants of Canada like to have the same treatment as was given to thousands and thousands of Canadians during the recession who lost their jobs, who had to re-open their collective agreements in order to maintain their companies' competitiveness and to try to weather the recession.
We have been very fair. Of course, zero per cent is not what they deserve, but it is what this country can afford at this particular time, and it is also showing a sign of concern about what is happening across the country.
When you say that in 1981 settlements in the private sector were at 5.5 per cent, for those who found the settlement, but in the first two months 146,000 Canadians would have loved to have a zero per cent offer.
He said we should need more public servants. Do we need to raise taxes, increase the deficit, borrow more money? Companies that are in opposition just fold up because they cannot afford to continue. We continue because we are a government. But we cannot overdo it. We have to be very careful not to go beyond a certain capacity. Otherwise, it is our very capacity to continue to maintain a good, strong public service that would be threatened.
Just remember that next year the interest only on our debt will be $41 billion. This is money that we do not have, that it is not possible to use for salaries, services to Canadians. We could increase it to $43 billion. For every dollar we get, 35 cents goes to servicing the debt. We can let it go to 50 cents or 53 cents, and what would happen then to the civil service?
So we need to balance this. We felt that at this time in the recession, when we made the budget, we had to look ahead and make sure that the government was sending out the right signals, and was making decisions that would help the economy pick up again, as it is doing now.
September 30, 1991

The hon. member says we should go back to the negotiating table. I would tell him that we have negotiated for 60 days. We have been in conciliation for 30 full days. We came back to the table after the strike for 35 meetings, and never did we get an offer from PSAC. In any case, they are the ones who left the table, not us.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are only three minutes left. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre.

Thank you, Madam Chairman. I hope the President of the Treasury Board is not suggesting it is normal to try and reduce the deficit by bearing down on those in the public sector who earn less than $30,000.

I hope very much that the President of the Treasury Board is not trying to solve the deficit question by attacking the public servants' salaries. As he knows, the money that the government pays to the public servant does not account for more than 12 per cent. In fact, it is less than 12 per cent of the total expenditure.
He alluded to the fact that next year we are going to have a deficit of $40.5 million. I hope that figure is not accurate. We have been hearing that the deficit was going to be reduced this year.
It was reduced. Interest on the debt.

Interest on the debt, okay. I will take this one back.
In any event, the 13,000 jobs we are talking about were lost. Whether somebody has been laid off or fired is irrelevant. Those jobs that were there are no longer there, so the people who have been doing them could be on UI or on the welfare roll.
I would like to ask the minister how he can justify penalizing 55,000 people in the Public Service who are earning less than $30,000 a year? How could he have the heart to expect those people to bite the bullet? The inflation rate was in excess of 5 per cent over the past year or so. There is no guarantee the inflation rate is going to be close to zero per cent. He knows it.
Government Orders
He knows as well that everything should be in line with the cost of living. Why would he just force the public servant to bite the bullet while everybody else is getting off the hook?
Why do 55,000 workers, Madam Chairman, who make less than $30,000 have to pay the price?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish an answer? There is not very much time.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the principle that they do not seem to understand on that side of the House is that there is something called the "capacity to pay".
When we arrived in government in 1984, for every dollar that was coming in, the government was spending $1.33. You can be popular with the Public Service. You can be popular with Canadians by borrowing money and spending more than you collect in taxes. We have turned that around.
We are paying the debt, and we think that by putting our House in order, we are providing a future for our Public Service. If we were not to do it, we would not be really caring for them. It would be very quickly threatened as are all our programs.
I do not agree with them at all that you do not pay into account. In which world do we live? The capacity to pay is not taken into account. We need more civil servants: I agree with him. How do we pay them, by borrowing more money? Do we go the way of Argentina, down the drain? We do not want that. We keep a balance.
It was a tough recession, and instead of letting it go with rates of interest of 22 per cent, inflation rates of 10 per cent and 14 per cent, we have taken the other direction: tighten up and leave some room for the economy to prosper. Do not take all the room that is available.
That is why we have taken this measure. It is not at all to punish anyone. It is a small contribution we are asking, compared to what Canadians have to go through. It is difficult. I understand that, but I think it is reasonable.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member wants to speak to clause 2?
