I just wanted to make sure that hon. members are aware of the motion introduced earlier today, which allows amendments to be tabled. If hon. members want to know what those amendments are about, it will be necessary perhaps, at one point, to suspend debate on clause 2 and move on to other clauses.
However, I do not mean to tell hon. members what to do. I just want to refresh their memory in order to make things easier for them a little later.
The hon. member for Laval East has the floor.
Point of order, Madam Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier has the floor on a point of order.

Madam Chairman, you just raised two important points. I do not want to interfere in any way with the hon. member's right to speak, but there is a practice which is common for Committees of the Whole and that I think we should follow in order to allow all hon. members of this House who want to table amendments to do so before supper so that we can see them, understand them and make a decision on each of those amendments.
The other point is this. I noticed that each time a member has the floor, the president of the Treasury Board takes 20 minutes, sometimes 15 minutes, to launch into a debate. He has been using this tactic since this morning. I think this is out of order.
Oh, oh!

Now listen. This is not in keeping with the usual practices of the committee of the whole. Standing Orders provide that each member has 20 minutes and the minister's answer must be included in this 20 minute period. What happened today, at least up to now, is that each time a member took the floor, the minister's answer was almost as long as the member's question. That way, fewer members will be able to participate. The minister will have to take into account the 20 minute constraint the way it used to be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member up to a point. The fact remains, I think, that when a member has the floor and wants to ask questions, he or she should keep in mind that there should be enough left for the minister to answer the question or questions. I can
understand the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier's point, but I think that, if a member speaks for 19 minutes and then asks 11 questions in a row, the minister cannot be expected to reply to all 11 questions in the minute that is left.
I think it is a matter of good will on the part of all members and I will remind the House again of the motion adopted earlier this afternoon to the effect that any amendment tabled with the Chair prior to 9:00 p.m. will be deemed proposed and be put without further debate at 10:00 p.m. Some hon. members may want to know about the contents of the amendments. So, all I had in mind when I suggested that we move on to other sections was to allow members who had made amendments to tell us about them in their speeches.
Resuming debate, on section 2 still. The hon. member for Laval-Est.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State and to Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I appreciate all the advice we have been given here today. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier has a lot of experience and I have great respect for him, but today's debate was on things people want to talk about, like their riding and the workers they represent.
I must begin, Madam Chairman, by saying that public servants are not found only in Ottawa. I heard members from the other side who represent the Ottawa area speak today. That is well and good, but there can't be public servants only in Ottawa. There must be some in Laval, in Abitibi, in Riviere-du-Loup, in Montreal.
So I was rather amazed to see how much those people had to say. I represent Laval, which has many civil servants. I must tell you that there are five prisons in my riding. These five prisons have many public servants. They are also workers who I think do an excellent job and are very unhappy about getting no increase. The only thing I can tell those people listening to us and who will read what I say is that I too am getting no raise. We are in the same boat. So what many people said is untrue, and I see the hon. member get up with a smile on her lips. She was the first to-I listened to the radio today; they were all public servants who called in and were asked whether they agreed with the strike. Certainly, they sometimes gave themselves away when they talked. They said that the government was stepping on them. That proves right
September 30, 1991

away that they are people who work as public servants. They were asked to answer the survey.
The hon. member even mentioned in some of her questions that MPs had voted themselves generous increases and then froze salaries. How many times have we heard that? How many times, and people believe it because someone said so.
Well, I would like to tell people that MPs here have gone backward, not forward, since 1984: they had an average annual increase of 2.9 per cent compared to inflation of 4.3 per cent.
Those of us who have been here since 1984 and made the calculations, taking into account the cost of living and the increases received, have found that the loss in salary is $7,000. But that is alright, we are just members of Parliament. I know many people will be delighted to hear that. As I stated in an radio interview this afternoon: "The listemers will be happy to hear that members of Parliament, ministers and even the Prime Minister are affected by the wage freeze. Figure that, we are all in the same boat."
I heard horror stories today, Madam Chairman. People come to see us at our offices and tell us: "We want to work." Some people are on strike, and they have the right to be. But others are not and want to go to work but are being prevented.
Day in and day out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Day in and day out, they are threatened. I was talking earlier, outside, to a fellow whose wife was threatened when she showed up for work. "Should she go in tomorrow? he asked me." My answer was: "Let her go to work tomorrow. I will escort her myself." Imagine, threatening people because they want to go to work!
The funny part of it Madam Chairman, is that people come to us and say: "I used to work for Air Canada, but I lost my job. I would certainly take a zero per cent increase."
Others worked for Canadian or other airlines and lost their jobs. They tell us: "I would sign a ten-year contract at zero per cent, just to have a job." That is when it dawned on me, Madam Chairman.
I have been in politics since 1984 and meet people at my office all the time, like everyone else.

Day in day out!
Government Orders

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
When they came to us. I ask them:"What can I do for you?" A common answer is: "I want a job, but I want to work for the federal, provincial or municipal government." Why? "Because I want job security." That is when it dawned on me that it is not so much a job that they want, but rather a position, a place where they are safe. That is what they are after, because they know that when you work for the government, there may be a zero per cent wage increase, but there is job security and many other marginal benefits.
So, people want two things: some want to go to work and others want a position. The concept of jobs seems to have disappeared. Yet, in my riding, people do want jobs and would be ready to accept increases below zero per cent to get one.
Remember what happened in Quebec. When I hear the Bloc on the other side say outside now, and the member for Hull, who is with the Bloc, whose leader cut Quebec public servants not 0, not 5, not 10, not 15, but 20 per cent. Today they are in bed together. They sit next to each other holding hands and embracing. Fine press conferences together. But do they really take the people for fools?
The member for Hull says anything, anywhere in any way, although public servants had their pay cut by 20 per cent.
He is not here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
He is not here? He will be back soon.
So, Madam Chairman, many people here today are talking in favour of the public servants, but I think it has much more to do with vote getting. Everyone wants to protect his own bailiwick, especially the members from Ottawa.
Today, I listened to an open-line radio show, just to find out. Of maybe 37 calls, 36 came from public servants, who were asked whether they agreed with the strike. They said, "Of course. The government is squeezing us. The Treasury Board President lied to us." However, if anyone behaved correctly, it was the Treasury Board President. The minister accepted everything. He put the bill on hold. He agreed with the NDP. He agreed with the Liberals. They agreed. There was a chance it might work. It did not. Now, what do we see on television-unfortunately, I saw it too-violence. I saw Daryl Bean say that there would be violence. He was the first to break down the door at the entrance here, even

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
though it is not his property. Daryl Bean used to be a mechanic. It hurts me to see people like that.
In my riding, for example, residents of Laval called us and still call us every day to say, "Send a message to the President of Treasury Board. Tell him not to give up and to maintain order." They have a good job. It is true that they deserve more; we also deserve more here. Everyone deserves more. But where will you get the money? There is no more money. The bag is empty. It is finished.
So what must we tell people? Be glad we saved 6,000 jobs. Air Canada employees in Laval would have liked to keep their jobs. They liked their jobs.
I see people who are glad that MPs' salaries were finally frozen. I told my son to take my MP card and to tell the director that I was a member of Parliament and that my salary had been frozen. But my son had to pay $1,500 nevertheless. I do not know if the director misunderstood him, or if he does not like members of Parliament, but my son, who is attending the University of Montreal, must pay $1,500 and not $500. It happened that my salary had been frozen too. That is most unpleasant. Such a freeze is not pleasant for the Public Service, and it is not pleasant for me neither.
That is not pleasant to see violence. I have organized strikes myself and I use it to put the baseball bats under the truck. There is always room for negotiation.
I would ask my colleague from Toronto, who has some lessons to teach me, to cool down. And I would suggest to him to go outside to calm down the civil servants instead of boosting them up because you are the one who are boosting them up instead of telling them the truth. Go and tell them to calm down. They have a good job and they should stick to it. It is not a job, it is a position. They have all the job security in the world!
They were negotiating and the President of the Treasury Board made a generous offer to them. Mr. Bean, whe should be called "Uncle Bean", had saved face. Mr. Bean came along and then left the table, all of sudden, and we would be the ones who are dishonest? The civil servants say that the government is dishonest. Who left
the table first? Is it the government? No, it is them who quit first.
Let us talk about the poor hon. members! We hear nothing but falsities here. I see unkindness and falsities when I hear those Hon. members say here that we have voted -And they give, as an example, the $80,000 bonuses! But they did not mention that those people had seen their salaries cut by 15 per cent, so that we could be in a position to give them bonuses if they were doing a good job.
I have always been with the private sector and I suggest that a man who works hard deserves a bonus. I am not against bonuses. But even the bonuses were frozen, as the minister has explained once more this afternoon. He said that it was a zero freeze for everybody. There will be no bonuses!
I have seen some extraordinary things since this morning. I heard civil servants repeat again and again that it was the government's fault. The opposition did such a good job at that, and I include the Bloc Quebecois, that if the Montreal stadium is falling part, it is Mulroney's fault there too. It is not him who sold the cement! I know who sold the cement to build the stadium, and it is not Brian Mulroney.
For some of my colleagues, it is always the fault of the poor guy who tries to fix up the mess you left us with. Somebody said, this afternoon, that we should have fixed that problem after 7 years of government. But the mess is so big that it will take more than 7 years to straighten things up, it will take another 20 years before we can pay up the debts we have inherited from you. Seven years is not long enough! The interest rates were so high- they had reached 13.5 per cent. You have not been in business much! Personally I have been in business for 25 years. Management is important.
I was talking about essential services. What is this nonsense about essential services? Who gives essential services? It is a joke. Let's go and see in the hospitals if they give you essential services. Let Mr. Bean go and see if his brother or his father were there! He would see what services are not provided to our senior citizens. Where are essential services for those who are in need? Nails have been thrown on the ground, people have been beaten, and pushed, essential services are provided- It is utter nonsense! There is no such thing as essential services. They tell people if you go back to work your
September 30, 1991

name will go up on the wall and next week we will give you a wallopping. I am looking forward to seeing these people. I cannot wait for the names to be out. Some people have the right to strike, others have the right to work, because their heart is still in their work.
Back home, we often heard people say: we were called- I do not know if they go to work, but send them back to work. The least we could do is send them back to the office! You know what people say: I am sorry you had to hit them with a law- You can take a horse to water but you cannot make it drink. But at least we are going to try. We are going to keep them from in front of the offices, because they are bothering those who still want to work, who still take their work to heart. I know some people in my riding office who give 110 per cent to their work. They come in at 5 a.m. to help our people. Those people want to work, let them be! If you do not want to work, step aside, stay on the grass, the weather is fine, Indian summer will be here soon. But these people say: Tell the minister to push, not to draw back, we are behind him. They say everyone is in favour of this strike, and that is not true. They will not shoot at each other. Come on! They have not reached such an extreme. But they shot themselves in the foot when they quit the bargaining table.
As the minister explained it so well this afternoon, they have settled for a freeze of zero per cent in Nova Scotia. That freeze has been ruled. In the Province of Quebec, a few years ago, the chief of the Bloc Quebecois settled once for 20 per cent less than what we can offer. Wage settlement has been less than 2 per cent in Saskatchewan, it is zero in Manitoba; and it is zero per cent for six months and less than 3 per cent for 1992 in Quebec. It has been zero per cent in Newfoundland, zero per cent in New Brunswick, and a limitation has been imposed upon wage increases in British Columbia. That is to say that some people understood before we did that that policy was necessary. Everybody has abided by the agreement and everybody is treated equally. You think that the unemployment rate is only-
Earlier today, I was looking at some information with my colleague from Abitibi, who said that in his riding, the unemployment figure is 12 per cent; it is 13.1 per cent in Lac-Saint-Jean and 14.8 per cent in Gaspe and we are talking at ways to go through some difficult times as far
Government Orders
as unemployment rates are concerned. There are eight areas; we find that one region, among others, has been hit for quite a while, and that is the important region of Montreal and Laval.
My colleague from Saint-Leonard is always making references to Montreal, but he never talks about Laval. He did not say that Laval sits just next to Montreal. There are always some windfalls, either economically positive or negative, but Montreal is often mentioned as the area. But when we talk about Montreal, as does my colleague, we must include Laval. It is true that we have gumption in Laval, and that we do not have the NPD style, that is to hate money and love the guy. We like everything, and if the guy has some money to invest at home, he is very much welcome. We have an extraordinary and enterprising mayor, and we are on the go!
There are some people in Montreal that do not see business that way! There has been some problems. My colleague from Saint-Leonard submitted to us a whole list of problems. He quoted every articles on that subject that has been published for the last six months. He did a good job at it since he told the truth, but he forgot conviently to mention the Merck Frosst Project. He did not mention that article, since it is positive news on a 300 job and $300 million project. He has also mentioned refineries. He said that four refineries closed their doors in Montreal. We are not responsible for the dismantling of those refineries. It is Marc Lalonde's policy, his Energy Program that did it. He closed 11 refineries in Canada, including the four plants located in Montreal. Things cannot go well with such a policy. It is obvious that they will be a little worst.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I rise on a point of order. You may remember earlier this day we passed a motion to set in place a somewhat different way of proceeding in Committee of the Whole to allow every member of the House the opportunity to make sure that any amendments they had for this piece of legislation would be put to the House before the close of business this day and have a chance to be voted on.
Because it is 6.30 p.m. and we are still on Clause 2, there have been discussions and I think you would find a predisposition, Madam Chairman, to next recognize the member of the Official Opposition who would be in a position to explain to the House a series of amendments which have or will be tabled with the Table shortly so that they are available to all members. There would be some explanation of that, followed by a representative of the New Democratic Party who would do likewise for its amendments.
There may be other members of the House who have tabled amendments and would like to explain them. We could conclude with the President of the Treasury Board who could explain his amendments and respond to any of the others that he chose to at that point. Then I think we would be in a position to move through clause 3, clause 4, and sort of speed it up a little. Hopefully members would then be disciplined in their questions and their responses to the clauses under consideration.
From that point on, those who had more general comments to make on clause 2 might find that opportunity as early as tomorrow on third reading stage. It might be more appropriate for 20-minute speeches to take place at that point and enable us to be targeted between now and seven o'clock, more specifically on proposals for amendment that could come from anywhere in the House.
I think that predisposition exists.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Madam Chairman, I would like to confirm that indeed there were discussions before the vote. It was agreed that a member from each party would introduce various amendments, as well as any other member who would wish to do so, in order that we can continue the debate and explain all of the amendments before 10 o'clock.

There were discussions and the proposal as put by the government Whip is acceptable to the NDP caucus.
I might say it is an unusual procedure, but I think it responds to an unusual situation, and for that matter an unusual interpretation of the motion which was adopted by unanimous consent earlier today.
Some of us thought at that time that it was simply a way of dealing with amendments which might not have had the opportunity to be moved from the floor, but the government had a different understanding. It has met the problem with that understanding by consenting to this particular arrangement, and I thank it for that because it will give everybody an opportunity to say what amendments they have tabled and why.

I think, given the limit on time for debate, it is relatively important that for the rest of our discussions in Committee of the Whole all members be aware of amendments that have been or will be tabled.
I would therefore like to move the following amendments in addition to the one already moved to clause 2. The first of those amendments would be, and I move:
That Clause 3 of Bill C-29 be amended by adding immediately
after line 31 on page 3 the following:
(e) persons engaged as independent contractors.
What this does is ensure that people engaged from outside the Public Service to perform work for the Public Service of Canada are treated exactly the same as those employed within the Public Service.
We in the Official Opposition see no reason for limiting employees of the government, whether term employees or continuing employees, to no salary increase for a year and only 3 per cent for the following year and for providing preferential treatment to persons engaged as independent contractors performing the same work. If the government were serious about fiscal restraint then surely that fiscal restraint applies to people hired from outside to perform the same work.
September 30, 1991

This offers opportunity for even more savings because independent contractors constitute a larger amount of spending at $5 billion than the entire payroll of the Public Service Alliance of Canada with which the government is now in dispute.
With respect to my next amendment, hon. members might wish to insert my proposed new clause 5 immediately after line 2 on page 4, following clause 4 and before the existing clause 5 of Bill C-29. The proposed clause 5 now deals with pay equity and reads as follows. I move:
That Bill C-29 be amended by adding after line 2 on page 4 the following:
5.	(a) Forthwith on the coming into force of this act
(i)	Treasury Board shall revise the classification system to incorporate fully into pay scales the compensation now paid to certain employees and groups of employees as equalization payments in respect of pay equity;
(ii)	Treasury Board will cease all actions before the Human Rights Commission in opposition to the Commission's ruling on any matter related to equal pay for work of equal value.
(b) One year after the coming into force of this Act, the Treasury Board shall revise classifications as necessary to implement full pay equity as agreed to between the Treasury Board and bargaining agents for the employee.
(c) For any employee or group of employees for which the Treasury Board and the bargaining agents have not been able to reach agreement pursuant to section 5(b) on new classifications to implement equitable pay scales, all disputes will be deemed immediately referred to the Human Rights Commission for binding resolution.
To put in simple terms what this accomplishes, it takes an archaic provision whereby the government provides token payments to female dominated groups of employees in lieu of fully equivalent salary. They are token payments. Equalization payments are not pay equity. Only pay incorporated in the salary scale is pay equity.
With respect to the amounts required to implement that, the amount available for pay equity is already being paid in equalization payments. It could just as easily be incorporated for the same amount into salary scales, and
Government Orders
one of the conciliation board reports has already determined that the government has set aside money for that.
This further provides that full pay equity will be implemented within one year after the coming into force of this act for a number of groups and employees for which pay equity is in dispute. After 14 years, it seems to me it is time to do that.
This amendment is put forward because the bill specifically contains provisions to allow for the implementation into the classifications of pay equity. This is an amendment to those provisions, but more from the point of view that the Official Opposition does not believe that pay equity is negotiable. It is the law. It is a right. It is not an item to be negotiated against any other consideration.
The fourth amendment I put forward is:
That Bill C-29 be amended by deleting everything after line 3 on page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
Forthwith, on the coming into force of this act, the chair of the Public Service Staff Relations Board shall name a mediator acceptable to both parties who will endeavour to mediate all matters referred to the mediator and to bring about agreement between the parties;
6.	The Chair shall refer to the mediator all matters relating to the compensation plan for any employee or group of employees covered by this act which has expired and for which no new compensation plan has been established.
7.	The mediator shall report to the chair on the resolution of all such matters on the date fixed by the board.
The effect of this amendment is to delete all the provisions of this act relating to the imposition of a wage freeze and wage controls and to delete all provisions of the act that suspend collective bargaining rights for employees of the Government of Canada.
It is also to substitute for those provisions the establishment of a mediation process to lead to the resolution of all matters in dispute.
The fifth amendment is:
That Bill C-29 be amended in clause 7 on page 4 by deleting line 33 and substituting the following therefor:
What this does is change a provision that the Canadian Human Rights Act, as it might apply to any of the provisions of this act, is superseded by or, in the words of the bill, "subject to the act".

That line 33 on page 4, be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
Rights Act, the terms
Therefore, deleting the part which would subject the Canadian Human Rights Act to this bill once enacted.
Motion No. 6 refers to clause 8, on page 5.
That Bill C-29 be amended in clause 8, by deleting line 42 on page 5 and substituting the following therefor:
award, including wage rates and other terms.
What this does is amend clause 8, which prevents any provisions relating to wage rates or conditions of compensation being included in any agreement that may be reached by arbitration or collective agreement. We believe that wage rates and other terms should be arbitrable or subject to collective bargaining.
The seventh amendment and second last, refers to clause 10, page 6. The amendment is:
That Bill C-29 be amended in clause 10 by deleting lines 20 through 42 on page 6, and substituting the following therefor:
10(a) by such amounts as are agreed upon by the parties as a result of collective bargaining.
What that does is take out an imposed settlement and allows for the possibility of compensation plans being implemented that are reached as a result of collective bargaining.
The final amendment I propose:

11(1) The previous compensation plan and wage rates may be adjusted by such amounts as are agreed upon by the parties as a result of collective bargaining and any wage rates so adjusted shall
The effect of that is to allow for the inclusion of compensation as agreed to in collective bargaining in collective agreements.
I table a copy of these amendments and commend them to the House. I particularly urge the government to look seriously at those clauses relating to pay equity and
to agree, after 14 years of a Human Rights Act in this country, that pay equity is not a bargaining chip.

That clause 9 be amended at line 5 on page 3 by striking the word "not" by an equal amount to the Canadian consumer, not at all. We are not prepared to legislate the Consumer Price Index. I have indicated that we have to fight this and make sure that we break the vicious circle which would carry us to higher deficits, higher taxes and higher debt. We are not prepared to accept that.
That clause 9 be amended at line 11 by striking the words "3 per cent", well this is a 3 per cent year and we will hold on to that.
Another item, that clause 9 be amended by the addition of a new subparagraph, I would say that this is a wage restraint bill, not a job security bill, which can be dealt with in the proper form which is the National Joint Council.
That clause 12 replaces the words "Treasury Board" with the word "Public Staff Relations Board", I beg to remind the hon. member that this is the employer. The Public Service Staff Relations Board is an adjudicative body which does not deal with matters such as the
enforcement of an act. Sometimes I wonder, I must say, but they are supposedly an adjudicative body.
Why don't you talk to the judge?

He said he wanted me to talk to them. I am not supposed to talk to a judge, you know. I did not. But everybody else has, it seems. I wonder.
On Clause 14, by inserting the words "being forced", this is not helpful and I do not think it would add anything to enforce penalties.
Again, Clause 25 is related to mediation. The effect of the last amendment on Clause 25 is beyond what is not in the agreement with what we are trying to achieve.

Mr. Chairman, these are roughly the amendments we are moving in an effort to tie up a number of loose ends in our bill. This is what I had to say about the proposals made by the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. Thank you.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I appreciate the comment made by the hon. member for Burlington, but having said this, it is nevertheless true that, since the beginning of our proceedings in committee of the Whole all hon. members dealing with clause 2 have taken this opportunity to deal with all the issues connected with that bill and I intend to keep the same flexibility and allow all hon. members to discuss clause 2 as well as any other features of the bill, when I recognize them in the House, if the House agrees. Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say on clause 2, and perhaps some other clauses of Bill C-29, an act respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada and to amend another act in relation thereto. That is the gentle characterization of what we are doing here today.
Government Orders
I suppose it is the nature of bill drafting that one has to be fairly innocuous or genteel in putting labels on those bills. I have no difficulty with that. But let us be aware that what the government seeks to do here today is more Draconian than talking about compensation in the public sector.
I listened with great interest to the gentleman from Laval Est-

-who just made a speech. The member for Laval-est said to this House: "We have nothing against those people", meaning the civil Servants who are now on strike. I would like to tell him this: What you say and what you do are two different things.

I want to say to the gentleman from Laval Est that his actions contradict what he is saying. We have an expression that says: "your actions speak louder than your words." It is not enough for him and others to stand in this Chamber and say: "We have nothing against those people," when every single action of the government, and those who toe the line over there, indicate clearly that it must have an awful lot against these people in the union, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, because how else, I say to him, can you explain the toying with them, the aggravation, the setting them up over the past few weeks?
My colleague and friend from Ottawa West raised the question today in Question Period on this very issue. She said in her first question that the government was much more concerned with its place in the polls, that these 160,000 people were pawns in a game.
If you look at the way the government has gone about this, it is a two-faced approach on this issue. The old "now you see it, now you do not" approach, the government changing the ground rules to suit its particular purpose at the time.
First, it told these employees there would be negotiations. Now it refuses to negotiate. First it said that salaries could go up, but it would mean job losses. Now it says zero increase and the job losses continue.
It is very difficult. It is always difficult to deal with a moving target. It is always very difficult when you have a government that places no stock at all in credibility, no

September 30,1991
Government Orders
stock in its word at all. To use the expression that is almost worn out, but still very revealing, a government that rolls the dice as it sees fit.
The sad result, of course, is that there are many thousands of people out there on strike in front of this building today, and countless other buildings, in Ottawa and the national capital region and across this country. Of course they are. I suppose, all of them, to a man, to a woman, do not particularly want to be there. That should come as no secret to anybody. They have been goaded into it by a government that does not care an awful lot about the pain or inconvenience it inflicts on people. It has goaded these people into this strike. It has been a contrived confrontation from the beginning.
I put it to you, Mr. Chairman, that this strategy was mapped out a long time ago. It was part of the contrivance, part of the plan, part of the way to grasp at straws, to hang on by the fingernails, to find a way for this government to redeem itself in the public eye, to play tough with a group of people, to go out there and show that there is going to be restraint, or else.
There is another side of this that needs to be put on to the record. I cannot get veiy excited about the way the government is handling this particular grievance. I heard some insinuations a few moments ago. At the same time, there is always the danger that because one criticizes one side one is thereby thought to be embracing all the actions of the other side.
I stand here representing about 85,000 or 86,000 Canadians who happen to live in the riding of Burin-St. Georges. Relatively few of those people, a mere handful of them actually, are involved as members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada. I suppose, on a per capita basis, I probably have fewer people in that union than almost any other member in this Chamber. My riding is a very rural riding of 158 communities. The largest communities have a population of are 7,000 or 8,000, communities like Stephenville and Marystown and Port aux Basques. However, most of them are much smaller communities of 50, 60 or 100 people. In those communities you will not find government services. I am not saying there is an absence of services, but there is an absence of a government installation. The services are usually delivered from outside the community, from
more urban centres such as St. John's or Comerbrook, or in some cases Stephenville or Halifax or Moncton or so on. On a per capita basis we do not have a lot of PSAC people.
But that is not the issue. Surely, members of this Chamber ought not to have their participation and debate determined on that basis alone. I also represent 86,000 people, including many thousands of taxpayers, who are going to be footing the bill for whatever settlement there is here. They are going to be putting up with whatever inconvenience or lack of service during the course of this strike.
As I have said, I do not have many of those members directly in my riding. I want to give an example, just to illustrate a point I think is important.
The point I alluded to just now is that because we criticize the government, do not, anybody, be under the illusion that somehow we embrace all the activities of PSAC on this.
For example, I do not at all embrace the way it has in a very partisan way tried to politicize the entire issue. I do not embrace that at all. I am sure that comes as no secret to many people in this Chamber.
There is something else that I do not at all subscribe to. I will give a specific example. My friend and colleague from Gander-Grand Falls has a community in his riding called Gander. I happen to go through that community to use the airport on a fairly frequent basis, last Friday afternoon being one of those occasions. It was just after the union had decided to go back on the picket lines.
I arrived just after a particular incident had taken place. I was not witness to this, so it is second-hand in this situation. I was informed about it by a person at the airport who did it mainly just to make conversation with me. We were passing time together, and that individual decided to tell me about this particular incident. I want to tell the committee, because it is revealing.
An elderly woman had approached the airport in a car as a passenger late in the afternoon, hours after the picket lines went up. She was a woman in her sixties. She was to take a flight from Gander to St. John's, a 25 or 30 minute flight, to have a CAT scan, a medical examination, for her particular medical problem.
September 30, 1991

Her case was known to the people on the picket line. Her age was known, it was obvious to see. Her circumstances were known. The importance of her getting to that airport to get that flight was known.
That woman was obliged to vacate the car in which she was travelling and walk for just about a mile, carrying her luggage, to get to the airport.
What point was served? If they wanted to do that to the President of the Treasury Board, make him walk a mile to get to the airport with a suitcase, I suppose it could be considered that they are aiming at the target.
What did that poor little old woman have to do with those people getting a settlement. I think we all know the answer.
I was talking a moment ago about this government engaging in a contrived confrontation. It is like an argument, it takes two. You cannot have a confrontation unless you have people on both sides willing to engage in the confrontation.
I have to say on this one in passing, before I get on to some of the other issues in this bill, that given the example I have just put before the committee, that woman approaching Gander airport last Friday, either the union leadership is not very bright, else it is just anchoring to get legislated back to work.
I do not believe for a fraction of a second that we have to embrace all the antics that are going on out there in the name of strike action. I would hope that the union leadership would smarten up and realize it is not those little old ladies I am talking about who are the brunt of its problem, but if it wants to take it out on this government, it has a duty and a right to do so. I will be there with it.
Let us come to some of the issues, because I just wanted to set the record straight on that one. It bothers me that some of the people out there are missing the real issue here. The real issue is to inconvenience the government. The real issue is to get the message home to the government.
I doubt the President of the Treasury Board even heard about that incident until I told him just this last minute, not that he should have, but I am just saying to the union that if it thought that woman, and she was mirrored many times across the country, was going to
Government Orders
bring the government to its knees, maybe it was mistaken on that one.
In this business everything is black or white. I suppose the reason I do not have a full bench of NDP members here is because they have all rushed out to call Daryl baby now, and get their latest instructions from him and tell him what little old Rog has said here in the Chamber about them. In the age of black and white, I suppose, I will now be blacklisted as a fellow who does not like unions.
I happen to like them very much. I just do not like some of their tactics. When they go interfering with the freedom of some senior citizen who wants nothing more than to get to a doctor on time, then it is time for them to have a little pow-wow and refocus on what their target is. I do not believe it is those people out there who are innocently suffering on account of some tactics of which I cannot believe for a second anybody in his or her right mind is actually approving.
I say to my NDP friends, while they are calling the union, maybe they could pass on a message or two. Maybe they could tell the union that yes, I, this member, supports pay equity. I happen to know people in my riding and people across the province of Newfoundland and Labrador and people across the country, carpenters and labourers, who are getting $4 less an hour than then-counterparts in Vancouver.
Here is a carpenter in Vancouver and he gets so much an hour for doing a job for the government. He is employed by the government, he is a civil servant, he is a member of PSAC and he is getting a certain wage in Vancouver. His counterpart in Newfoundland, doing the same thing, driving the same size nails, drawing out the same nails, squaring off the same board, using the same kind of a Skil saw, maybe wearing the same brand of overalls, is getting $4 less an hour.
What is the difference? Is the fellow in Newfoundland doing a sloppier job than the fellow in Vancouver? That is entirely possible, I suppose, because the law of averages says that you are going to have some sloppy carpenters in Newfoundland, some sloppy ones in Vancouver. You would not mind if they were paying the sloppy ones $4 less. All the carpenters in Newfoundland who work as members of the PSAC union for the government are getting that rate. What is their sin? Is

September 30,1991
Government Orders
their sin that they are sloppy, as opposed to competent? No, no, oh, no. Their sin is that they are living in Newfoundland instead of in Vancouver.
You talk about discrimination. This government is paying a carpenter in Newfoundland $4 less an hour than if that same carpenter were in Vancouver.
To extend the example, this government pays the carpenter in Newfoundland $2 less than his counterpart in Ontario. You do not need a strike. You do not need negotiations to tell you that fair is fair. This government says to women librarians that because they are women it is going to pay them several thousand dollars less. It is happening right in this city to librarians.
Again I make the point: it is not on the basis of whether they are sloppy or incompetent or thorough or experienced or a novice. Oh, no, none of the above. The only question in effect is: are you a women or are you a man? If you are a woman you get paid several thousand dollars less a year than if you were a man.
We do not need strikes. We do not need collective agreements. We do not need negotiations to settle those questions. These were settled in the minds and hearts of Canadians many, many years ago. That is addressed in one of the amendments put forward by my colleague from Ottawa West. Take those things off the table. Pay equity should not even be a negotiable item. That should be a given. The government will now say it as it should have said a long time ago, and oh, yes, it said it, the Prime Minister has said it many times. Like so many other things, he has not exactly put his money where his mouth is.
Let the government say now that it recognizes its error on this. It is not a matter for negotiation that a carpenter in Newfoundland should be paid less than one in Vancouver; that a woman librarian in Ottawa or wherever should be paid thousands of dollars less than a male librarian. That is disgusting, it is absolutely disgraceful. It is unthinkable.
Let us not get these things wrapped up in government's ability to pay. When we get to the stage in this country at which we have a government that can justify discrimination on the basis of the pocketbook, can justify using the public purse to discriminate against people because they happen to be female or happen to be living in one part of the country or another, it is time for
somebody over there to smarten up. This has nothing to do with Tory politics or right wing politics. Certainly, lowering the agenda is not that right wing. It cannot be. That has to do more with basic insensitivity, basic stupidity.
Does the President of the Treasury Board not actually have some women in his riding who voted for him at one time. Surely, he is not expecting them to vote for him again if he keeps up this nonsense.
Does he not have some carpenters, some labourers in his riding who are getting less money than they would if they were living in some other province in Canada?
If the minister had nothing going for him, only an instinct for survival, forget looking after the deficit and all the other things he is worrying about these days, if he only has an instinct for survival, an instinct to stay alive, he should rush out there and cure this one, this pay equity issue. This has nothing to do with negotiating. When you have to negotiate something like this, it shows how out of touch with reality you really are.
There are so many more things I could say about this bill, given the time. I see by the signal that my time is up. Perhaps I will get another crack at it later in the evening.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to congratulate-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Did you have your dinner?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
No, not yet, I am still waiting for my three limousines!
September 30, 1991

I would like to congratulate my colleague from Burin-St. George's for his remarkable performance in French. I was quite impressed when he started his remarks by answering a question from my colleague from Laval, and I invite him to do so more often. He did extremely well, indeed. He reminded us that the hon. member for Laval said we have nothing against these people, meaning public servants. In French, he said: What you say and what you do are two different things. I understand, of course, that a 0 per cent increase or a salary freeze, is not, on the face of it, the most pleasant way to tell our employees we greatly appreciate their work. That is the reason why, as the months went by, I took so much time, as did the government, to explain to our employees that was one of many measures we had to take, a difficult, painful, but still necessary decision to make. The hon. member said we have tried since the beginning-

He said it was a contrived confrontation that we had been seeking for political purposes to confront the unions. I will tell him that if one were to look at what other Liberal governments have done this year in other provinces, they have not taken the decision we have to sit down and negotiate. They have just legislated zero per cent. We chose to try and make an effort to improve it.
He said: "You have been shifting the ground rules or changing the ground rules by saying first it will be three and then it will be zero. In February, what we said was that the wage budget would remain at zero, but if we could soon enough come to some agreement where we could balance 1 per cent against 2,000 positions, we could give 1 and then 2 and then 3 per cent. It would be a very high cost. This was not considered by the union. When we sat down, and June came, it was too late. We could not find a saving within the wage budget to proceed this way. We have been, I think, very fair and very consistent. We did not change the rules.
He mentioned a lot about pay equity. I wonder where the members of that party were over the last decade. We are the government which decided in 1990 to give $370 million, in a lump sum payment, for pay equity. We have also agreed to pay, on an ongoing basis, $81 million to
Government Orders
allow for catching up. We are not only talking about pay equity as they do, but we are acting. I would certainly compare our record to that of the Liberal Party any time.
He also refers to regional pay. He said it was unfair to pay carpenters in his riding less than what is paid in Toronto or in other provinces in Canada. We have a policy, in certain areas of regional pay, which seems to be fair. I do not see why the Canadian government, which gets its money from the taxpayer, should create a totally unfair competition at the regional level. We try to follow the market pressure in each area and react accordingly.
This, in my view, seems fair because we have to compete with others in that particular area. We do it, I think, as a way of managing well. This is a fair and accepted way.
On the whole, I would like to repeat in closing, we have not chosen confrontation. Far from it. We have chosen negotiation. It is sad that finally the union, as it said the day before the budget: "We are never going to accept this if they so decide to freeze our wages. We are going to go on strike," and they said: "This is a political strike."
It is their problem. For us it is not a political decision. It is a good sound fiscal decision we have taken.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a couple of words for the minister. I could not help but interject after the minister stated a moment ago that it is okay to pay people in the Public Service less in the province of Newfoundland, for example, or Nova Scotia, or New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island than people are paid in a similar job in other parts of Canada.
In other words, what the minister has just said is that one's wage rate should depend upon where one works, that is, in what province one works. That is quite a statement from the President of the Treasury Board. The President of the Treasury Board speaks on behalf of the government for all policies relating to wages.
In other words, does it mean that the Government of Canada now is trying to pay secretarial staff, clerks, radio announcers with the CBC, who are in competition with private radio, clerks who work for the federal government, who are in competition with clerks in the private sector, secretarial staff, managers, all of our profession-

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
als what it figures is the going rate in that particular province?
That is totally unacceptable. That is discrimination of the worst kind. That is discrimination depending upon where one lives, where the border is. I notice in section 7 of the bill it refers to work-sharing agreements approved under the Unemployment Insurance Act. Right now under this government you collect unemployment insurance depending upon where you live, not where you work. In other words, you take the government's policy and depending on where you work, that is the sole determinant of how much money you get.
Then when you leave your place of work and you go home to draw unemployment insurance, it depends on where you live, where you take up residence, as to whether or not you qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. In some places it is 10 weeks, other places it is 14 weeks, other places it is 20 weeks, and so on.
It is an outrageous form of discrimination, Mr. Chairman, and the minister just verified it. He said that it is only fair to the private sector in the places affected. I want to remind the minister that some of these employees qualify because they live in those same areas for environmental bonuses, or what is commonly referred to as isolation pay. Why? Because they are living in an area in which the cost of living is higher than if they were living in another area where the cost of living would not be so high.
On the one hand the minister turned around and said in this Chamber a few moments ago that they are going to pay carpenters less if they live in Newfoundland than if they lived in some other province, they are going to pay pipe fitters because they do less if they live in Newfoundland than if they live in some other province in Canada, they are going to pay tractor operators less if they live in Newfoundland-oh, no, work in Newfoundland. Excuse me because it is not where you live. It is where you work which is the sole determinant of how much money you make.
I bring up this point simply to point out that this is one of the things that has demoralized people in the Public Service. You wonder why somebody would willingly go out on a picket line and remove their income from their family. It has to be pretty important to these people to
say: "I am going to give up a day's work, or week's work now. I am going to give that up and I am going to have it docked on my next pay cheque". They are being docked on their next pay cheque for the days they were out on the picket line in September. Why would you want, in this day and age, in this country, to lose a week's pay?
The reason for it is because of the demoralization of the Public Service. This is one of the things the minister just said a moment ago and it is enough to make you angry. Regional rates of pay, he says, are okay. You live in Newfoundland, he says you should get paid less for doing the same job than if you lived in the province of Quebec.
What an outrageous statement for the President of the Treasury Board to make on behalf of the Government of Canada. What an outrageous statement for the minister to make.
It is not only that why people go out on strike and sometimes do things they should not really do. The other part of the story is connected with the way the government has treated these employees. After this period is over, this bill will re-enact the same types of agreements, same wage scales, same rapport they had with union members prior to this legislation.
Three years ago the Government of Canada brought in a system under the orders of the President of the Treasury Board to get rid of employees in the Public Service. When you make a decision to get rid of employees in the Public Service, the people who get hit the worst are of course people who live the furthest down the line. They are the first ones to go.
We had upper management in the Public Service being paid money called "productivity bonuses" to get rid of employees in the Public Service. How would that make you feel?
Here you are, sitting in an office in Grand Falls, Newfoundland, sitting in an office in Gander, Newfoundland, or in St. John's, Newfoundland and you know that this President of the Treasury Board has approved a system whereby certain managers along the way will get bonuses if they meet the government's guidelines of getting rid of person years in the Public Service, because that is what was in effect.
September 30, 1991

In other words, you had one manager ordering other managers to get rid of employees so that he could get his bonus. Then, further down the line, you had managers wondering whether a manager above them was ordering him to be got rid of so he could get an extra bonus.
In other words, you had everybody looking back over their shoulder wondering who was getting paid off to get rid of you. What a system to be living under. The President of the Treasury Board could rightly be called the terminator because he was terminating people by giving bonuses to upper management in the Public Service.
That certainly is not a very good working environment for people in the Public Service. Here they are now, some of them, getting less pay than people in other provinces, and the President of the Treasury Board stands up here tonight and says: "That is the proper thing to do. You should get less pay because you live in the province of Newfoundland, or Nova Scotia".
If you lived in Quebec or Ontario, you would get higher wages. If you lived in British Columbia, you would get higher wages still. That is what the President of the Treasury Board just said.
On top of that, a system of pay-offs for lay-offs in the Public Service. We can understand why the Public Service has been totally demoralized and why the public of Canada are the real losers, because public service to the people of Canada has gone downhill ever since this government took office.
They stand in this Chamber and they say once a year: "Here is a report from this auditing firm saying that it takes two days for a letter to get from one province to another." Canadians are sitting out there and wondering why it takes their letter two weeks to get there. Of course, the reason is that the things that they are judging are only the letters that are pumped out of a computer or a typewriter and have the address exactly in the centre of a letter so it can be read by a machine.
The grandmother who sits down and writes a letter to her granddaughter at university somewhere writes it. She does not type it. The letter takes two weeks to get there, or three weeks. A Christmas present takes a year sometimes. We come across these cases.
Government Orders
People applying to universities, and their student loans going between one province and another. Every member of Parliament has cases now of the mail not arriving at all because public service to the people of Canada under this President of the Treasury Board and under this Government of Canada has gone downhill. Service to the people of Canada has been substantially reduced because the Government of Canada will not treat its public servants properly.
It is not very good to be working in a job today and not know when you are going to lose it or when some manager somewhere is getting a Christmas bonus to take your job away, and wondering why you are making less than somebody in another province and why the President of the Treasury Board stood up here tonight and said: "That is great. That is fine. We are in total agreement with it." Shame on the President of the Treasury Board.
I want to ask him one question. I want to just get this straight on this bonus business that was brought up recently. I just want to get it straight. He can stand up and say yes, that is correct, or no, it is not correct.
If I understand him correctly, what he has said is this: There are really three types, of bonuses. One is a performance pay by managers in the Public Service. Of the 4,700 managers in the Public Service, 97 per cent of them qualified for performance pay this past year. Now, that is one type of performance pay. That runs from 3 per cent to 10 per cent, as I understand it, Mr. President of the Treasury Board through you, Mr. Chairman. Now, that is one type of bonus, which is really a part of, as the President of the Treasury Board explained in the House, the salary. The President of the Treasury Board said that that was negotiated years ago and about 15 per cent was taken off of their range of the salary scale and that amount of money which would have been spent anyway was being used as performance pay for management in the Public Service. That is the massive number-4,600 public servants. That is one group.
Then there is another group which involves Crown corporations, people who sit on boards and commissions; in other words, mostly Order in Council appointments. In fact all of them are. That is a completely separate group now from the public servants. If the minister understands me correctly, am I to understand that the bonuses for both those groups will be removed from April 1,1991 to March 31, 1992, for that working period? Did I understand him correctly when he stood up in the

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
House that that is what he said? Is that correct, I am wondering, Mr. Chairman? Is that correct, or is it not correct? If it is correct, it is oui, it is yes, and that will settle it.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Yes, exactly. The hon. member talked a lot about the performance pay, and he said that I had decided that people who work in Newfoundland would get less. Not at all; they may get more, for all I know. What we say is that we try to adjust a certain number of our categories of employees, a very small number in all, if I may say so. Because out of a quarter of a million employees there are 26,000 to whom these regional pays apply, in nine occupational groups. This policy which, from listening to the comments of the hon. member sounds so horrible, must not be so horrible because it was implemented by the Liberal government.
If I may go on and explain why we maintain this. First of all, when there are occupational groups for whom the outside pay data indicates significant regional variation from the Canadian average, this is taken into account. Where you have occupational groups where the area of recruitment and the mobility of employees in the Public Service is limited, and when occupational groups for which regional rates would contribute to the achievement of fair and competitive rates of pay in the labour market, these are the elements on which we base our decision. In my view this is a fair approach.
On another aspect of the issues raised by the hon. member, he said that since we arrived in power the
service has gone downhill. I would like to remind him that when we came to power, for every dollar that Canadians were paying in taxes, the Liberal government was spending $1.33.
They were playing at being Father Christmas, which is all right for a while, but obviously, at one time or another, one has to face this reality and one has to act accordingly and try to bring one's expenditure within one's capacity to pay.
This is what we have been trying to do, I must admit with great difficulty. The opposition has opposed every one of our proposals to try to bring our fiscal situation to a better position.
Basically, we are trying to improve service, to find new ways of providing services, and to use the best possible methods. I think that we should be commended for this. In the reform program I introduced in the House, PS 2000, it says that people are looking behind their backs at the bosses, and so on. This is what we are trying to change. We want to empower people and allow them in the regions to get on with the job, find good people, help them get the best training, and then let them get on and not have Ottawa on their back all the time.
This is what we are trying to do because we find it is a good way of using our good employees.

speechtext:

He talks about NATO. It is always a difficult and costly operation to make such a transformation. So I do not think there is any savings there to be accomplished.
We have already indicated otherwise that we are proceeding with some changes in Europe and they will be dealt with as expeditiously as possible. We can say that they have already been booked and provided for.
As for the Department of National Revenue, we have, indeed, granted additional persons to tighten up and make sure that there is a better enforcement. But I would also like to remind him that members of his party have been getting up, over the last little while, talking to us about bankruptcies. Much of the reasons why we have this income tax which is theoretically due, but cannot be easily collected, is because of that. This is an impact when companies or individuals are in difficulty and cannot meet their obligations. So we have granted additional human resources and a budget to do that.
I would say that in the bill that will be introduced, if it has not been done so by my colleague, the Minister of Finance, on the spending limits, we make provisions for spending which brings in additional revenue. We will certainly look at that as one way possibly, but again I would say that we have tried to have as efficient an organization as possible. We tried to improve enforcement, but this is an end of a recession and of course it is not always easy to collect all the money which is owed the government.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I heard this from the NDP source, large corporations are running away. They fail to recognize that this government is the one that imposed a minimal tax on capital, which had never been done before. We have closed about 200 different loopholes which existed. So we have done our share.
As for the number of corporations or so-called companies, most of them are small companies that are marginally profitable and have great difficulty carrying on. We can put the pressure on them and have more of them go into bankruptcy.
The banks and the financial institutions for the first time have a minimal tax on assets. This brings in $2 billion. It was not there when we came in. We have not been giving any gifts. The hon. member mentioned, and it is frequently heard, high dollars.
One of the reasons we want to tackle the deficit and the debt, and it is not that it is fun per se, is because it is one of the major causes of the high dollar. We are all borrowing heavily.
The provinces, in the first six months of 1990, have gone on foreign markets and have borrowed $10 billion in foreign currency. This currency, in turn, is changed into Canadian dollars and so there is a huge demand for Canadian dollars and the price goes up. This is the reality of it.
It is very interesting. You can sit down, not invest in a company, buy government certificates and go sit in Florida. We want to change that. We want to make room for entrepreneurs. We can find cheaper money.
This is why we want to fight the debt and the deficit, not for the fun of it, but because it is central to the well-being of Canadians and a sound economic policy is necessary. It is tough because we get requests from the NDP to spend, spend, spend.

(3)	Is this another escape clause for the government to help its friends?
(4)	Does this mean after this legislation is passed the minister might cherry-pick his way through and lift this legislation for some, maybe for department heads, or deputy ministers or some other group the minister favours?
Those are the questions that will have been placed on the table and will be provided to the minister to which certainly we crave answers, answers to which in our submission all Canadians are entitled.
It is unfortunate that such answers will not be forthcoming prior to the final consideration of this bill by this House, because the answers might, just might, cause some of the members in this House to rethink their opinions with regard to this bill. It is a long shot, but as a New Democrat from Alberta I am used to long shots.
Before sitting down, which I know is the event at this point most hon. members are having the greatest hope for this evening, I would like to point out just two things. First, even allowing that this bill is obscenely unfair on the face of it, there are provisions within it that render it obscenely unfair squared, raised to the second power. I refer specifically to subclauses 7(2) and 3(4).
These clauses together allow the government at whim to exempt virtually anyone it chooses, any group of people, any area of the Public Service, any individual.
The government clearly has no intention of achieving fairness even in the application of this odious bill.
