speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I rise here to speak to this back-to-work legislation. I fear I do not have the knowledge of clauses in the bill that my predecessor has. However, I must say that it is not the clauses that bother me as much as the whole bill and the politics behind the bill.
This is not a bill based on rules. This is the Conservative philosophy of politics based on power, sheer power over who is going to do what, who is going to listen to whom, and who is going to be the patsy. I think about the poor person who will bear the brunt of this government's terrible legislation.
I would venture to say that it is not going to be this government's and I say Conservatives' powerful friends, absolutely not. They would have us believe that this is a bill to fight the deficit. Maybe it will fight the deficit, but it is not really about fighting the deficit. It is about who is going to pay the price. That is what this is all about.
How can they talk about controlling the deficit? On the one hand they have money to pour into the Spicer commission that travelled the country first class. I mean, hey, these were all friends of the government; this is fine, there is no problem, expense has no limits. Do you want to live in a first-class hotel? Who are we to question? You are working for the Conservative government, the holiest of holies.
On the other hand, you have the poor typist over there. Well, I am sorry, you cannot have an increase because we have no money; we are so pure and we do not spend money on ourselves.
September 30, 1991

"Forget the fact that the day before the budget we voted bonuses and pay increases for our top management. I mean that was last year and they were our friends. We have to look after our friends." This is about power, let nobody forget this. It is about power. I have no illusions because power knows no rules. When you are in power and when you want to have the upper hand and you have it, you do what you want when you want. It has nothing to do with people. Rules have to do with people.
Where are the rules in this one? You have a budget and you announce 0 per cent, 3 per cent and 3 per cent, and we are a perfection. You go to your backbenchers and you say: "You know we have to fight the deficit." I have to tell you that in my previous occupation I understood about deficits, yes, and I commend you in your fight for the deficit. I believe that we have to control the deficit, but not at the expense of the poorest of the poor, of the lowest wage earners. Come on now. If you had led by example, I would have been the first one to say what great people you were. That is the worst mistake of all. How can we go to these people and say to them: "I am sorry, we have no money for you. We have money for everybody else and we have had money for everybody else." All of a sudden, notice there is an election in B.C.: "We have money for the KAON TRIUMF project, don't we." Do we have money for that KAON project?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Sure we did. Now we are going to move something to Saskatchewan, there is an election there.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Oh, that is a coincidence.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Coincidence, purely coincidence. We have money for those things and I expect that there will be money for other pet projects of this government.
This is not co-operation. This is power. It is saying: "This is what I like, this is what I don't like. These are the people who are expendable." That is wrong.
These people across the way talk about being in tune with business. I come from Sudbury, which is perhaps the union capital of Canada if not the world, and the big businesses in my municipality learned a long time ago that the worst thing that you can do is turn everybody in the union off by decreeing that it shall be that way and
Government Orders
going out and spending the money the way you feel like it. All that does is create more problems.
How, when you are in business, can you expect people to work for you in a good and in a happy manner and be productive? Productive is the word of the 1990s. You have to be productive and you have to be competitive. How can you be happy and do these things when you are being ordered from above? How about co-operation? How about conciliation? Why not appoint a mediator? Why not? There is nothing wrong with that.
I know we are proposing that kind of a motion. There is nothing wrong with that. I know the government is afraid that it is going to cost it a little bit more. Just cut back a little bit on some other expenses on the other side, some of your friends over there, some of the contracts that you let out. That is the other sham about this whole thing: "We have cut back on civil servants, are we not good?" We forget we have got all these contractors on the side and they cost as much. You do not have control over how much that costs you. Every time you subcontract it is take it or leave it. You have no choice at that point.
Do not tell me that you run a tight ship just because you have got numbers to prove it. There is creative accounting and then there is magic of accounting and you can make things say beautiful things if you want to and it is all in the eye of the beholder if you can manoeuvre it.
I ask the minister one question: Why will he not consider a mediator? Why not? I think it is a very important point.
Before I sit down and let you answer that question I have another one, a big one on my side.
The other question is: How are you going to control costs of the subcontracts you let out everywhere? You just tell me for one second how you are going to control the costs? How about the cost of the advertising that you have?
I notice that all of a sudden there is money for a big advertising campaign because it is going to make you guys look good. Believe me, I can understand you need to look good. I believe it. You really are in need of looking good.

September 30,1991
Government Orders
That is not going to help you, because you are misjudging the people of Canada. They know what this is all about. There is a new reality and that is that people are aware. You cannot treat them like fools. They understand. They really understand.
The other thing about pay equity is that everybody bandies pay equity around but it is a real thing. It is not a make believe project. Why does it have to be part of negotiations? If you are worth something, you are worth it. You should not have to negotiate for it. What is this? I understand about being a woman and sometimes having a bit of a rough time. I can take that. I can take it from you because I can dish it out as well or better. That is okay.
There are many people out there who need to have that recognition. I ask: when and why is that a part of this package? It is like the inherited right to self-government by the native people. It is a right. Why does anybody have to negotiate it. It is there. Why do we need to have an understanding about it?
These are some of my questions, and I really am preoccupied with these things because I feel that you are trying to impose your will. You are being sanctimonious about fighting the deficit and the debt. What kind of grand gesture are you prepared to make to convince first me, and the rest of the people out there, that this is not just using lower echelons of the Public Service to achieve your ends while at the same time controlling the agenda, controlling what comes to you and your friends?

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, this all sounds very good but I wonder what the hon. member will say when I tell her that Liberal governments in Canada have done worse.
We have negotiated for 90 days, and this week we had 35 sessions. Clyde Wells did not negotiate 90 days. He legislated zero. New Brunswick legislated zero. Some governments have done it for two years. We tried to negotiate with our members.
Far from doing the power trip you describe, we could have done it easily, we sat down and negotiated. This is the difference between them and us. Today, we are being reproached for going on a power trip. That is easy. We just order it. We could have legislated zero at budget time.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You did.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
We did not. We said we would introduce legislation if the need was there to negotiate. There were many other aspects that could be offered in a deal. We sat with our unions and tried to make a deal. We worked at it this week again during 35 different meetings. We made new offers on Thursday that were not even considered.
Basically, if we are a Conservative and if we try to reach agreement on the basis of zero, three, we are terrible people. If a Liberal had dictated that through legislation, it is good I suppose. This is why I do not accept at all this nonsense about looking for power. It would have been easy to use power.
We tried negotiating within a very difficult framework, therefore she said that we cut back but we spent more money by giving out contracts. Why have we managed to turn around a $16 billion operating deficit? We could not even pay the salaries. We had to borrow money. We turned it into a $14 billion surplus. It is a $30 billion turnaround. This is what we have done, and we are very proud of this.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I listen to this and I think to myself, where does he live?
Did you not listen to your own leader's budget speech? I was sitting here. I heard 0, 3 and 3. We will bring in 0, 3 and 3. We will allow you to legislate. That is like holding the gun to the head and saying: "We will not let you talk to us. Say exactly what we want, or else, pow." What kind of negotiating is that?
You talk about the provinces and say: "They gave 0 per cent." They negotiated. They did not decree first and then say nothing to anybody.
They did not give everybody else a big raise and then turn around and say "no way". There is a difference. Wake up, wake up. How many more polls do we need to have in this country for this particular government to wake up? The people of Canada want you to listen and to co-operate and stop with this decree. That is no way to govern. That is not democracy. Just because you say so does not mean it is right.
I was at a number of functions this weekend in my riding and one of the things they said was "why can these people not sit down with you and talk reasonably?"
September 30, 1991
They don't know how.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I agreed: Why? It is a frustration out there. I know you mean well and I am going to give you credit for that; I know you want to do well, but you do not know how. You talk about past governments and past deficits and past all this stuff. I have to tell you that since you have been in power you have had some of the best growth years. As a matter of fact, before the election in 1988, how crass can you be? You loosened up your fiscal policy, you let the interest rates come down, you brought down the income tax rate, and you went on a free for all. You paid and you bought and you gave and you had a great time to try and get re-elected. You did not win the election on all those giveaways before the election. That did not win it for you. What won it for you was the free trade debate and the outside influences which came and actually bought and scared people into voting for free trade. You did not even have a majority there.
What I want to say is this: As soon as the election was over and this government came back in 1988, all of a sudden you had a tightening of fiscal policies and you had an increase in everything. Then we had to have a recession, we had to have a recession.
When are you going to start taking responsibilities for your own actions? I am not saying we have always been perfect, but what I am saying is you are not either. Let us sit down and work at this together because this is our country; this is not just your country, this is our country and we want to make the best of it. It is high time that you realize that this is a two-way affair. I do not want to blame you for all my troubles and you should not blame me for all of yours.
I think you should take your responsibilities and start admitting that there are times when even you have made mistakes. I am willing to admit that we have made mistakes, are you willing to admit that you have made mistakes? Obviously, this is a big mistake you are making now, because when you have legislated these people back to work what kind of productivity do you think they are going to give you? What kind of love of their job do you think they are going to give you? What kind of Public Service 2000 are you going to have? Do you think we are going to have this whole new public service in which we are going to be very good and we are going to give you authority? Authority to do what? To do nothing.
Government Orders
I am asking you, how do you expect Public Service 2000 to work when this is all over? Are we going to end up worse off than we have ever been because you had one of the best unions working for you? It did not demand high settlements. It has taken less than the average for the last number of years. What have you done? You have turned it from a very reasonable union to this very unhappy, terrible force that is taking over. What have you done with this confrontation? How are you going to solve these problems? Putting them back to work is not going to solve your problems.
What kind of programs do you have? After you have decided and decreed them back to work, what are you going to do then?

speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I understand that hon. members have been a little all over the place. My feeling is that we had agreed that we would proceed this way. This is extremely important for our bill.

September 30,1991
Government Orders
We were faced with a very difficult situation, much more difficult than that of Newfoundland, for example, where our debt is much higher, our deficit is higher. Therefore we had to take tough measures. But we were not as tough as Newfoundland, and I do not hold it against them.
It is very relevant that the premier of Newfoundland, the government of that province, passed an act in April 1991 that there would be no salary increases, no benefit improvements. We have accepted to increase the benefits for employees.
What he did, a horrible Liberal government is it not, was cancel previously negotiated increases due in 1991-92. We did not do that. We proceeded very openly at budget time and we said that we had a mandate to go and negotiate other things. They were on the table. We negotiated for 90 days and again last week for 35 different meetings. We tried to reach a negotiated settlement and I would not like the hon. member to hold this against us.
The alternative would have been perhaps to do like Nova Scotia: a two-year freeze on wage increases. In Quebec the unions have said: "Yes, it is a reasonable thing to do in these times and places," and they have agreed to a 0 freeze for six months and 3 per cent for 12 months.
Basically, this is in the ballpark of efforts that all Canadians have to make at this time to help our country get out of this recession quickly and get on with the recovery.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The 20 minute period is over. The hon. member for Portneuf is rising on a point of order.

Madam Chairman, since this morning I have been listening carefully at the two opposition parties and I must say, Madam Chairman, that I am far from being edified by these people who should stand for those who in fact have no means to defend themselves right now.
I never heard these opposition members defend the interests of the workers involved in this dispute. I heard no opposition member tell Mr. Bean that he was responsible for the loss of 4 per cent of his members' wages. Normally, the opposition members should have
stood for those people. But they have not done it, Madam Chairman.
The ten days of work that those workers lost, they lost it because their union reresentatives have badly informed them, because their union representative want to play politics.
Madam Chairman, perhaps it would be time for some union leaders in Canada, rather than hiding behind workers, to have the courage to do like me and the other members of Parliament and to run for election, try to get elected here to make sure that the laws are implemented as they should be for the greater welfare of all Canadians.
They probably forgot to do something else. They forgot to say something that probably the workers and unionized members of the Public Service do not know. The President, Mr. Bean, gave his union's unionized staff at 3 per cent increase this year, but to do so, he cut 20 jobs. Probably the union members would have accepted a freeze this year to save their jobs. But it was all right. It was fine because a union leader was subjecting his union's employees to it. That is called union solidarity. But it is not really that.
Madam Chairman, it is time to let the voiceless speak. This morning's Le Soleil says that 609,500 people in Quebec are on welfare. There will soon be a million in Ontario. Those people do not have an average salary of $33,500 a year. They are on welfare, Madam Chairman. The opposition did not talk about it. Of course not. They say, "Thke from these people and raise the salaries of those who are already well protected." Those people do not have job security.
The MUCTC will cut 500 jobs. Why? Because it seems that the union representatives do not want to accept certain adjustments to the agreement that would save 500 jobs. Sacrosanct "acquired rights" mean that those who came in before the 500 concerned are protected. They do not care about the others. I am not sure that union members care about their neighbours. However, it seems that the union leaders want to save face, not try to defend the basic interests of working people.
In my riding, Madam Chairman, it was announced that 50 jobs would be cut at Domtar at Donnacona, in addition to 53 others a few weeks ago and 35 a few months ago.
September 30, 1991

Since December 1, or perhaps I should say between January this year and next January, about 130 jobs will have been lost. That is at the paper plant. I am not counting the 135 jobs that were lost on August 2, again in Donnacona, when the Domtar insulation board plant closed its doors.
I am not talking about 500 IVI employees in Val-Belair, the only plant in that town. I am not talking about Bois Sylve in Saint-Raymond, a small municipality with a population of 6,000. Bois Sylvex: 225 workers. Saint-Raymond Paper: 250 jobs lost. They don't talk about these people. Of course not. You think they had job security? No, they didn't. Job security was part of the collective agreement they had with the company but the company no longer exists, and that was the end of their job security. We hear the same refrain in my own riding and across Canada. These people are not defended by the opposition. What the opposition is doing here is protecting their friends. What they are doing is making political capital out of all this. That is what our NDP and Liberal friends are doing today. They couldn't care less about the bottom of the pyramid.
Well, I can tell you that at Domtar in Donnacona and at IVI in Val-Belair and throughout the riding, those people would have accepted a three-year wage freeze to keep their jobs, three years, without making a fuss. Even that didn't help. When it was announced the plant was closing, they agreed to re-open the collective agreements. Everything was on the table. The plant was closing down. Why? Because these plants have to compete. That is a fact of life people have to live with every day in that area. I didn't hear anyone mention this in the House today. Of course not. They are defending people who are much better oganized.
The average Public Service salary is $33,500 per year. The average salary in Canada is $27,400. We are asking people who earn an average of $27,400 a year in this country to raise the incomes of those who have job security.
I read in today's newspaper what is offered to them. "A $500 lump sum payment to approximately 35,000 employees earning less than $27,000." But, workers in the private sector, earning that salary will not receive such an amount this year.
Government Orders
"Guaranteed Employment for employees laid-off as a result of contracting out or privatization." In the private sector, such things do not exist.
"A guarantee of a reasonable job offer to all other employees affected by workforce adjustments, as long as they are mobile and able to recycle." Such a guarantee does not exist in my riding.
"A commitment to assume all dental costs and to raise the ceiling for orthodontic services from $2,000 to $2,500." Such things are unknown to people in my riding, who work for $15,000, $16,000, and $18,000.
"An increase of the employer contribution to disability insurance premiums from 75 to 85 per cent." They do not know that either. When you do not have a job, it is not part of your contract.
"An increase of on-site day care facilities from 10 to 15."
"From April 1,1992, six-week annual vacation after 29 years of service." As far as I am concerned, some people back home are now on holidays for life.
"Shift bonuses increased from $1 to $1.10 an hour and weekend bonuses, from $0.75 to $1 an hour, as well as meal bonuses, from $6 to $7." In my riding, there are people who are working and who do not get meal bonuses. Really, there are limits.
Will the Official Opposition of this House, which is supposed to defend the people without a voice, say that these high officials have a higher status than anybody else in Canada? I am not the only one who says it; in an other editorial, today, they talk about the Spoiled Children of the System. What I find sad is that Mr. Bean's behaviour has caused some editorialists to denounce public servants and workers who do a damned good job.
I have been working with people at the grassroots for 7 years. Not with the union representatives, in Ottawa, who drive around in their little car, with their expense account and salaries that the people at the grassroots don't even get. I work with people who know what it means to be serving Canadians. These people know it, except that Mr. Bean says: "If you don't walk out, we will make you walk out."
That is true.

If you don't walk out, we will take care of you afterwards if we can't now. These are threats. Is that union democracy? Is that what the NDP and the Liberal

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
Party are defending? Is that what Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition defends, violence on the pickets lines?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: No, no. I already talked about that.
Really, there are damned limits.
Right.

Companies, Madam Chaiman, are presently facing a terrible problem. In the Gaspe Peninsula, Donohue just went bankrupt which means loss of 600 direct jobs and 1,000 more in related industries. It is these people who are going to pay for the wage increases. They too would have accepted a three year freeze.
You have to draw the line somewhere. I think that comes a time when Her Majesty's loyal Opposition must be able to clearly tell Mr Bean: "You are organizing your people and we are not going to be a party to it." That's it, you should denounce him but you don't. He has really cost his members 4 per cent, but you don't talk about it. Then, I am going to say it. There are people working for the Public Service who live in my county and who do not agree with Mr. Bean's behaviour, not one bit.
In mine too.

They have only been partly informed. People who work for the Public Service have told me: "It seems 62 per cent voted in favour of the strike, but I have never been consulted." How many are there in Canada who have not been consulted either? Their representative in Ottawa, God the Father, has decided for them, and he told them if they did not strike he would force them. This is not the way to do things, Madam Chairman. I cannot accept that in this House the majority of hon. members do not stand up for those who cannot speak here. It is unthinkable. They try to have the Canadian people believe that we want to score political points at the civil servants' expense. What do they think we are, fools? These people work with us every day. Am I going to turn the civil servants against me on purpose? Come on, it does not make sense.
It is obvious.
It is stupid.

Yes, it is stupid to believe that. It makes no sense, but that is what they are trying to put across on
the radio and TV. They have open-line shows to lead everyone to believe that everyone agrees, when we know very well that it was rigged; we know how it's done. There are specialists who know how across the way.
But there are limits! People must not be taken for fools or for imbeciles either. There are problems, due to a misunderstanding of some people who lead public servants, be they at the municipal, provincial or federal level or for school commissions; it is always the same story. They say that essential services have to be negotiated. Are any services provided by the federal, provincial or municipal governments not essential? Can anyone tell me that a government service at any level is not essential? All these services are essential. Were they not, private enterprise would provide them. It is as simple as that. They are all essential.
I think that they are quite well paid and you can compare it with anyone. But I rather get the feeling that what bothers you in the opposition most is that you are affected too; your salaries are frozen as well and you don't seem to like that. Your salaries are frozen and will go up 3 per cent next year if things are going well, as far as I am concerned. There are limits, and we are not close to being poor.
But, you seem more disturbed by the fact that you should receive the same treatment as the average man. We are paid by the taxpayers, who give us money, but we owe them some explanations. I will not ask my constituents, who can hardly make a living for their families, to raise my salary, oh no! And I think that people are aware of that.
Many companies, Madam Chairman, are now negotiating. Unions have asked bosses what they could do to save their companies, to save tomorrow's jobs. These negotiations are presently going on back home. But, you get here and, because this is government, there are no negotiations. The key to the success is to hold the people hostage. The dissatisfied bus driver stops driving his bus. Who is walking? The moron taxpayer. Not me, I have my own car. But there are many people who do not own a car and who need public transportation.
What happened last week in Toronto? The population was taken hostage. On what grounds? Could these citizens object in any way? No! What happens during a public hospital strike? Who are the first to suffer? Are
September 30, 1991

they the workers or the people who are taken hostage in the hospitals?
If you were to conduct a poll across the country, you would see that more and more people believe that those who choose to work in the Public Service should not have the right to strike. I hear that comment more and more. I think that we pay them pretty well. It is easy for you to ask us to pay them, but you still have not told us where we should take the money. Indeed, you would simply print some more.
You not only mortgaged your grandchildren's future but that of your great-grandchildren as well. If someone is paying the bill today, it is the workers, the 609,000 welfare recipients in Quebec, the million of them in Ontario. They are the ones who are paying the bill now for all the nonsense done over the last 20 years.
You pride yourselves on standing up for the poor in this House. But that is not true. You are not standing up for the poor, but for the best paid workers in Canada. I find your behaviour unacceptable. You should denounce Mr. Bean much more severely than you have done up to now, especially you, the members of the NDP, because he is betraying his own members, giving them incorrect information, improperly transmitting the message to the base and preventing workers from going back to work. These workers are willing to end the strike since they fully realize that you cannot ask the taxpayers for more money. Mr. Bean tells them that, if they do go back to work, he will deal with them physically.
Well, this is not true, Madam Speaker. It is time to put an end to this nonsense. I hope that by 10 o'clock tonight someone from Her Majesty's loyal Opposition will rise and properly defend these people.

I love it when I hear the complaints about Ian Deans being appointed to that job. I wonder who it was who appointed him.
I want to just reiterate that when the government throws mud in a fan it is going to get some of it back in its face.
I hope the President of the Treasury Board will be coming back. I have some things I wanted him to hear.
Government Orders
I am very concerned about the way this strike has progressed. The President of the Treasury Board and the government obviously have precipitated this strike and then chose to go back into negotiations, but not really meaningful negotiations. I think that has really exacerbated the problem.
When one looks at the federal government's advertisement about: "Here's what the Public Service Alliance of Canada walked away from", it is really galling to see what the government purports to be an offer to these people.
For one thing, the $500 lump sum payment to approximately 35,000 employees earning less than $27,000 a year. The government has said it guarantees employment for employees whose jobs are transferred to the private sector, as a result of contracting out or privatization. Those who chose to work for the contractor would receive six months salary to compensate for lower benefits in the private sector. This is not meaningful negotiation.
The next one is a guarantee of a reasonable job offer to all employees affected by work force adjustments. One would expect that if there were going to be work force adjustments, that there would be a reasonable offer of employment. But we do not have the government's definition of what "reasonable" is. When we look at the track record of this government, "reasonable" in its eyes is completely different from the definition of "reasonable" that most of us have become accustomed to. I do not think one can look at the government when it is bargaining and use the word "reasonable" with any kind of assurance. I am sure the striking Public Service did not.
The most incredible one was that the government mentioned payments totalling $81 million, now made under equal pay to be incorporated in employees base salaries, thereby increasing the dollar value of future raises and pensions.
Why would the government not do that in the first place? It would be the decent thing to do instead of using it as a bargaining chip at a time when the workers were expecting meaningful negotiations.
Considerable work went into this by all parties, hoping that there would be an equitable settlement to this strike. We thought the government was sincere when the offer to go back to the bargaining table was made. That

the government was sincere in doing something to bring about an end to this strike.
Then, we heard about the bonuses that were paid to senior members of the Public Service and to the heads of the Crown corporations. It is absolutely incredible that these people would receive that kind of an increase. I know it has been going on for some time. That kind of money was given to these people without justification. The government did not do anything about it, until it was actually confronted with it. It said it was just going to freeze the bonuses. Then, finally, it was embarrassed into doing away, with these bonuses.
Is Mr. Lander, the president of Canada Post, paid a bonus per post office closed?
Probably, with this government.

Is Mr. Lawless, the president of Canadian National Railways, paid per mile of railroad track that is taken out of service? Is he paid because he sold a CN route to a private company which went bankrupt in 15 months, with 2,000 people unemployed, without any kind of benefits? They would be wiped out completely and not even be able to make the payments on their trucks. They and their families would be absolutely destitute. There has been no response from this government. For the government to take three years to get an RCMP report, is that how they measure the benefit of the people they pay those bonuses to?
There is not one bonus to Mr. Lawless, but two bonuses to Mr. Lawless because he was also president of VIA Rail. The fact is they were not going to leave it at that.
The first offer was that the government was going to freeze the bonuses. Oh, yippee, yippee. That meant that it was going to actually increase the bonuses.
Mr. Lawless in all his magnificence was going to get more than he had got before. Why not? He is going to sell the rail line in eastern Nova Scotia. That has got to be worth at least $30,000 in the minds of the government. He is going to get rid of a railroad that has been in existence since the mid-19th century on whom people in eastern Nova Scotia depend.
It was going to sell it to somebody of substance, some worth-while company that had the revenues to be able to take it over. It is not as if we have not heard that before with Route Canada. There was supposed to be a marvellous company. It was supposed to carry on the trucking firm, but it did not.
It is one thing to cut off the services, to destroy the Canadian symbols, but it is another thing to insult completely the intelligence of Canadians from coast to coast.
The measure of this government is: "If you are a big shot, you get paid because we need you to keep the little person under control. We want to keep the small person under our thumbs". That is the thinking that Canadians from coast to coast attribute to this government.
The government wonders why there is a strike at the present time. It is because the mood is sour, because Canadians do not trust this government. They are fed up with this government and they do not believe anything this government says.
The only thing they will absolutely give any credit to is what this government does and it has done very little, if anything, to try to fix this very tragic situation.
Why is the government not including independent contractors in this? Last spring, when his own officials were asked, they said that the independent contractors were paid more than public servants, yet they did not know really if the independent contractors were saving any money for the government. They did not know if this was saving any money for the government, because they did not keep track. They did not keep track.
We do not know what this whole government thrust of giving money to the independent contractors is doing. We do not know if it is helping the country or not, because the government does not keep track. It does not want to keep records.
Has the President of the Treasury Board got a hold of his department? Does he know whether the step of giving work to independent contractors is saving money?
I want to know if he can give us some examples of that so that we can have information we were not able to get last spring.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has covered a lot of ground. I will try briefly to go over each of his points.
He said that he had the feeling that we entered this round of negotiation without really being serious and that we had not gone through meaningful negotiation. I would like to disagree very strongly with him. He knows full well that at a time when hundreds of thousands of
September 30, 1991

Canadians are thrown out of a job, job security is something very precious.
When I sat with Daryl Bean to get the negotiations going again, I spoke to him very bluntly about the wage budget. We explored together the areas where we could make some progress. Certainly this was a central issue. That is why it is there. It is for the union. At a time when everybody in Canada is worried about his or her future we felt that we could move on that and do our best to try to give some job security to our employees.
I would say that on that point we have a good record. I did not feel we needed to go very far. We are Canada's largest employer. We have nearly 225,000 employees working under Treasury Board rules. Out of those, at a time of deep recession as we are reminded every day by the opposition, 106 employees had to leave against their will, and in most instances it was because, for reasons I respect, they could not move. We were prepared to retrain them. We are prepared to spend two years with our employees to retrain them and help them find other jobs.
Even though we have tried to remove or limit the weight of government from 1986 until now, in a work force of 225,000 people we have lost only 1,500 persons who had to leave against their will. This is a very good record, and I do not know of anyone who has a better record. It is a better record than Daryl Bean's record in his own staff.
Listen to Daryl Bean a few months ago when he said: "Oh, these are tough times; I cannot go beyond this. I have to close positions". We are all going through rough times and trying to deal with them as best we can. We thought that job security, being something well identified, we could move on that.
You said: "We thought the government was sincere". We were sincere, and the lump sum payment is not something indifferent. It is something that was reasonable in our view for the lower income people who of course have to suffer more because of the zero year. We were quite happy to put that on the table.
Government Orders
We did not do like some other Liberal governments in Canada that have removed all benefits this year. We tried to improve them: dental care, medical and, as you have stated, a long list of benefits.
The hon. member says that we are trying to destroy the Canadian symbols. I would like to remind him that when we came to power in 1984, for every dollar that Canadians were paying in taxes to Ottawa the federal Liberal government was spending $1.33. Of course you can make a lot of people happy. Of course you can throw money around that you do not have. But sooner or later it catches up with you in a huge debt, and this is what we have been trying to tackle.
We would like to give more to people, but do we need to borrow it, increase taxes? We have asked our employees to do their share. Somebody said on the NDP side: "What is significant, $200 million?" Of course, they have a printing machine out there. We do not have it.
It is important. It is tough on the employees, but it is their one share. We have taken many other measures at budget time. We have dealt not only with unionized employees, but we have announced that we would cut 10 per cent of our managers. This is a very difficult decision.
We are trying to live within our means, and we feel that Canadians have too much government that they have to pay for. This money comes from thousands and thousands of Canadians who are without jobs. We wanted to set an example. It has been followed by many provinces. It has given the right direction and we can see now that the economy is picking up again. Because interest rates are down, this is helpful to the economy and we can hopefully create better conditions where we can protect the future of our employees. To do otherwise would not be useful.
As for the independent contractors, we have said that we will continue to look for the best possible ways of providing services at the lowest possible cost. This is reasonable. When you are as broke as we are, with a $400 billion debt and a $30 billion deficit, you have to find ways to try to cut your spending. Otherwise it is only down.
We looked at that as one of many options of reorganizing, going to special operating agencies, as we have done with great success and using various means of trying, if we have a limited responsibility which is limited in time, to deal with it without committing ourselves to a forever

September 30, 1991
Government Orders
salary, a forever benefits and so on and so forth. Each department has been asked to look at that, but in the process we said we would protect our employees and the numbers I have given you indicate that we have done so.
We have abolished many positions, thousands of them, cutting money, but we have done it through attrition and we have not done it by firing people. We have been very careful to manage well and I am very proud of our record in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, you would swear that the government was the saviour of the Canadian economy. I have never heard anything so completely nutty in my whole life.
The debt has more than doubled since this government came to power and it had good economic times. Not only has the debt more than double, but in 1984, when the debt was approximately $180 billion, only 17 per cent was being financed outside Canada. Now it is over $400 billion and 38 per cent is being financed outside the country. We do not even have control over our own economy.
This government has to sell Treasury bonds to keep the country going from week to week or we are out of business. He has to give a high interest rate and that is the reason the Canadian dollar is high. If we did not have the high interest rate you would not sell the bonds and the country would be out of business. It has put us on the rocks economically. It is blaming poor public servants and the inflation rate. I have never heard anything so full of hogwash in my life.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member takes the time to look at the numbers, he will understand that the deficit has not doubled. It is much below what it was with a much larger economy. We had to borrow $16 billion to make the payroll. You had a $38 billion deficit plus a $200 billion debt. We started trimming down, being opposed every step of the way by people across this room. Now we have, this year, a $14 billion surplus and we intend to continue trimming governments for the great protection of our own employees.

As you know, Mr. Chairman, I am at this point but the first of the three amigos to come in the next 20 minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the member for Portneuf, if I can remember correctly where he was sitting and if he is still in the House, strenuously defended all these people he was enumerating who were laid off in his constituency and those who are unemployed. The opposition, and in particular the NDP, certainly did defend those people.
Do you forget the debate on free trade? Why on earth do you think those people are unemployed? Why do you think they have been laid off from their jobs? Why do you think those people have been laid off? They have been laid off because of the free trade agreement and the companies they have worked for have moved south of the border. That is why they are unemployed. That is why they are losing their jobs.
In any event, this debate is not about fighting the deficit. I submit to you that the deficit is a very fortunate turn of events for this government. It gives it the opportunity to be able to do something. The question was asked and I made the answer. I think I received the answer to that about nine months subsequent to asking the question.
This is not about a large deficit and it is not about wage restraint either. This debate is about wage suppression. What a marvellous opportunity to bring in legislation, and there is no question whatsoever that this government has not bargained in good faith with these people from the moment the budget was brought in, a budget that brought in by law a constraint on the government's employees which guaranteed with the majority the government had that there was no way fair bargaining could possibly take place. Fair bargaining was pre-empted the moment that the finance minister read the budget, and there is just no question about that.
Turning to the deficit itself, I do not know who requested the survey or the study that Statistics Canada did. It is one of the most reputable adjuncts to the

September 30,1991
Government Orders
government. I do not know. I wonder if employees of Statistics Canada are going to be subject to this legislation as well. Probably they are, unfortunate bunch of people. Anyway, Statistics Canada and the exemplary employees who work for it found that 44 per cent of the debt of this nation was caused by successive Liberal and Conservative, particularly, governments having given away tax breaks to corporations.
Fifty per cent of that debt is directly attributable to high interest rates. That leaves 6 per cent and Statistics Canada did find-and I will readily admit that is what it said-that 6 per cent of that debt is directly attributable to Canadians living beyond their means, which is very roughly and quickly translated as the social programs, the unemployment insurance, medicare, and so on.
If we listen to the finance minister, if we listen to the President of the Treasury Board, if we listen to the Prime Minister, we find that they are blaming the whole 100 per cent on Canadians living beyond their means or, if you will, the social programs of medicare, unemployment insurance, and so on. No more deceitful lie has been perpetrated on the Canadian people in all of Canadian history or for more devious reasons. The only reason that this action is being taken is in order to suppress wages.
I am going to conclude very quickly so that the member for Beaches-Woodbine will be able to get his points in. There are a couple of other interesting sets of figures. Since this government was elected in 1984 inflation has gone up by 29 per cent and corporate taxes have gone up by 17.7 per cent. I am not even going to give you time, Mr. Speaker, to guess how much it is; I am going to tell you. For the individual, taxes have gone up by 103 per cent and they wondering why people are angry. Are they wondering why they are at 15 per cent in the polls?
I would like to point out that in the sixties the disposable income of Canadians went up by about 34 per cent. In the seventies the disposable income of people went up by 22 per cent, and in the eighties, dominated by this free enterprise, free wheeling capitalist government which was going to bring in free trade, this panacea of prosperity, the disposable income of Canadians has risen by .5 per cent. And they are wondering why Canadians are angry. They are wondering why Public Service
employees are so angry. There has to be some way for these people to be able to capture some of the wealth that this country is supposed to have offered.
If you started working in 1980, Mr. Chairman, your disposable income has risen by .5 per cent, andi they wonder why Canadians are angry.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great care to the discussion that took place in the House today, and particularly the comments by the hon. member for Portneuf.
When that hon. member spoke about the unacceptably high welfare rolls in Montreal and in the Quebec province, I can also point out to him that there is an equally unacceptable level in Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, Newfoundland, and the Atlantic provinces, and there is good reason for that.
There is not an economist in this country who would not agree that the recession that Canada is still in is a made-in-Canada recession by this government. Perhaps the Fraser Institute would not agree but every other reasonable economist in this country would agree with that.
I want to say something that is absolutely offensive to me, and I think to most members of this House. Since 1984 this government has never made one initiative without finding a scapegoat for it. Every initiative this government comes forward with is accompanied by a scapegoat. In 1985 it wanted to reduce the deficit. It blamed pensioners and it attacked pensioners and tried to deindex their pensions. Later on, when it wanted to blame the unemployed, it attacked the Unemployment Insurance Program. Again, when it wanted to reduce the deficit, it went after family allowances. Then, again, as recently as last Monday when the Prime Minister announced his constitutional initiatives, who did he blame? He went after housing.
If you combine all these things together, no wonder there is an unacceptable level of people on welfare and unemployment in this country. Today we find the government blaming public servants for the deficit.
I listened to that hon. member who said that he was trying to talk to principles here, and did nothing but try to set the Public Service unions against the unemployed, the Public Service unions against people on welfare. The
September 30, 1991

real question here is this government's role in negotiations with Public Service workers; it is as simple as that.
I have listened to the President of the Treasury Board try to justify the government's actions in these negotiations. There is not one major media outlet in this country that I have seen in the last three or four weeks that has not clearly seen through what this government is trying to do. Look at the editorials if you do not believe the people on the opposition benches and what we have been saying for the last couple of days. The Globe and Mail: "Ottawa should respect the right to negotiate", a whole editorial attacking this government's credibility with its own public servants. In The Globe and Mail again: "Tories do the almost impossible to spark sympathy for public servants". That was written by Jeffrey Simpson.
The Vancouver Sun, hardly a bastion of the left, put this in: "Don't freeze out public servants", and then it goes on to attack this government's credibility in negotiating under law with its own public servants. "Provoking a strike" says the Edmonton Journal, there is another real lefty. The Citizen-. "Back to work legislation, there must be a better way."
I heard the President of the Treasury Board today say that the government would not agree to the appointment of a mediator because it will not accept some third party that had nothing to do with the negotiations so far intervening in these negotiations, helping these negotiations, because the third party may very well dictate what a settlement should be. I find that to be the height of ignorance and one that is not acceptable to any right thinking Canadian who believes in the free bargaining process.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words before the debate ends. I wanted to review very briefly the government's mishandling of this case, because if there was ever a situation that cried out for incompetence, this is it. I will have to be brief because of the time. It is a shame I cannot go on at length because it is a disgraceful record and the President of the Treasury Board should be ashamed of the government's record in this regard.
Government Orders
I want to go back to the budget of February 26, 1991 when the Minister of Finance who has since been replaced-he is now the Minister for International Trade-made the following statement concerning the situation of the Public Service in this country.
The government will continue to bargain with its employees but, as
any employer would do, it will at all times be cognizant of its bottom
line as dictated by the seriousness of the federal fiscal situation.
It was a federal fiscal situation, I might add, that was seriously exacerbated by seven years of Tory mismanagement.
It then said: "The deteriorating deficit situation dictates that for the next fiscal year available resources simply will not allow the government to increase operating budgets to compensate for wage and salary increases. This means that any wage increases resulting from the collective bargaining process will have to be funded through a corresponding reduction in Public Service employment.
With a Public Service work force of approximately 215,000, each increase of one per cent in pay could lead to a loss of approximately 2,000 jobs." That is what the minister said in this House in his budget speech. He did not actually say these words, but it was printed in the material that he distributed in the House at the time.
He went on: "To contain the loss of Public Service employment, and to ensure continuation of the provision of vital public services to Canadians, the government is not prepared to contemplate wage settlements exceeding three per cent a year over the next three years. Negotiated settlements of three per cent are consistent with this environment of severe restraint and are in line with the government's inflation targets. The alternative to a firm wage bargaining stance would be a much deeper reduction in public sector employment including layoffs."
In other words, 3 per cent was the figure that was given out and it was understood at the time that if there were negotiated settlements of less than 3 per cent there would be lay-offs to take their place.
Well the government apparently abandoned this scheme and it abandoned it, of all places, at the negotiating table. Imagine, you announce it publicly in the House what your bargaining stance is and then you go into the

September 30,1991
Government Orders
negotiations and you turn around and say: "Sorry, we were wrong, it is now zero per cent."
Do you know why? It is because the President of the Treasury Board suddenly realized that he could not afford to part with 6,000 public servants.
The government pruned the number of public servants by 15,000 over six years and it boasts about it. Then all of a sudden he is confronted with a situation where he could lose 6,000 more if he ended up with a 3 per cent increase according to the Minister of Finance. So he abandoned that policy at the table and said: "You are getting zero."
Who did he say it to? He said it to all the lowest paid workers. Just before the budget came down on February 26 it gave a big increase to all the higher paid workers who were not negotiating with them in a union. That is what it did.
Now the government suddenly realizes its error and said: "Oh boy, we are going to apply this freeze." In June, the minister had the gall to stand in this House and say he was extending the freeze of zero per cent to everybody because he had realized the blunder he had made in giving the increase in January and February to these people.
Then, having recanted that far, the minister says zero per cent now applies to everybody, except the bonuses. He did not say that, of course, but we drew it to his attention and the unions drew it to his attention. He said: "Oh well, the bonuses are included too, it is all zero now."
That is what he wanted all along, but he did not have the nerve to admit it in the House, in the budget, in February. His predecessor did not. He was the one dictating the terms at the time. He did not have the guts to admit it in the House in June.
It was only when the unions pressed him to come out with a fair policy for everybody that he then said zero is the rule. But what he had done is give a substantial percentage increase to the highest paid ones in a year when the inflation rate was 6 per cent. He then says to the lowest paid: "You get zero this year. You may get three next year, but for the year when inflation is 6, you get zip." The others all get 4.2 or whatever it was that was given.
It was a shocking abuse of power by this government and a total mismanagement of the Canadian government that has cost us and cost us dearly in terms of jobs and that is why we are facing this legislation here today.
I have here some quotations from some experts in the labour field, a quotation from the Kingston Whig-Standard. These people are experts and professors at Queen's University. I will read the story:
Ottawa has badly bungled its handling of the public service labour dispute, two labour relations scholars say.
Dictating a wage freeze and forcing civil servants back to work is an ugly move that could have been avoided, say professors Pradeep Kumar and Donald Carter of Queen's University.
The scholars, who teach industrial relations, say the federal government's mistakes as an employer over the past few months could very well:
Demoralize civil servants.
Scuttle efforts to make the public service more efficient, flexible,
and responsible.
Promote a more militant public service union with more militant
and politicized members.
While they see some things differently, the two scholars agree that Ottawa has erred by imposing wage restraints under the guise of collective bargaining, a cherished labour principle under which unions and management jointly define employment conditions.
These are experts in their field. They say the minister has bungled this and bungled it badly. I say I agree with them and so does every member on this side of the House, and so does the Canadian public. This government is incompetent and should resign and get out. It is no good. I have got more.
Then, we have the Minister of Supply and Services who represents an Ottawa riding. He says: "Public Servants have nothing to complain about." He represents an Ottawa riding, and he has lots of public servants. Listen to what this man says. This is an unbelievable set of statements.
"They did not get laid off. They simply did not have their wages rolled back," says Dick, supply and services minister and Ottawa area's lone representative in the cabinet. I may say he is the only Tory in the whole Ottawa area, the people of eastern Ontario knew better than to elect this bunch.
He went on: "They did not have their plant shut down. They do not have to work-share. The Tory MP for Lanark-Carleton makes no apologies for the government's freeze on the salary of its employees in spite of the fact that the freeze only applies to the lowest paid".
September 30, 1991

This government is a disgrace. This government has botched this affair so badly that it amounts to nothing but a national disgrace. I say to the President of the Treasury Board through you, Madam Chairman, that he should get up and withdraw this bill at once. He has no business forcing this kind of legislation on the public without a mediator, without following the usual practices of labour negotiations. He knows that is his responsibility.
I would love to be able to quote more, but I know that my time is running out.
More, more.
